WHEN a man owes a good round sum he some- times finds it difficult to square up. A MAN, in looking around a shoe factory, ex- claimed: "Well I I declare This machinery beats awl ! " WHY are women extravagant in clothes 7—Be- cause when they buy a new dress they wear it out on the first day. WIFE : "Women are often criticised for wearing loud colours. What would you call a loud colour 2" Husband: "Yeller, I suppose." THE BRUTE I—A "great brute of a husband" advertised in the morning papers for a strong, able- bodied man, to hold his wife's tongue. "SARAH, why don't you wear earrings ?" "Be- cause I haven't had my ears pierced." "I will bore them for you." "Thank you; you have done that enough." "I DON'T think, indeed, that you are very smart," said a wife to her husband, to which he responded: "No, indeed, wife; but everybody knows that I am awfmly shrewd." GASKET: "Yes sir; I'm a self-made man:. Smothered voice; "Then you cheated yourself." " OH 1 you have the paper; please look and see if any one we know—has been horn." MR. CURTIS : "I tell you what 'tis, you could have a far worse husband than I 4am." Eunice (his wife: "I don't want one." "I LIVE mostly within myself," said a conceited fellow. "I understand," replied his neighbour at the table, "you occupy a fiat." A SCOTCH GIRL at an examination gave a pretty definition when asked: "What does patience mean 2' "Wait a wee, an' dinna weary." SMART ATTORNEY : "You say the evening wore on. What did it wear on that particular occasion?' Witness: The close of day, I presume." "I WANT to write a letter to the secretary of the navy. Shall I address him as Your Excellency 7" " "Oh, no; use the term, 'Your Warship." A TRUE LOVERS' QUARREL.—He : "Come now, let's kiss and make up." " She : "No sir; I won't." He: "Well, let's kiss, anyhow." (They make up). "How is it you have so few deaths on your hands, doctor?" "That's easy enough. When I find I have a bad case I order the patient to take a trip abroad." BJONES : "That young fellow seems rather pessimistic." Merritt: "Yes. He's an amateur Photographer, and always takes a poor view of life." A LITTLE girl in Piedmont, W. Va., who was given a drink of fizzing mineral water the other day, took a sup of it and then exclaimed, "It tastes like your foot's asleep!" CONCEITED YOUTH: "I, also, am very musieal. I sang 'Woodman, Spare that Tree,' last night, and there wasn't a dry eye in the room." Cruel Young Lady, "Were you alone ?" "I CHARGED a battery myself once," exclaimed an ex-sutler. "You did," replied an Oa artillery. man, who knew him; "you charged our battery fifty cents a drink for mean yVhisky." AN instance of throwing one's self about was wit- nessed a few evenings ago at a party, in the case of a young lady, who, when asked to sing, first tossed her head, and then pitched her voice. JACK: "Tom, were you at Charley's wedding 9" Tom: " Yes ; but the father of the bride did a mean thing." Jack: "How was that 2" Tom: "Why, he gave her away before the whole company." GILLY : "Sad affair over at Jones's." Smith: "What's the matter ?" Gilly : "One of the twins has died, and the worst of it is, the people don't know whieh of them is dead, they look so much alike." JOE: "I was insulted this morning by my grand- father." Jack: "Why he died a week ago.' Joe: "Precisely. His will was read to-day, and all he left me was his withering curse." HuRBY : "What kind of stuff do you call this r Wife: "Why, my dear, that is angel cake." Hubby: " Umph I I suppose it must be. I knew it was never meant for a mortal." POSEYBOY (sneeringly): "So you have gone and got engaged to that old Dollargrab ? I suppose he is worth a million 7" Miss de Smith (contemptu- ously): "Yes, of such as you are." LORD CHATHAM said of John Wilkes that be was a cosmopolitan who was aisle and willing to make himself at home in any country where claret was and sheriff's officers were not. HENRY: "So you asked old Growler for his daughter last night, did you, Fred? And how did you come out " Fred "It was a window, I believe, Harry. That was the best I could do, though." A GENTLEMAN asked a friend if he could tell him how to cook a canvas back duck, and he re- plied: "I haven't got as far as that yet. How to buy one, at present prices, is the problem which troubles me." MERCHANT (on collecting tour): "Mr. Brown, can you tell me why my errand here this morz,iug is like a well-baked loaf of bread 7" Brown: "No, I cannot. Why is it ?" Merchant: "Because it's dun Brown." Brown paid the bill. "MARY," said her mother severely, "If I am not mistaken I saw your head on George's shoulder. What sort of an attitude is that for a young lady?" Mary (ecstatically): "Beatitude 2" "How did your husband meet his death 7" "He Yell through a trap." "In the dark, I suppose." "No, it was broad daylight, hut there was a black cap over his face and he couldn't see, poor man." ! LADY (to gentleman who had been thrown from his horse): "I am so sorry for yon." Gcr.-ntleman : "It isn't so bad, madame, as it seems. I assure you I am much more comfortable now than I was in the saddle," " MAMMA," said a four-year-old reflectively, " did Vrod make me ?" "Yes, Harvey," answered mamma, soberly ; "God made you for mamma's little boy." "Humph 1" said Harvey, after a little, "God did a pretty good job that time, didn't he 7" EDITOR.—" That little item of yours yesterday reminded me strongly of some of Shakespeare's works." Funny man (blushing)—" Ali, thank you. It is kind of you to say so. In what respect may I enquire?" Editor (coldly)—" In age, princi- pally.' "You are poor, are you not, young man?" "Yes, air." "And if you marry my daughter you will take her from a home of luxury and splendour to a humble sphere of life, where she may be very un- happy." "I have thought of that, sir," responded the young man, with deep emotion, "and it occurred to me that if Clara should be unhappy we could live with you until I should be able to carve out fame and fortune worthy of the beautiful girl whom I adore." A LADY having asked Dr. Johnson what was the way to secure comfort in a storm, the old moralist replied: "Madam, comfort in a storm is best insured by taking shelter in some friend's house about the time he is going to dinner, ruakin; him bring out his best port, and cracking walnuts by the fireside afterwards, Madam." Miss SKEE7.4 : "Where did Tna graduate from, Mr. Gill 7" Mr. Gill: "From the School of Phar- macy." Miss Skeen (with surprise): Is it possible? What a strange choice for a young man brought up in the city I But, if I remember rightly, your grand- father was a farmer, too." SCENE.—The gaming table at Monte Carlo. Young English lady with her little sister and a gentleman whose acquaintance they bad recently made while travelling. Young Lady: "Now, I shall just try one 5-franc piece on the number of my age," putting one on number eighteen. Number 27 wins. Little sister: "Oh, Mand, what fun. Now, if you had put it on your right age you would have won, wouldn't you ?" YOUNG WIFE: "You are not going out to-night, are you?" Husband "Yes, inv dear ; I must go back to the office and post my 'books. I'm afraid I'll be kept late." Y. VT.: " 2,Tot going anywhere except to the office 7" H.: "No o." Y. W. : "Well, then, step into Strong Smell and Co.'s around the corner from your effice, on -your way down. They'll be open until eight o'clock. Get a couple of mackerel and bring them home with you when you come." H.: "Ye-es, my dear. Good night." Y. W. (to herself, as her husband departs) : "He won't do much theatre-going with those mackerel in his pocket. NOT. SUSCT.RTIDLE OF DEMONSTE aTeeea—Perri- wink : Aw, Mr. Hardhead, is it true that cigawettes affect the bwain 7" Mr. Hardhead : "No. Those who have brains do not smoke cigarettes."

Air. Broadhurst is slowly recovering from his at- tack of rheumatism. Ile is now able to take a little out-door exercise along the Cromer cliffs.

The Prince of Wales has postposed his annual visit to the Riviera until Easter, and according to his present arrangements, he will start on Satur- day, March 21st, for the Monte Carlo, where Baron llirsch and Sir Frederick Johnstone are anxiously awaiting his arrival.

Lord Brabourne has given notice that he will move the rejection of the Tithe Bill in the House of Lords. Lord Brabourne is a landlord first, and a Unionist afterwards, and no one more deeply resents any legislation which appears to affect injuriously the position of the landlords.

The Prince of Wales entertained a party of twenty-four at the Marlborough club on Sunday night. Amongst the guests were the Duke of Fife, Prince Leiningen, Dr. Russell (of the "Times "), some dramatic celebrities, including Mr. Henry Irving, Mr. Charles Wyndham, Mi. Wilson Barrett, Mr. Arthur Cecil, and Mr. Augustus Harris.

Ether-drinking in the North of Ireland has been the subject of representations to the Government by the Society for the Study of Inebriety. The society have received replies stating that the Irish Government have given instructions to schedule ether as a po.son, so that it may not be sold except by chemists licensed to retail poisons under proper legal restrictions.

An extraordinary purchase was made at Christie's a few months ago. An "old waster" begrimed with dirt was knocked down for £7. It was promptly resold for £BO, and again for .E7OO, and it has now been acquired for £2,000 by a Continental gallery, and turns out to be a magnificent Terburg. This artist, it may be remembered, spent some time in England and left behind him some of his finest productions.

Two Ministerial pensions, of £2,000 a year and £1,200 a year respectively, have fallen vacant since Lord Salisbury came into office,the one having been surrendered by Lord John Manners when he be- came Duke of Rutland, and the other by Mr. Shaw- Lefevre. The £2,000 a year pension has just been assigned to Lord Cross, and the other to Sir Michael hicks-Beach. These pensions are not drawn by the holders when they are in office.

Grasse, the town which has been selected by the Queen for her sojourn abroad in the spring is about ten miles inland north of Cannes. The Grand Hotel, which is being fitted for her accommodation, faces full south,and is completely sheltered by the moun- tains which rise behind it. The town itself is a heap of crooked buildings piled up on the bill side, and though the neighbourhood provides some most pleasant walks and drives, it is :not particularly picturesque.

Not long ago a fashionable calf was holding a bank at baccarat, when there was a stake of £1,500, about which there was a dispute, and which the players held ought not to be paid. The calf, however, being fully convinced that it would not. do for him to fall out with his fashionable friends, said that the matter only concerned him as bank- er, and paid the money. lie was a wise calf, and he knew the conditions under which he was re- ceived in the ' hupper suckles."

It is a comfort to see a sort of semi-official an- nouncement in Tuesday morning's papers that the Lord Chancellor has had brought under his notice the judicial scandal with which rumour has been busy in legal circles for weeks past, and that "it is expected that Lord Ilalsbury will forthwith take action in the matter." It is now an open secret that the scandal in question relates to the mental con- dition of one of the judges, ana a state of things more fraught with danger to the public can hardly be conceived.

The division on Mr. John Morley's Resolution 1 taken in the house of Commons on Tuesday morn- ing went on strictly party lines. Both sections of the Irish Nationalist party voted against the Government, who were supported by Lord Harting - ton, Mr. Chamberlain, Sir Henry James, and a diligently whipped-up muster of the Dissentient Liberals. Mr. Cunninghame Graham, who had given unexpected pleasure to the Conservatives by a personal attack on Mr. John Morley, rounded off his eccentric interposition in the business of the even- ing by voting for Mr. Morley's motion.

The Government majority, 75, was one of the smallest yet known on an important division affect- ' ing Irish policy.. In 1887, on Mr. John Morley's amendment against giving precedence to the Coercion Bill, the Government majority was 89. On the first reading of the Bill the closure was carried by 108, and the second reading was passed by a ' majority of 101. In 1888 an amendment moved by Mr. John Morley condemning the administration of the Crimes Act was rejected by a majority of 92,and in 1889 an amendment, also proposed by Mr. Morley, condemning the system of administration in Ireland was defeated by a majority of 79.

The Government do not intend to set aside a day for consideration of Mr. Russell's amendment to Mr. Morley's resolution on the Administration of the Law in Ireland. The consequence will he that matters will be left as they remained after the divi- sion on Mr. Morley's resolution, and before Mr. Healy moved the adjournment of the debate. This will have a curious result upon a page of the jour- nal's of the House. Nothing is left of Mr. Morley's resolution but the preamble :—"That in the opinion of this House the action of the Irish Executive in connection with the recent prosecutions at Tipper- ary and other proceedings—" Since Mr. Russell's amendment will never be added in place of the declaration omitted, this sentence will never be completed

Canon Mandell Creighton, Ow tww Bishop of Peterborough, after taking high classical honours at Oxford, devoted himself to historical studies.' His best know' work is the "History of the Papacy during the Period of the Reformation," which, by its impartiality and learning, brought him a highly appreciative notice from Cardinal Manning, and later Ow first Dixie Professorship of Ecclesiastical History in the University of Cambridge. Ile started I the "English Historical Review," which he has edited during the five years of its existencP. Dr. ME.tgee's successor is only forty-eight, and besides being an active Churchman has displayed the tact and commonsense which should render his pastorate a success.

There has been an outcry lately against publicans insuring their customers, lives of the customers, and the sys- tem is vicious enough. To all appearance the pub- licans would be much better employed in looking after their own lives. A gentleman who has been sounding the life assurance companies on this point finds that eight offices—including the Hand-in- Hand and the Scottish Widows'—refuse to insure publicans on any terms. The large majority of offices charge them 1 per cent. above the ordinary rates; several more charge ss. and 10s. per cent.

The labour struggle at Cardiff will certainly re- veal one figure of the greatest strength and import- ance in the person of Sir W. T. Lewis, the manager of the vast organisation of industry known as the Bute Docks. Sir William is barely fifty, but he is already one of the great labour captains of England and in Wales he is certainly the foremost industrial figure. His origin was extremely humble, for he began life in a mine as a common" door boy" at the ventilating shaft. Since then he has worked himself up to a position of confidential adviser to the Marquis of Bute, now in failing health, and un- disputed manager of his vast possessions at Cardiff. His private fortune is also a very large one, being estimated at between £300,000 and £400,000, and few commercial undertakings in Wales are com- plete without his co-operation or advice.

The movement against gambling in high places is making much headway, and it seems likely that good will come, after all, out of the baccarat scandal. I am credibly informed that before answering the questions that were addressed to him in the Rouse of Commons on Monday Mr. Stanhope had an interview with the Prince of Wales, and that at this interview an understanding was arrived at that in future more strenuous efforts should be put forth to discourage gambling amongst officers of the Army. Mr. Stanhope in his reply spoke as if the regulations of the Army only referred to what takes place in barracks or in camp. This is not the case. There are two regulations on the subject. The first says that "all gambling in garrisons, camps, or cantonments is forbidden," but the second is more general in its terms, and provides that "the cow.- manding officer is to discourage any disposition in his officers to gamble."

div.head: "BIGOTRY REBUKED" AT RUNCORN.
div.p: "BIGOTRY REBUKED" AT RUNCORN.

A REPLY TO CANON WOOD. The Rev. 11. Davenport, of Frodsham, on Sunday occupied the pulpit at the Greenway-road Primitive Methodist Chapel ; and in the evening the title of his discourse was "Bigotry Rebuked." - He took his text from St. Luke ix. 49-50, "And John answered and said,Master, we saw one casting out devils in thy name, and we forbade him, because he followeth not with us. And Jesus saith unto him, Forbid him not, for he that is not against us is for us." Mr. Davenport said this little incident in the life of Christ reveale4 the breadth of his soul and the range of his sympathy. It testified Christ's attitude to- wards bigotry. What was bigotry? It was the devil of narrow-mindedness ; it was obstinacy, prejudice, the essence of stupidity. The correlative term of bigotry was self conceit. The bigot's depreciation of others might always be fairly measured by his complacency in himself. But the bigot said "There is only one way of worshipping and serving God and that is ours. If you are not worshipping God and serving Him upon our lines and by our methods then you are not acceptable to Him." Precisely because it was self-conceited and con- fident bigotry was ever intolerant and despotic. It loved to exercise authority, to be dictatorial ; and dogmatical bigotry would have no dissent; its dictum was " Conform to my standard or I will crush you." What right had any man outside the clerical order to have any conscience? The claim to private and inde- pendent judgment was little short of blasphemous pre- sumption that must be crushed out as soon as possible. The authority of the supposed Apostolic succession must not be questioned. Down with Dissent: that was the cry, and that the principle of the bigot. The policy of bigotry had been too long a policy of prohibition and repression. Centuries ago, imprisonment, confiscation, and martyrdom were the favourite methods of repres- sing and silencing men. Why were these methods not used still? For the simple reason that they could not be. Forcible repression was nnt now a practical policy. But bigotry and intolerance were not dead ; they had simply altered their tactics; and if they could not now forcibly repress they could censure and dis- countenance ; if they could not coerce, they could by- cott, and that was the latest development of religious bigotry, in the person of a supposed minister of Him who came to seek and to save that which was lost. They were advised to have nothing to do with Metho- dists. These Methodists are sinful schismatics : they were to have nothing to do with them, but stand aloof from them. This showed what bigotry would do if it could ; it went to the extent of its power. In the text they had disclosed the root idea of endless conflict and bitterness, it waa not the idea that there could be only one true church ; that was true enough ; but that the one true church could only have one manifestation, one constitution, one polity, one order of service, one method of operation, was not true. When the clergy of the Established Church said that Wesleyans and other Methodists were not parts of the Church of Christ, be- cause they did not subscribe to the 39 Articles and use a liturgy,and hold the doctrine of apostolic succession,they made themselves appear ridiculous. The Methodist might with as good reason say that the Establishment was not a true section of the Church of Christ ; but they were not so foolish. They admitted it to be a real branch of the one Catholic Church, though like other branches it was not free from error. So far from these things constituting her the true church she would be more like the apostolic church if she were rid of her state fetters, unchristlike ritual, and sacer- dotal vestments. As to the dogma of apostolic succ2s- sion,a third standard schoolboy knew that it was a mere idle pretence. He did not believe Christ ever intended to have one uniform church, or He would have had it. Ills plan was unity in diversity. That there were thousands of men unfed, unclothed, • uneducated, degraded to the lowest depth to which sin does degrade them, did not trouble the bigoted clerical one fiftieth part so much as that those who were heroically seeking to raise this "submerged tenth had left their community and become Dissenters and Nonconformists. Instead of coldly censuring those who had left her that they might have a larger field of service and had discarded her methods in favour of others that offered a prospect of better results, let her go and do likewise. In conclusion the preacher advised his hearers to meet bigotry with charity, and if the church would not reeognise the Non- conformists' efforts to extend Christ's kingdom,to recog- nise and assist those of the c,vurch. Above all things let them " put on charity" which was the mark or charac- -eristic of perfection.

div.head: HORRIBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: HORRIBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.
A WIFE SHOT DEAD

A terrible tragedy was enacted at Stone; North Stafford shire, late on Tuesday evening, when the manager of the Falcon Inn, a fully-licensed house, situate in the High-street, deliberately shot his wife with a double-bar- relled breech-loading gun, and afterwards shot himself. For the past three months William Strefford, aged twenty-six, and his wife, Ada Mary Strefford, aged twenty-seven, the latter being a Liverpool young woman whose maiden name was Ada Mary Perks, have been managing the Falcon Inn for Messrs. Montgomery and Co., brewers, Stone and Liverpool. Latterly they have lived unhappily, and frequent quarrels have taken place between the two, and as late as Saturday night Strefford attempted to stab his wife, but he only succeeded in inflicting a wound on his wife's shoulder. About a month ago an infant child was found dead in bed, and this seems to have affected Strefford, for since then he has given way to habits of drinking, and his wife has been afraid of him. About 10.25 on Tues- day night Strefford was alone in the back vaults of the house, which is entered from a yard. At that time there were in the house a man named Shardlow, a barber named Flowers, Mrs. Strefford, and her sister-in- law, who acted as assistant in the house. Strefford, it appears, sent for his wife, and there can be no doubt that he deliberately premeditated murder. On the wife entering the vaults, her husband must have deliberately taken up the double-barrelled gun aril fired. The shot must have struck her in the throat just under the chin, destroying the tongue, and entering the base of brain about the centre. Strefford then, no doubt, held the gun upright to his chin and fired, bisecting his head verti- cally. The first that was heard of the report of firearms was by Flowers. He did not think at first that it was the report of a gun, but on hearing a second similar noise he rushed to the back vaults along with the man Shardlow, They there saw a horrible sight. The bodies lay feet to feet, and the discharged gun was by the side of them. The heads of the couple presented a frightful spectacle. Not a shred of the features of the man could be seen, the face being simply one mass of flesh and blood. The only features of the woman that were visible were her eyes, forehead, and part of the nose, the lower portion of the face being completely shattered. With regard to the motive for the crime, all that can be said is that Strf- ford was a very passionate man, and had lately been drinking heavily and appeared strange in his manner. His wife, it is stated, was very jealous of her husband, and had frequently upbraided him for alleged infidelity.

div.head: NOTES FROM MANXLAND.
div.p: NOTES FROM MANXLAND.
BY F. R. R.

THE CONTEST IN PEEL. It is said that Dissent flourishes best in the shadows of a cathedral. Certainly it is in a healthy state in the ancient city of Peel. The cathedral, it is true, is in a dilapidated state—its roof is gone: what remains ot its walls is covered with moss and ivy; its tombs are shapeless mounds, and the , broken fragments of its memorial stones retain but faint traces of the recording chisel. The venerable pile is nothing more now than an interesting monu- ment of antiquity to the tourist; and to the enter- i prising fisherman of Peel it is an abiding attraction which supplies him with the means of turning over an honest penny in the way of ferry charges. It must not be concluded, however, that the church which since the Reformation has been iden- tified with this ruined pile is in a similar state ot decay in our capital city. On the contrary never, at: all events within recent years, were the interests o "t-

div.head: HORRIBLE MURDER IN AMERICA.
div.p: HORRIBLE MURDER IN AMERICA.

John M‘Mullen, of Wilkesbarre, Pennsylvania, has murdered his wife, mutilating her in a skocking manner. When the body was discovered in M‘Mullen's house it was naked, lnd a red hot poker had been thrust into it a dozen times, and with red hot tongs he tore great strings of flesh from the body. The room is described as resembling a slaughter-house. After committing the murder IVl'Mullen fled from the house like one insane, and threats of lynching him were heard.

div.head: CRIMES ACT DIVISION.
div.p: THE CRIMES ACT DIVISION.

s . he Church "so well looked after and her minis- try so popular there. In the place of the old cathe- dral a span-new, commodious, and comparatively speaking, handsome, Gothic church is doing duty, and is well filled with a congregation largely com- posed of the members of that class of society which styles itself " good." But,as elsewhere in the island, the shopkeepers and the fishermen are Dissent- ers, and, as tkey constitute the larger half of the population ot Peel, the same state of things exist there as in all the Manx towns, namely, that Dissent is the predominating social force. It is 1 difficult to give your readers an adequate idea of the meaning of this fact. You have nothing like it in your large towns. I have met with it in some of the old agricultural towns of central England, but to a Lancashire man of to-day it is almost im- possible to realise how completely the religious question is the wall of partition in Manx society. A Manxman is either a Churchman or a Dissenter. I He never becomes an Atheist. Ile could more easily I become a Heathen Chinee than a Roman Catholic. He has no politics. You can only give him two names, first Manxman, second Dissenter or Church- man. It should further be stated that " Dissenter " is practically synonymous with " Methodist" throughout the island. It follows that the vast majority of Manx working-men are staunch Dissen- ters, devoutly religious men whom it is by no means uncommon to hear discussing the latest " conver- sion" in a railway carriage, or singing hymns at street corners, and who, however forbearing and patient they may be in other things land they are wonderfully so) will not tolerate an insult or a slight put upon their religion or their church. All this will help your readers to understand the nature of the contest in Peel. The sitting member is a bigoted Churchman. And strange to say he holds the dignified position of High-Bailiff of the I very town he represents in the Keys. This office in no way resembles that so worthily filled in Warring- ton, for it has nothing to do with "bums "and dis- traint and other machinery of your county courts. Our High-Bailiffs are stipendiary magistrates, administering justice in the several towns of the island.. Whether the High-Bailiff and Member of the House of Keys for Peel has been emulating the freaks of your J.P.'s and thus brought discredit upon himself I cannot say, but the public feeling of Peeltown has been expressing itself lately in terms unfavourable to the combination of the functions of magistrate and member in one man. But the contest turns mainly on the religious question. Mr. Laughton (the member in question) has thoroughly disgusted the Dissenting portion of his constituents. A few months ago,when the vexed question of the appointments to the magistracy was raised in the Keys by the eloquent member for Ramsay, Mr. Laughton distinguished himself by a clownishness of utterance and bigotry of abuse which gave the greatest offence in Peel. But if- Mr. Laughton was to be opposed,who was to oppose , him? To secure success a strong man must be found. He must have, aa required by law, a property quali- fication which °minded all but comparatively rich men, and the trade of Peel does not supply such , men in conspicuous numbers. But a deus es tnachina' ' appeared in the shape of a returned colonist, a man who had made a huge fortune abroad, and had come home to spend the remainder of his days. Mr. Joseph Mylchreest rejoices in the soubriquet of "The Diamond King." Twenty years ago he was a ship'S carpenter in his native town. Out of work, be left Peel,to seek his fortune in Africa, and, making his way to the diamond fields,speedily succeeded in ae--I hieving his object,. He is the reputed owner of fabu- lous wealth, and it is certain that he is giving evi- dence of its possession in extensive purchases-of land and houses here. His popularity in Peel is immense. He is a man of great stature, and appa- rently equally herculean strength. His energy is tremendous, and he seems to be just the man to shock the susceptibilities and expedite the tardy movements of our easy-going and,locally speaking. aristocratic legislative authorities. The poor of Peel have already found that a helpful friend is in their midst, and even the fairly well-to-do feel a sort of buoyancy in the consciousness of the nearness of such a massive personality and such great wealth. 'Moreover, Mr. Mylchreest is a " jolly good fellow." I was in Douglas station yesterday when he came down for his train. It was amusing to watch the horizontal expansion of every official face. All the guards and porters-present found something to do ' near Mr. Mylchreest' s carriage,and apparently their labour was not in vain. A lad who had followed the worthy gentleman with a parcel left the station in a state of unutterable satisfaction. I looked out of my window as the train left, and the nods, smiles, and winks or the men in velveteen corduroy seemed to indicate that Mr. Mylchreest, Zeus-like, had descended upon them in a shower of, not gold perhaps, but silver. The fight is being hotly fought. The only thingl that can save the sitting member is that the Gover- ' nor should not dissolve until the fishing season has begun, when the men will be off to the Irish coast. Mr. Mylchreest de/ores he will charter a steamer and fetch them back in that case, and I have no doubt he will. There are about 650 voters in Peal. ' The other day an old fisherman was asked how these votes would be bestowed. " Laughton would get 150" said he.. "So many?" answered his inter- rogator, sarcastically. "Aw mon," replied the old salt, taking the remark seriously "there are always plenty of gaughs (fools) in the worli." Next week I purpose giving your readers an account of a political meeting held by Mr. Mylchreest's supporters ashort time ago in Pee's.

There were exactly 100 members absent from the divi- sion on Tuesday night on Mr. J. Morley's motion impeaching the administration of the Crimes Act. The 247 supporting the motion were-176 Gladstonian Liberals, 45 Anti-Parnellites, and 26 Parnellites. The majority of 322 consisted of-260 Conservatives and 62 Liberal Unionists. The absentees were-47 Conserva- tives, 5 Liberal Unionists, 33 Gladstonian Liberals, 6 Anti-Parnellites, 7 Parnellites, and Messrs. Dillon and , O'Brien.

div.head: GREAT AMERICAN WEDDING.,
div.p: A GREAT AMERICAN WEDDING.,

NEW Yonx, WEDNESDAY.—The wedding,!) of John Jacob Astor and Miss Eva Willing was the most elaborate that has ever been held in this city. if not America. Pre- sents which are estimated as worth 2,ooo,ooodols,include a furnished house in Fifth Avenue, New York. The young couple will spend their honeymoon on a yachting tour to the West Indies.
TWO PERSONS KILLED BY A LUNATIC.

NEW YORE, WEDNESDAY.—At a train bound for Little Rock was leaving Baldknob, Azkansas, yesterday, a male passenger suddenly fired at Isidore Meyer ,a commercial traveller, killing him instantly. The conductor pulled the bell to stop the train, when the man fired at and killed him alto. He was: secured and proved to be John Greater, of Vincennes:. Indiana, an. escaped luna- tic.

div.head: LACROSSE.
div.p: LACROSSE.
WARRINGTON V. WITHINGTON A.

After an enforced idleness caused by frost and the necessary cancelling of fixtures through cup ties, the Warrington men, true to their engagement, turned up at Withington,on Saturday last, to meet the local organisa- tion. Unfortunately the visitors were poorly represented having five of their best men away. As a consequence their attack was considerably weakened. It was only the stubborn resistance of the defence that prevented a bigger score. The centres faced at about 3.30 and the home team commenced to attack,butthe visitors' defence was too strong for them. Spelley ran down the field and sent into goal, but Barker saved in brilliant style, and shied down the field to one of the Warrington attacks who threatened danger, but the ball was dropped at the critical moment. For some time the visitors were severely pressed, the ball rarely going beyond centre, where Dunn was doing some useful work. Turner gave Spelley a pass, and he ran up and sent in a stinging shot. William- son, who put in some good defensive work, got posses- sion of the rubber, passed it to one of the homes, who transferred to Evans,who ran up the wing and equalised with a good sh3t. At length Withington broke away and after some neat passing between the homes scored again, after which half-time was called, the score being 2 to 1 in favour of the home team. In the second half, the game was much of the same character as before, With- ington pressing. Their attacks played a neat passing game and kept Ora visitors' defence hard at work, and thus ran out winners of a hard-fought game by 4 goals to I.—Warrington team: H. Barker, R. Garnett, W. A. Kiernan, S.Wilson, F. H. Williamson, E. Parry, J. Dunn, R. E. Garnett, H. H. Evans, C. Spi-nks, L. Thompson, and C. H. Woods.
WARRINGTON WATERWORKS COMPANY,. THE HALF YEARLY MEETING.

The ordinary half-yearly meeting of the share- holders of this Company was held, on Wednesday afternoon, at the offices of the Company in Cairo-st. In the absence of both the Chairman and Vice-Chair- man (Lord Winmarleigh and Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P.), Mr. J. C. Carr, presided. There were also present Messrs. John Geddes, P. Stubs, Thcmas Barham Forster (Manchester), J. Wal- ton Mellor (Ashton-under-Lyne); T. J. Ridg- way, W. Fairhurst, J. Shaw Green, H. Neild, E. J. Nicholson, and John ROss, secretary. The directors submitted their report as follows : "The Revenue Account shows a balance, including £1,209 14s. 3d. brought from the previous half-year, of £5,480 7s. 10d. The Dividend en the 2.401,000 preference stock amounts to £9OO, leaving a balance of £4,580 7s. 10d., out of which the directors recommend that there be paid for the half-year a dividend at the rate of seven per cent, per annum on the £3o;oo9ordinary seven per cent. share capital ; a dividend at the rate of seven- and-a-half per cent, per annum on the £15,000 ordinary seven-and-a-half per cent. share capital ;.and a dividend at the rate of ten per cent. per annum on the £30,000 ordinary ten per cent. share capital,. with a further dividend at the rate of two per cent. per annum thereon, so as- to make up the maximum statutory dividend of ten per cent, for the year 1890, the dividend paid thereon for the first half-year of 1890, having been at the rate of eight per cent, per annum. The balance remaining to be carried forward is the sum of £2,167 9s. 10d., as against 21,045,55. carried for- ward at the end of the year 1889. The Warrington Txtension and Water Act, 1890; which passed through both Houses of Parliament last Session, received the Royal Assent on the 14th of August, 1890, and thereupon became law. Bv virtue of its previsions, the undertaking of the Company will be tranafferred to and become the property of the Corporation a Warrington on and from the Ist day of July, 1891., The Directors who retire by rotation are Sir Gilbert Gre,enall, M.P., Mr. Thonaas Barham Foster, and Mr. Henry Neild, who are eligible and offer themselves for re-election. The auditor who retires by rotation is Mr. William Silcock, who is eligible and offers himself for re-election." The report, on the motion of the CnAteltANl.seconded by Mr. PRTER STew, was unanimously adopted,.and dividends according to the recommendations of the directors were declared. The retiring directors were • unanimously re- elected, and Mr. William Silcock was re-elected auditor. A vote of thanks having been accorded, proposed by Mr. RtDGWAY and seconded by Mr. GEDDES', the meeting terminated.

"It looks suspicious. But the men must be there this evening. He shall not escape me now." "There is no fear of that, my lord. I will see that he is apprehended as soon as he returns." "Right, Savotano—right ! And now to the other matter. lamto be married this afternoon !: "Ah—so soon 2"

" Yes ; I waste no more time. What is the use 2' "None, my lord—none at all." "Then you must remain, for the ceremony shall be performed as soon as possible." "And does the countess know of your determin- ation ?"

"Yes. She knew it ere she retired last night. I told her she should not escape me again till she could carry my name with her. By the masc, sir,she sealed her own doom! Ha, ha, ha,—the Duke of Tula will have his coffers filled again. Money must come somehow, and how else so easily as this?" "Sure enough," returned the priest, with that old coarse, wicked smile. "Sure enough, my lord— how ?"

"In no way. Ho, I'll put the seal upon that bud- get, and stamp it—mine!' So here you remain until lam married. To-day—until that ceremony is per- formed, I am not sure; but to-morrow they cannot harm me. Oh—she shall be mine, Savotano. To-day she is my wife—to-night she shares my bed—and to-morrow all heaven and earth and hell combined cannot undo the work. I have waited long enough. ' I have worked and schemed, and have puzzled my brain to one great Purpose; and yet each step I had marked out has failed me. Damonoff lives—the gun-maker lives—the Black Monk lives—But /, too, 'live! hve, Savotano ; and now the work shall be done as it might have been done at first had I been so disposed !" The duke had arisen to his feet while speaking thus, and his manner had been frantic and excited. As he ceased speaking he sank back into his chair and gazed the priest in the face, lie was all iron now. Every nerve and muscle was set, and a fierce determination was in his soul. There is is one more scene in the ducal palace, and it goes on at the very time while the duke and his tool are together. Valdimir the monk was in the chamber of the countess, and the fair occupant and her maid were there with him. "And you are sure he means to make you his wife to-day ?'" said the monk, in continuation of a con- versation which had been goinc, on for some moments—" that he will have the ceremony per- formed whether you consent or not ?" "'Yes, sir," the countess murmured.. She gazed into the strange man's face a few moments after she had spoken, and then, starting quickly up, she threw herself upon her knees before him. "Oh !'? she cried, with her clasped hands raised towards him, " can you not help me in this bitter moment ? Do not say no. Oh, I know you have some strange power—and you may help me. You cannot know the misery I suffer. Oh, earth has no pangs moreeruel ! mall the long catalogue of woes there is nothing more bitter Sir—" and the maiden raised both hands towards heaven as she thus con- tinued—" sooner than be that man's wife I. would with my own hand let ray life-blood out were not the act a sin against my God !' But you may help me." "Alas, lady, ..I'cannot assure you now." "Oh—say not so. You can help me flee from here—you cairfine some hiding-place—some place where my days can be spent in safety from this great evil." "But how ean I'help you away, lady ?:' "Because you know some secret entrance to the palace. You know some secret passage, else you would not be here now." " True," the monk replied, in a perplexed tone, "I do know such a way, for by that way I came, and by that way shall I return; but I. cannot con" vey you away thus. lam sorry that—" The monk stopped here, for at that moment heavy footfall sounded without. He had started q from his seat when the door opened, and the stou_b duke entered. The countess uttered one low, quicx cry, and sank down. She would havesunk to the floor had not Zouobie caught her and bore her tin the couch. The monk stood erect, with his arms folded across his breast, but his right hand was hidden in the bosom of his robe. The duke started back like one thunderstruchi and it was some moments ere n 0 could gain the power of speech. He turned first as pale as death, and then the blood mounted hotly, fiercely to his brow. "By the living God!" he gaspedi.in a hissing, frantic tone," how came ye here V' " To learn of your wickedness, Duke of Tula, calmly responded Valdimir. "ha! do you beard me in my very palace, dog But you have ventured here once too often. As We as there is life in me you go not hence alive !" "hold, Olga !" spoke the monk,—and so strange and powerful was the tone that though the duk.es had turned towards the door, yet he stopped. " lady tells me.you mean to make her your wife. it so ? " "Out accursed monk ! Who gave thee right to question me ? " "By my soul, proud Duke, you shall know Os: anon. But listen: If you force this lady to the,, thing you do it at your peril! You had better see': the fabled ' potion of the gods; and. drink and be dog. thando that thing ?" "Hold &moment monk! "• cried the duke, 110,.6 nearly blind with passion; "you go not hellY, alive !—What ho, there! Without I say !—Zeuoblv.! pull that bell-cord—quick .P—Back, monk! yar, pass not here alive !—Whatho !‘ Without there' "Beware, Olga! " spoke the monk, as calmly eSI before, at the same time drawing a heavy pist° from his bosom and cocking it. I would she(); you as I; would a dog! Offer, me one motion 0e impediment to my passage, and , you die on instant Instinctively the duke moved to one side. There was something in the look., and tone of the stroll man that he dared not cope with then. The molle passed.out, but as soon ae.he was gone the sprangto the bell-cord and pulled it till he broke.rd In alew moments morethe servants came rushl'

"-Out, dogs! "the madman shouted. "and st°,Sl that monk from leaving. the palace. Sill hima us,o tho•spot where you find, him if he dares to offer t" least resistance! Kill him—you have my ordetlb end t am alone responsible! Thus speaking the duke rushed from the aPartt; ment to start up more of Ms household. First thegate of the court: he went, but the monk not there, nor had ha been there. Then he rusiws;/ to the postern, but that was locked, and the so° was untrodden befcre it. Ile returned to the 11,11,kiv and one by one the•servants came back frora search. No monk could be found ! ger At first Olga was-temped to believe that his --ho 'glints deceived him, ;. but he quickly set tPO, thought aside, for' he could see by their collo aces that they were as much astonished as he. search was rem-wed,, but the strange man was,am tobe found! There was some wonder, and—s" uneasiness.

div.head: BY SYLVANTIS COBB, JR.
div.p: BY SYLVANTIS COBB, JR.

CHAPTER XVIII. STRANGE AND COMPLICATED. Ruric Nevel dreamed that he was a great general, and that lie was upon the eve of an engagement. He gained a view of the commander of the oppos- ing army, and he saw that it was the Duke of Tula. Yet the duke had an enormous hump upon his back, and instead of the usual uniform he wore the garb of a priest. This was very strange—at least so ran Ruric's thoughts in the dream. Soon the engagement commenced, and the loud-monthed artillery opened its thunder. The din was deafen- ing and strange, and Ruric shouted in vain to his aids, for the roar of cannon drank up his words , direct from his lips. Louder and more loud grew the crash, and finally Runic started for the charge. His horse was shot under him, and with a quick leap he reached his feet. "Runic! Rune ! My master !" lowly the youth opened his eyes, and Paul stood by him in his night clothes. He gazed about him, and found that he had 14-sped from his bed, and now stood shivering upon the floor. "Don't you hear that racket at the door ? " asked Paul. " What ? Ha—there is some one knocking,' Runic uttered, as he heard the sound. " And have you not heard it before ?" "No." "Why did you leap up thus ?" "I was dreaming ?" "I thought 'twas the noise below. Why they've been making a perfect thunder of noise down there Shall [go down ?" "Yes, go, Paul; and I will: dress as soon as possi- ble. What time is it ?" "It must be near daybreak," And thus speaking Paul turned and went to his own room, where he threw on an outer garment, and then he went down. At the door he found a stout man wrapped up in furs, while close by stood a sledge with two horses attached to it. In the east the golden tints of morn were already visible. "A gun-maker, named Nevel, lives here, does be not ?" asked the applicant, after having first made some passing remark on the trouble he had had in starting some one up. Paul feared that there might be something out of the way, but he dared not tell a,falsehood where it could not possibly be of any use, so he answered in the affirmative. "Then let me see him as speedily as possible." "Ile is preparing to come down sir. If you will walk in you may see him very scon. The stranger followed the boy into the kitchen, where it was quite warm, the fire in the furnace having been burning all night. Ere long Ruric came down, and the visitor started up, How I.!'nttered the gun-maker„starting forward and extending his hand. "Demetrius ?" "Aye, ray friend," the Greek replied with a smile, "I am an early visitor, eh ?" "I should say so; but, early or late., you are wel- come." "Thank you. But we must not, spend much time here now. My sledge is here at your- door, and I wish you to accompany me." "But wherefore is this ?" asked:the youth in sur- prise. " What has happened now ?". "I'll ten you: Last night Olga, the duke, came to see the Emperor. I had just been giving his majesty some exercise at the sword, so I was pre- sent at the interview. The duke wished for power to arrest you; and in explanation of the request he stated that you were at the head of a bond of rob- bers here in the city, and that you had already com- mitted several robberies. I needn't tell you all he said—but he made you out to be a most unmitigated villain, and with this the Emperor granted his Aquest. Olga wished for power to execute you at once, but Peter would not go so far as that. He gave the power of arrest, but ordered the duke to bring you before him." Ruric e3:.00d for a few moments like one con- founded. "Then he must carry me to the Dimperor," he said at length. " Ah." returned Demetrius, with a dubious shake of the head," be not too sure of that. Bsaw a look upon his face when he turned away that meant more than he daded to speak. As sure as fate he never means that you shall see the Emperor.. I know it —I saw it in his evil eye." 'But will he dare disobey the order ei" " Yes. fur he hopes to escape by falsehood. How easy for him to swear that he had to kill Toll to take •ou."

" I see-1 see," uttered Eric. " Then.come with me." "Did the Emperor send you ?" " No ; but I take the responsibility.. I will take you to him: myself. Be sure the duke's hirelings will be here before long. Trust to me andall shall be well." Runic pondered a few moments, and he saw that his friend was right. "Let me go and see my mother," he- said, "and then I will go with you." "But make haste," urged the Greek, "for the duke's men may be hare soon, and. 1 do not wish thee to see you. And—tell your mother to inform whoever may call, that she knows not where you are gone, but) that you will be back at night.".' The youth nodded assent, and then went into his mother 4 room, whereho-explained to her what had. happened and what he was about to do. "Ant how long must these things be ?t' the mother uttered, gazing eagerly upon her son. "Not long," returned Runic. "1 may do much towards settling the Taatter to-day. But fear not, for I" am now safe, Lied shall be until I see yott again."' The-widow promised all that her son asked, and soon became assured: that all was well; but Paul was -left with the duty of attending to those who might come for Runic, though they; might see the widow if they pers7:sted. The boy nromised to tell all that asked for his-master that he-had gone away on business, and wculd not return till evening. The mother came-out before Runic was ready to start, and her examination of the Greek's counten- ' anee seemed to be satisfactory, for the anxious look left her face, and she looked upon the visitor kindly. As Ruric entered the sledge thedawn of day was plainly announced- in the east, and, the stars were paling in the ski. The Greek: did not take the direct road to the Kremlin, but struck off to the westward, and so-entered by the Neglina. An hour late7r a party of five men drove up to the gun-maker's cots. They were dark„villainous-look,- ing men, and murder was plainly stamped upon, their faces. They entered the dwelling, but they. found not theirprey. They stormed and swore,but to no purpose,. and when they were convinced that the gun-makerwas not there-they went away. An hour later still, and another party drove up-to the same cot.. /t consisted of. two men in a double - sledge, one-of whom was Valtlisrair the monk. The fat, mystic man entered the- cot, and there ho-re- mained for-, some time. When he came out the widow and Paul accompanied him ; and they all; got nto the sledge and drove off together. What did it mean?

It was noon. The proud Duke was once, more alone iii his private room;. and he was pacing un- easily to and fro. There was a cloud upon his brow, and trouble in his soul.. His lips were firmly set, and his hands clenched. Ever and anon he mut- tered.to, himself, and when he did so his hands would work nervously and emphatically. He looked often at his watch, and often he stopped near the door and hearkened. At length came that well-known shuffling, un- certain, cat-like tread. He threw °pea his door, and the dark priest glided in. "Ila, Savotano, rve waited for you," the duke uttered sinking into a chair, for his nervous walk- ing had made him weary. "sow tea me the work .is done. Oh, for God's sake, don't tell me again of failure ! " "Alas. my lord—" "hold Savotano . By the host of hosts, you are not going to tell me of failure ! " "Not really a failure,my lord," the priest returned nervously, "But our men did not find the gun- maker at home. He had gone when we got there, and no one knew where." "No one knew? Did not his mother know ?' "No. She said he did not tell her where he was going. He only left word that he was going on business, and should not return till evening.: "By heavens! I think he has fled. "No, my lord. Ido not think so. I think be must have had business." "But what time were you there ? " "Shortly after sunrise." "And he gone then?" "Aye —he had been gone an hour,"
