div.head: IMPERIAL PABLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PABLIAMENT.

--- - - - HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNnaT. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the wool-sack at a quarter past four. EAST INDIA OFFICES BILL.—VISC,OUDt CROSS moved the second reading of this Bill, the object of which, he ex- plained, was to enable certain high officers in India to return to England when necessary on public grounds 'without incurring the penalty of losing their commis- sions or appointments. The Bill was then read a second time. EDUCATION OF THE BLIND AND DEAF.—Lord CRANBROOK moved the second reading of a Bill, which, he said, was similar to that introduced by him last year, the object of which was to enable the blind and deaf to be educated at proper institutions, the cost to be defrayed by Govern- ment grants or out of the rates. After some observations from Lord Horton, Lord Her- schel', Lord Egerton of Tatton, and the Earl of Powys, The Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at a quarter past five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. NEW MEMBER.—Alderman Manfield, the new member for Northampton, took the oath and his seat amid cheers. THE BACCARAT SCANDAL.—Mr. STANHOPE, replying to questions, said he had received no communications which could enable him to contradict the statements in the newspapers regarding the baccarat scandal. It was not proposed to allow any officer connected with the case at present to retire. MR. MORLEY'S RESOLUTION. Mr. MORLEY then moved that, in the opinion of the House, the action of the Irish Executive in connection with the recent prosecutions at Tipperary.and other pro- ceedings is calculated to bring the administration of the law into contempt, and violates the civil and constitu* tional rights of Irish citizens. The right hon. gentleman contended that the present was an opportune time to bring forward his motion, especially when the spectacle was witnessed two days ago of two hon, members of that House being conveyed through London to undergo a term of imprisonment. He almost entirely confined his comments to the proceedings in connection with the prosecutions in Tipperary, which ended with the im- prisonment of Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien and asserted that cheering or hallolng is made a pretext dispersing the Irish crowd. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL moved as an amendment that in the opinion of the House the action of the Irish Execu tive in connection with the recent prosecutions at Tip- perary, and other proceedings, has been rendered im- perative by the existence and activity of an illegal con- spiracy directed against the civil rights of a large section of her Majesty's subjects irilreland,who had been subject to cruel persecution and great loss in following their lawful callings, and that the House rejoices in the suc- cessful vindication of the law at Tipperary and elsewhere which has gone far to restore freedom to the individual in every part of Ireland. Mr. GrAnsrolmsaid it was a superlative stroke to have secured the closing of the prison doors on Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien at a time when their country had great need of their services. The Government would be re- membered in Ireland for acts which were neither desir- able nor laudable. Mr. W. H. Salim followed, and characterised Mr. Gladstone's speech as the more reckless and unscrupulous that had ever been made in .the House. Mr. BALFOUR and otherspeakers having addressed the Rouse, Mr. Morley's motion was defeated by a majority of 75, the voting being—For the motion 245, against 320. The House divided. For Mr. Morley's motion 245 Against
Majority for the Government..:. 75

On the amendment being put by the Speaker, Mr. T. HEALY asked for further time to consider it. The Irish members wanted more time to testify that they were not so grateful forthe administration as the amend- ment represented. Not a single word had been said upon the amendment, except what Mr. T. W. Russel said him- self. He therefore moved that the debate be now ad- journed. Sir W. HARCOURT seconded the motionas most reason- able and necessary. Sir CHARLES RUSSELL hoped Mr. fealy would go to a division. Mr. BALFOUR said it was undei stood through the ordinary channels that the debate would close that night. The debate was adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. THE WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE BILL.—Lord DENMAN moved the second reading ol the Women's Suffrage Bill. The MARQUIS of SALISBURY, in moving that the bill be read a second time that day six months, said it was not com- petent for one House to undertake the reconstruction of the other. The bill was rejected without a division. POWERS OF COUNTY COUNCILS.—Lord HENNIKER, reply- ing to Lord Dunraven, said that under the Local Govern- ment Act of 1888, the various County Councils were empowered to appoint one or more medical officers of health within their jurisdiction' and the Local Govern- ment Board were aware that in the case of some of the county councils such appointments had been made. There was, however, no obligation on the County Coun- cils to report to the Local Government Board as to any appointment they might make. Correspondence on the duties of the medical officers was proceeding. The House rose at twenty-five minutes past five o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly after three o'clock. QUESTIONS. &C.—Mr. PICIEERSGILL gave notice of a motion calling upon the Executive to put into operation the existing law on betting and gambling against all classes of her Majesty's subjects. Sir W. HART DYKE, answering Mr. David Thomas, said the Education De- partment had refused to sanction the readmission at Bangor College of the student whose impertinence was stated by the inspector to have been the immediate cause of the recent outbreak. Sir. JAMES FERGUSSON informed Mr. W. James that there were no grounds for making a formal representation to the French Govern- ment regarding the recent arrest at Algiers of the British steamer Arib Brothers on a claim for salvage. The pro- posed " Oological expedition" to the Shetland Isles and ithe Alabama indemnity formed the subject. of further questions, Mr. W. H. SMITH informing Mr. Atkinson that It would be contrary to the Treaty of Washington, 1871, for this country to request the return of any money from the United States under the Alabama award. Mr. W. H. Siam replying to Mr. Sexton, said the Govern- ment was perfectly satisfied with the debate on Mr. Morley's motion, but if hon. members wished to go into it again, it would be for the Government to consider what their action would be. Mr. Surrn informed Mr. David Thomas, in regard to the establishment of district councils, that legislation on the subject would entirely depend upon the progress of business. Several bills were brought in and read a first time, and a desultory discus- sion took place upon Indian affairs, Mr. W. Smith pointing out that it was impracticable to take the Indian Budget earlier in the session. Swims BANRS.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer obtained leave to introduce a bill to amend the law re- lating to savings banks, and it was read a first time. BRINY: PUMPING COMPENSATION.—The Brine Pumping (Compensation for subsidence Bill) was read a second time, and on the motion of Mr. Brunner it was referred to a select committee, four members to be nominated by the house and three by the Committee of Selection, with Power to send persons, papers, and records, three to be the quorum. The House adjourned at five minutes past twelve o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock. RAILWAY BILL.—The Glasgow, Yoker, and Clydebank Railway Bill, the Plymouth and Dartmouth Railway Bill, and the Rhyl Gas Bill were read a second time. FACTORY AND WORKSHOPS BILL.—Sir HENRY JAMES, in moving the second reading of the Factory and Work- shops Act (1878) Amendment Bill, explained that its objects were to give the operatives better sanitary sur- roundings, including ventilation, greater safety from outbreaks of fire, greater protection from injuries in con- sequence of dangerous machinery being unfenced, better opportunity of testing the accuracy of payments for piecework, and the imposition of something more than nominal fines for offences under the Act of 1878. The Government had introduced a bill dealing with the Factory Act, but it did not deal with the difficulties his bill met with, and until he knew•more of the Government bill and the intentions regarding it he would be committing a breach of duty by abandoning the vantage ground which the chances of the ballot had given him. Mr. Oldroyd and Sir W. Heuldsworth spoke favourably of the bill. Mr. Caleb Wright advised that it should be sent with the Government measure to a Se- lect Committee. Mr. Byron Reed supported the second reading ; and Mr. J. A. Bright felt great satisfaction in not being called upon to oppose the bill. Mr. J. M. Mac- lean spoke agattist the bill. and Mr. Matthews suggested that Sir Henry James should endeavour to engraft its Provisions on that of the Government. Mr. Illingworth, Mr. Addison, Mr. Hoyle, Mr. F. S. Powell, and Mr. Mun- della having spoken, the bill was read a second time, and committee was fixed for next day. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Registration of Electors Acts (Amendment Bill and the Museums and Gymnasiums Bill 13;cre read a second time. The Teachers' Registration Bill was under discussion at half-past five, when the debate stood adjourned. Bills providing for the regula- tion of vans, vehicles, and tents used as dwellings, and •!or the amendment of the law relating to outdoor relief in Ireland, were read a first time. The House adjourned at 20 minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS, THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. THE Tuerme BILL.—The Marquis of SALISBURY moved 1,119 second reading of the Tithe Rent-charge Recovery ITI• Ile said the most important change that had taken Pytee since its first production was the abandonment of attempts to legislate on the question of tithe redemp- uon. It must not be supposed that the Government in

the least degree renounced the opinion that there were Ino evils in regard to tithe redemption. Lord HRABOURNE moved that the Bill be read a second time that day six months. The Archbishop of Canterbury and the Earl of SELBORNE supported the measure, which was read a second time. Tan PRICE OF BREAD.—On the motion of Lord Stan- ley of Alderley, an address was agreed to for copies of reports recently received from her Majesty's diplomatic or consular agents abroad relating to the price of bread in the countries to which they are accredited. Their lordships rose at seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TnunsDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Lord GEORGE HAMILTON, in answer to Admiral Mayne, stated that a Committee had been ap- pointed to inquire into the condition of the Royal Naval Reserve. Baron BE WORMS explained to Mr. Staveley Hill the position of the Newfoundland fisheries question. Sir T. Sutherland and Mr. W. P. Sinclair asked questions regarding the outward American mails, the first question 4- having reference to the missing of the connection at Warrington, and the second to the suggested adoption of the Stranraer and Larne route to Queenstown instead of by Holyhead. Mr. Raikes promised to look into both matters. Further questions had reference to discharged soldiers, the use of petroleum spirit, responsible govern- ment for Natal,disturbances in Arklow,compensation for slaughtered animals, and the West Highland crofters. VOLUNTEER OFFICERS.—MT. STANHOPE replying to MT. Howard Vicent, said there was at present vacancies in the Volunteers for 49 field officers, 161 captains, and 1,194 subalterns, and it was difficult to devise a remedy for this deficiency. THE ARMY,&C.—On the order of the day for going in- to Committee of Supply, Mr. HANBURT called attention to the falling off in the number of recruits, and moved a resolution embracing a modification of the conditions. Major Rasch seconded, and General Hamley hoped that the startling nature of the emergency would be quietly but promptly met. Mr. Stanhope under- took to consider the practicability of providing soldiers with free sea kits, and would do his best to extend their facilities for learning a trade during their period of ser- vice. After further discussion, the motion was with- drawn. A motion by Mr. Howard Vincent for the ap- pointment of a Select Committee in reference to the difficulty of securing rifle ranges near large towns was negatived. Mr. Marjoribanks moved a resolu- tion pointing to the necessity of making experiments with other patterns of rifle than the " magazine.' After some remarks from Colonel Nolan, who was still addressing the committee, the Chairman left the chair at twelve o'clock, no vote having been obtained. Mr. STANHOPE, in reply to Mr. Campbell Bannerman, said the consideration of the Army estimates would be re- sumed on Monday. GAME BILL.—Sir J. Dorington obtained leave to intro- duce a bill to amend the laws in reference to the illegal possession of game. It was read a first time. The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock

div.head: WHITECTIA.PEL MURDER.
div.p: THE WHITECTIA.PEL MURDER.

IMPORTAN r ARREST. The energy with which the police had entered upon the investigation of the circumstances of the murder of Frances Coleman and the search for,the culprit was on Saturday rewarded by two arrests, one of which turned out to be of considerable importance. In the other case the man, being taken to Leman-st. Police Station, was able to give a satisfactory explanation of his movements, and he was accordingly at once liberated. Sadler, the man arrested, had been identified as the man who was seen by Police Sergeant Edwards on Tow- er Hill shortly after the murder, when there was blood on his clothes. He had also been identified by a White- chapel coffee-house keeper as a man who visited his shop an hour afterwards; whilst it had been ascertained that he has not been in England for the last 18 months, a period which corresponds with the date of the last Whitechapel tragedy. Edwards, who had not heard of the murder, questioned Sadler ss to the blood on his clothes and accepted his explanation that he had been assaulted at the docks, and allowed him to proceed ; but from information subsequently received Sadler was ar- rested on Saturday at a public-house in Upper Smithfield and conveyed to Leman-st. station. Telegraphing on Sunday night a corrrespondent says, it now appears that despite the utmost vigilance on the part of the police authorites they have discovered but little to throw any definite light upon the authorship of the latest Whitechapel tradedy. On Saturday they effected an arrest which at one time seemed to be of an important character, but careful inquiries, it must be said, tended to support in the most material particulars the genuineness of the man's story. When asked to explain his movements he readily agreed to do so. He said he was a sreman on board a steamer in St. Katherine's Docks, and had known Coleman for some time. He met her on Wednesday, and after they had been about drinking during the day they went to what is known as a "double" lodging-house in Dorset-st., Spitalfields, where they passed the night. On Thursday he was about with her a good deal, and they undoubtedly had too much to drink, consisting principally of gin and cloves. She asked him for some money in order to buy a hat, and he gave her half-a-crown. She bought the hat, which cams to about 2s. The two in course of their wandering about the district, came late in the evening to Thrawl-st., where they went to a common lodging-house but they afterwards left, as the woman wished to go Lack to Dorset-st. in Thrawl-st., they had home argument, in the midst of which a woman came up and struck Sadler on the head with some instrument which caused him to faint. In corroboration of this he drew the attention of the police officers to his head,upon which was a nasty wound from which blood had ap- parently freely flowed on to his clothing. More people he asserted came up and added to his ill-treatment. When he came to again these people had gone, and only the woman Coleman remained. He upbraided her for not having attempted to defend him, and charged her with being the cause of the assault. They quarrelled, and he left her. This was between ten and eleven o'clock at night. He made his way to the docks with the inten- tion of going to his ship, but when he got there the gate- keeper refused to admit him because of his intoxi- cated state. For some time he lingered around the gate abusing the officials. In the midst of this some dockers came along, and he at once fell foul of them, and in all probability would have been roughly handled by them but for the presence of a police sergeant and constable. His next move was towards the Victoria gpme for Sailors, with the intention of seeking shelter for the night. In this he was also unsuccessful on ac- count of his drunken behaviour, and after pouring out some more abuse upon the porter, he went away in the direction of Tower Hill, where he met the police officer who accosted him. This in effect is Saddler's account of his movements. While giving it he appeared to have a particular good recollection for a man who had un- doubtedly been worse for liquor during the time that the chief incidents had been happening. Saddler has the appearance of having led a hard life. Though only middle-aged, he is described as looking nearly sixty. When telling his story he mentioned all sorts of little incidents likely to prove its truth, and when interrupted for a moment by the officials put- ting a question, quickly resumed his narrative at the point where it had been broken off. Prominent police officials are prepared to admit that they have been able to ascertain little to substantiate the earlier suspicion against Sadler. In the first place. it is pointed out that when he was met soon after two o'clock he was some distance away from the scene of the crime, which had been committed only a few minutes before. Sadler, Moreover, was weiring heavy boots, which would render noiseless and rapid flight an impossibility. When, there- fore. the information which appears to be in possession of the detectives is summed up, it seems that the arrest of the undoubted " Jack the Ripper" is as remote as ever. This the police are themselves ready to admit. THE INQUEST. The inquest on the murdered woman was opened on Saturday afternoon by Mr. W. E. Baxter,at the Working Lads' Institute, opposite the London Hospital, in White' chapel. Superintendent Arnold and Inspector Flanagan watched the case on behalf of the police. The sum- monses to the jury described the deceased as "a woman unknown." Several jurymen did not attend personally to serve on the jury, but sent substitutes. The Coroner, however, declined to accept any substitutes, remarking that substitutes were no good in a case like this. It appeared that of the twenty-four jurymen summoned only eight apoeared personally. As the result of some conversation the Coroner agreed to accept some substi- tutes, on being assured that the jurymen they repre- sented were unavoidably absent, and that the substi- tutes were respectable local residents. One man whose services were declined demanded to know the reason, and on the Coroner remarking that he simply declined to accept him, the man said in an iritated tone : Because I am chairman of the Vigilance Committee you won't accept me. You accept others and will not take me.— The Coroner: You are not a representative, like those I have accepted. The man: Why ? —The Coroner: I decline to give you a reason.— Police Constable Ernest Thompson deposed that he went on duty at ten o'cicck on Thursday night. His beat was in Chambers-street and Preston-street. He went down one of the passages about 2.15 on Friday morning, opposite the Catholic schools in Chambers-street. The first thing he saw was something lying on the roadway about midway through the arch. He went up to it and turned his Winiz on, whenhe saw that it was a woman. He noticed some blood, and saw her open and shut one eye. He then blew his whistle three times, and two con- stables came up in about three minutes. He had heard footsteps when going up Chambers-street. They were going in the direction of Mansell-street at a walking pace but he saw no one. He was then eighty yards from the arch. Nobody was going in the opposite direction. He could not say if the person whose footsteps he heard had come from the arch. As soon as the constables came up doctors were sent for.—Police Constable F. Higham and Police Constable Elliott also gave evidence, and the case was then adjourned till Tuesday. The inquest on Frances Coles, the victim of the list Whitechapel murder, was resumed on Tuesday morning, wpen Mr. Charles Matthews, barrister, appeared for the public prosecutor, and it was agreed, at the suggestion of Mr. Wynne Baxter, the coroner, that Mr. Matthews should examine the witnesses.

div.head: TnE EXNMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 21, 1891.
div.p: TnE EXNMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 21, 1891.

James William Coles deposed that he was an inmate of the Bermondsey Workhouse. He had identified the deceased as his *daughter Frances, who was about 26 years old. He last saw her on February 6th. Lorenzo Hawkes said the deceased, who was "three sheets in the wind," came to his mother's shop on Thurs- day night, at Bethnal-green, and bought a hat. Sadler looked through the window while the purchase was made, and walked away with deceased. Samuel Harris gave similar evidence to that given at the Police Court, on Monday, as to seeing Sadler and deceased at 8, White's-row, Spitalfields. He had no doubt about Sadler's identity. A witness name Gyver, living at 8, White's-row, Spitalfields, stated that Sadler slept at the house with Coles the Wednesday night before the murder. On the Thursday night Sadler came in again while Coles was in the kitchen. They were both intoxicated, and Sadler could not rouse Colas from her sleep. Sadler left, but Coles remained until half-past one or a quarter to two, and then went out, this being the last time witness saw her alive. Just after three o'clock in the morning Sadler came back to the house. He asked to be allowed to come into the kitchen, but was refused. Blood was running down his face, his clothes were dirty and disarranged, and he said he felt faint. He said he had been knocked down. Mr. Matthews said they wanted to sift other evidence, and the inquiry was adjourned until Friday. PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. At the Thames Police Court, en Monday, before Mr. Mead, John Thomas Sadler, 55, marine fireman, Victoria Lodging-houses, Upper East Smithfield was charged with wilfully causing the death of Frances Coles, hy cutting her throat with a knife or some sharp instrument, at Swallow Gardens, on the 13th instant. The fact that the prisoner was to be brought up on Monday having become generally known, the courthouse was surrounded by a large crowd eager to catch a glimpse of him. Owing to the defective cell accommo- dation at Leman-st., the prisoner was taken to Thames- at. Police Station shortly after midnight. The formal charge having then been made prisoi*x was placed in' the dock at 2.20 He was wearing a blue serge jacket and dark trousers. His face was still very dirty, and there were still indications of old scratches on his cheeks. He wears a dark beard and moustache. On being conducted into the dock the prisoner as- sumed a careless attitude, and stood with his hands in his pockets. Inspector Arnold, addressing the magistrate, said,—l have engaged with the Public Prosecutor, who has directed me to request you to grant a remand after tak- ing evidence of the arrest. The Magistrate.—l must hear some evidence. I cant not tell until I hear the evidence whether it is sufficien- to justify a remand. You may put before me what evi- dence you please. Samuel Harris, a young man, deposed: I am a fish curer, and live at 9, White's-row, Spitalfields. I was in that dwelling-house on Thursday night it 9.30. I had been there about an hour when I saw a woman whom I knew as Frances. She was sitting on a form, and had her head upon the table. It was the kitchen of the lodging-house where she sat. I remained in the kitchen till 11.30. Prisoner came in, and at'once sat down beside Frances and asked her, "Have you any lodging money?" She looked up, but made no reply. The prisoner then said, " I've been robbed, and if I knew who did it I would do for them." At 12.30 prisoner went out, but the woman remained in the kitchen. Before going away prisoner showed me a discharge document. Prisoner, thinking I was the governor' showed me the document and asked me to let him go to bed, and he would pay when he got his money. I did not permit him and he went away. About three or four minutes afterwards I saw Frances put a black crape hat under her dress and leave the house. I did not see her again alive, but have identified her body at the mortuary. Police-constable Westley (7 H) saidonFriday morning, the 13th, I was on duty on Mint-pavement shortly be- fore two o'clock, when I saw the prisoner. He was than, in my opinion, drunk. I could see he was suffering from a cut over his left eye. He was standing on the pave- ment holding his side. He said he had been knocked about by some men at the dock gates. William Jewett, night porter in the receiving room of the London Hospital, deposed :—A little before five o'clock en Friday morning prisoner came in with a lacerated scalp and a small cut over the eye. While washing his face I asked him how he came by the inju- ries. Prisoner replied, "I've been with a woman, and she's done me." I asked him how much it was for. He said, "Only 7s. or Bs. and a watch. I should not have noticed that if they had not knocked me abont." He trembled, and on my asking him why, prisoner replied, " I'm cold; I've been walking about. Unfortunately, I've got no lodgings; this is the first night I've been ashore, and I haven't secured any lodgings. On my asking where ithappened, prisoner said, "In the small street down the highway, near the bottom if Leman-st. I have been to one or two places to try and get a few halfpennies for refreshments." The question of remand arising, the Magistrates' Clerk asked whether Sir Augustus Stevenson had wished for any particular date. Abreply being given in the ne- gative, the magistrates appointed that day week at two o'clock for the resumption of the hearing, and the pri- soner was formally remanded till that day.
SINGULAR LETTER FROM SADLER. A correspondent sends us the following letter, received from Sadler on Thursday morning by an official of the Seamen's Union :
"MM. Prison, Holloway, 1891. "Mr. Wildgoose, from T. Sadler, a stoker and mem- ber of your union—Burnt Island Branch, No. 311 (my last payment was made at Town Hill last

Friday, the 13th) : wishing prosperity to the union. I must apply to you to act as my friend, as I have no claim on anyone else in particular. My wife was always a doubtful friend : my mother is too old; I have no brother or sister, or public-house palls worth a d—. I should like a reporter connected with" Sea- faring "or the " Star" to watch over me. The police wish to hurry ray case on to suit their own ends, and anything turning up in my favour will be squashed. All the money and sense of Scotland Yard will be used to hurry me to a finish. What a Godsend my case will be to them if they can only conduct me, innocent as I am to the bitter end. The whole detective system of Scotland Yard will be whitewashed in the sight of the whole world. Money presents will roll in to them. But on the other hand, if I have any true friend in a reporter to see that I am not talked down or sat upon entirely by the police and court I hope to walk out as I deserve to do. The knife business is false. I have neither bought or sold any knife. I had one knife and .fork only—a pair given me by my old mother a few months ago.—J. T. SADLER."
MR. F. MONKS ON "A VISIT TO
AMERICA."

The fifth meeting, for the present session, of the Literary and Philosophical Society was held on Tuesday evening in the Museum lecture-room. The Vice-President (Rev. Gibson Smith) occupied the chair and there was a large attendance of members and friends. Mr. F. M. Appleton, Bruche Hall, was elected a member of the society. Mr. FREDERICK MONKS J.P. (president of the society) read a paper entitled "A Visit to America." He observed that for a long time a great deal had been heard about American competition, the excellence of American tools, and their great productions. In his own mind, he had resolved to go over and see for himself at the first convenient opportunity, and judge how far the Americans were ahead of the English. When the American iron-masters invited the members of the Iron and Steel Institute to hold their autumn meeting in America, he at once decided to take advantage of the opportunity to visit the States. He started on the 20th September from Liverpool, sail- ing in the Cunard steamer Servia. After eight days' steady steaming, New York was reached. As tke con- conveyance in which he travelled to his hotel rumbled through the streets, he was made acquainted with the condition of the roadway. He held on to his seat, ex- pecting every minute to experience an upset. (Laugh- ter.) He was surprised at the speed and . ease with which the trains travelled on the elevated railway. In tramcars he discovered that overcrowding was both systematic and excessive. A car was never full so long I as there was standing room for any more passengers. New York was no exception, for the same indifference to personal comfort and convenience was general through- out the States. The patience with which the people bore that and many other inconveniences was simply amazing. He did not hear a ward of complaint from anyone. It was all borne in such good humour that it increased the difficulty of explaining it. In a country where Jack was as good as his master, and all men were equal, he supposed they had to take what they could get and make the best of it, for there seemed to be no appeal from the tyranny of the democracy. The abstention of the best class of men from municipal public life haft left the management of municipal affairs entirely in the hands of the party wirepullers, whose nominees were expected to vote and act in accordance with instructions from a party caucus. Around that system had grown a network of private interests, which made it a most complicated and diffi- cult question to deal with. There is a large foreign ele- ment under the control of the party managers. How- ever plausible the arguments may be for the payment of members of Parliament, and town and county coun- cillors, his opinion was that that the payment of salaries to aldermen and councillors and members of Congress was one of the causes of the political corruption and jobbery in municipal and national politics in the United States. (Hear, hear.) The American protective system, he said, by increasing the cost of living without increas- ing wages, and by making employment more precarious, deterred the better class of workmen from emigrating to a country where he had to compete with the negro in the south, and with the Italian Hungarian, and role in the north. There was a limit to America absorbing such a foreign element as yearly flocked to her hospitable shores, and lie thouguit that Congress would be acting wisely if they required from every emigrant some guarantee of his or her fitness to become a good citizen. (Hear, hear.) American hotels were not what he expected they would be. They were neither so well managed nor so comfortable as hotels in this country. He was afraid he could not say much for the press. The little time he had for reading newspapers did not give him many opportunities for judging it fairly: What he did see was very poor in comparison with London and provincial papers. Americans were very much below the English standard in literary merit. (Laughter.) The American system of railway travelling was best suited to the long distances which had to be covered. Going South from Chicago and entering Tennessee, the visitor found a region of 20,000 square miles of coal and ironstone, easily accessible by rail, and worked at a very small cost. At Knoxville every inducement was offered to manufacturers to go and settle. There was an abun- dance of coal and ironstone in the hills adjoining, to be had at very cheap rates. On his way to Big Stone Gap, he stopped to examine the side of a mountain spur some 6ft. or Bft. high, containing an excellent ore of 40 to 45 per cent, suitable for the manufacture of basic pig iron used in manufacturing basic steel. In scores of places pieces of ore were lying exposed, and in some places where a spade and pick had been used, he saw the bed of ore lying within 3ft. of the surface of the hillside. Having spoken of the regard in which England is held, her sons being welcomed in America. Mr. Monks said he was afraid that the condition of the negro popu- lation had not improved very much by the change. What;was to be the future state of the negro race it was difficult to say. They were a people by themselves, with their own schools and teaching staff and places of wor- ship. They were increasing in numbers much more rapidly than the white population, and they had a char- acter for being docile and indolent, rather than energetic, self-reliant, and combative, like their Anglo-Saxon neighbour. He had few opportunities of examining the educational institutions, but he noticed as he travelled through the country that every villiage seemed to have a school house, and that in the larger towns every opportunity was afforded to those who desired to I take the higher subjects; and there was no diffi- culty in any student going to one of the universi- ties and taking his or her degree. Boston furnished the means of education most liberally. Its public library was a magnificent one, and would be as magni- ficently housed. The technical school was really a tech-

div.head: DARING JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT
div.p: DARING JEWELLERY ROBBERY AT
NORTON PRIORY.

With regard to the robbery from Norton Priory, the residence of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., some par- ticulars of which we gave last week, it now appears that the thieves carried away about twenty articles of gold and silver jewellery, but the case also contained £2OO worth of other jewellery concealed in a false bottom, and this the robbers fortunately overlooked. In the dressing room is a Chubb's Safe in which were secured diamonds of the value of £2,000, and the rob- bers have the keys of this Safe in their possession, and the owners are unable to open the safe to ascertain whether it has been cleared of its valuable con- tents. To cut open the safe,which is the only course, is a difficult operation which will occupy no less then ten hours, mad an experienced man commenced this task, and until he has finished,the family are in suspense as to the fate of their diamonds. On the night previous to the robbery and also on the night of the robbery, two strange men were seen in the locality, and they are strongly sus- pected of being the authors of the robbery. They arrived at Norton Station by the 5.37 train from Chester and departed by the 10.25 p.m. train to Frodsham. They arc thus described. The first, 40 to 50 years of age, 51t. sin. high, broad features, beard and moustache cut short, stout built, wearing hard felt hat, and dark mixture suit. The second 22 to 25 years of age, sft. sin. high, slight built, moustache, wearing hard felt hat, and short light drab overcoat. The safe was successfully opened on Saturday morn- ing about 11 o'clock, and those interested in the matter were much relieved to find the valuable diamonds safe. It would seem that the thieves were disturbed before they had an opportunity of using the keys they had ob- tained, and it transpires that a servant, hearing some person in the room knocked at the door and was sur- prised to receive no answer. At this time the family were at dinner, and she raised an alarm which no doubt caused the unwelcome visitors to take a hasty depar- ture. We understand that Sir Richard Brooke values the booty carried away at an amount under £2O, so that the affair is not so serious as appeared on the first inquiry.

div.head: DARING BANK ROBBERY IN LONDON.
div.p: DARING BANK ROBBERY IN LONDON.

£11,500 STOLEN. A daring robbery was committed on Monday after- noon in London, from a clerk in the employment of the Bank of Scotland. About noon two clerks in the employ of the Bank left the chief office in Lothbury, and pro- ceeded together in the direction of Bishopsgate-St. One of the clerks, named Mc'Kenzie went to the National Pro- vincial Bank of England in Bishopsgate-st., his compan- ion going to the Capital and Counties Bank opposite, the arrangement being that they should meet after perform- ing their duties, and return to the Bank of Scotland to- gether. Mc'Kenzie. who is only 17, entered the National Provincial Bank of England and proceeding to the counter, laid his satchel' upon it. At that moment he felt a touch upon his right shoulder, and turning round was asked by a man of gentlemanly appearance standing near. whether he could direct him to the Union Bank of London. M'Kenzie replied. A moment afterwards turning to the counter he found to his dismay that the satchell had disappeared. M'Kenzie was almost stupi- fied when he realised the great loss which had been sustained and the responsibility which rested upon him. He looked anxiouslv about the bank, but there was no one leaving in a hurried or suspicious man- ner. He immediately made his loss known to the officials and clerks at the National Provincial Bank, but the theft had been committed with such skill that no one noticed it. The satchell contained Bank of England notes to the amount of £11,500. A clerk named Hagan, who was in the bank at the time, heard of the robbery dur- ing the afternoon, and attended at the Bank of Scot- land, and stated that at the time in qaestion he noticed a man with a light overcoat and felt hat standing near Mackenzie. and that a taller man was with him. Both the men are described as foreigners. Superintendent McWilliams, and Inspector Outram, of the city police, have the case in hand, and regard it as the work of a gang of robbers who have been engaged in similar tran- sactions.

In conclusion, Mr. Monks said: I wish to give PATENT the audience the net result of my visit from purely a BALSAM OF HONEY, business point of view, which may possibly have an in- euenhievmersailly Science p lar as a Family Medicine all over the World. Thousands of opuin- terestin- terestto somein this room. If I returned a little more !List oisndeeo. ftithreds,e soonerDls e o voerr ileast to become or re-assured, it was not because I under-estimated that progress which had been developed on the other side of the Atlantic, but because I have had an opportunity of Testimonials to Hand. examining in detail and comparing the conditions undeg which both our English and American manufacturers ;lit working. When we observe the very large output of a blast-furnace, we comprehend mere accurately how it is accomplished, but we also see that the same methods are open to our own manufacturers, with the same results, if they cared to spend the money re- quired to provide each furnace with separate blast- engines of sufficient power to give the very high pressure required. It is a question of management and economy; but where blast-furnace plant is about double the cost, it may pay to do it in one case but dot the other. -So also in steel manufacturing, it may pay to drive a plant to its maximum capacity, even at extra cost, but, so far as we could judge, they have adopted the English practice, with such improvements as a larger experience and local circumstances have decided. In the manu- facture of bar iron they are wasteful to an extent that would ruin an English firm, and in both finish and pro- duction are not abreast of our best English mills. They make an excellent hoop, but in some of the works the Knights of Labour have such control as to limit the pro- duction; and, of course, under such circumstances, the best is not possible, and no faiT comparison can be made. In wire-drawing their mills are in no way better equipped in plant or machinery, but they have adopted a different system of working, which gives them a larger output and greater economy in working; but even here it is only a question of time as to how long our English wire- drawers will continue to submit to an old prejudice in the presence of new conditions, which have altered and made possible a readjustment which will improve the position of both masters and men. With such a con- sumption in one works alone as 2,500 tons per week of wire rods, it would be surprising if they had not been stimulated to make their wire-rod mills as productive as possible. In several mills they are doing exceedingly well, far in advance of anything in this country ; but it is only fair to say that the mill is a combination of a forge-train and rod-mill, possible only when dealing with soft steel in very long lengths and in very large quantities. In their machine, tool, and nut and bolt worksthere is little difference to be noticed, except in details, which would apply to both countries. There are many novelties, but novelties are not always improvements, and many of them did not seem to commend their adoption to some of our hard-headed Lancashire machinists. In structural ironworks they are well up, both in theory and practice, and are developing this branch of industry very much, and even now are successfully competing for export work. Their engineers seem to be content with strength and stability, and are not so exacting in details, which add nothing but cost and appearance. The universal system of driving every- thing to its maximum capacity largely explains how it is that the American workman is content to work longer hours and work harder than the same class of labour in England for little, if any, better pay. The skilled work- man is doing well at present, and earning high wages ; but the great bulk of the labour employed, taking the cost of living into account, is no better paid than in Eng- land. With the increasing demand for labour of the better class will arise the difficulty of getting the well- trained artisan as heretofore, as present conditions offer no inducement to the average workman to emigrate, so long as he can find regular employ- ment here. At present we have nothing to fear from American competition with a fair field, but so long as they are bolstered up with a high protective tariff, it may suit many manufacturers in bad times to sell a part of their production below cost in order to find employment and keep cost down upon the balance. Still no man who has seen the immense deposits of coal and ore and other minerals, and seen also how easily and cheaply they can be got, but must feel that the day will come when American competition will be a struggle be- tween the two nations as to which of them shali supply the world at large with its manufactures. There is time for every prudent man of business to put his house in order and be ready for the struggle when it may come, and in the meantime fer us as a nation to develop our technical schools and those educational advantages which shall assist in maintaining thelead in industrial progress. We left the Americaushoresfeelingthat e better under- stood the American character, and that they, too, might feel, that, if we were a fair specimen of the Englishman at home, they would like to see more of him to share with them that wonderful prosperity which is un- doubtedly theirs in the future. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Monks for his able lecture, said America afforded opportunities for amassing immense fortunes that no king or any other man in Europe could hope to get together. It was a country full of contradictions. The people were, as had been said, "rough and ready ; " but they must consider the age of the country. It was scarcely yet out of its petticoats, but they might look forward to immense developments. Mr. LONG seconded the motion, and gave several in- teresting incidents connected with his visit to America some years ago. M.r. TROMAS BIRCHALL supported the vote of thanks, and said he paid a short visit to America eight years ago. There was a great deal of ingenuity exercised on the part of the Americans, though in some cases the ingenuity was thrown away. We accomplished certain operations with simple machinery; but the Americans had evidently a desire for effect, and what they did in certain cases was like employing an elephant to pick up a pin. (Laughter.) With reference to the wire manufacturers of England, their machinery had been much improved, and they might fairly be said to be in all respezts abreast of the best American manufacturers. (Applause.) The Rev. F. K. FREESTON also supported the motion. The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously. Mr. MONKS, in reply, said there were a large number of really first-class men in America, who deplored the political oorruption as much as anyone could. The great difficulty was to get out of the bad rut, particularly when these party managers had control of the foreign element. American Government (and American politics) was the very essence of Toryism, and with regard to liberty in the sense in which they understood it, he doubted very much whether it existed there. The meeting then terminated.

• SENSATIONAL DIVORCE CASE. • The London correspondent of the "Freeman's Journal" says there was a reporti on Tuesday night that a sensa- tional divorce case, n which a Government official is connected, is pending. Efforts are being made to pre- vent it from coming into court, but so far without suc- cess. PARNELLITE MEETING. Mr. Parnell presided on Tuesday over a meeting of his supporters in Committee-room No. 15, and gave a full account of the recent negotiations between him and Mr. O'Brien at Boulogne. On the motion of Mr. Mahony, seconded by Mr. John O'Connor, a resolution was adopted approving of the policy pursued by Mr. Parnell. MESSRS. DILLON AND O'BRIEN. The Press Association's Tipperary correspondent tele- graphs that Mr. John Dillon, M.P., and Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., were on Thursday morning removed from Clon- mel Gaol to Galway. They were taken from Clonmel at seven o'clock in a saloon carriage attached to a special engine. As the train passed Tipperary at 7.30 a cheer was raised by a few persons wile had become aware of the removal of the prisoners. The remainder of the sen- tence will be completed at Galway. The special train ' reached Galway shortly before noon. A. crowd had gathered, and cheers were given for Mr.. O'Brien, with counter-cheers for Mr. Parnell. The prisoners were con- veyed in a carriage to the prison. MEETING OF NATIONALISTS. A meeting of the supporters of Mr. Justin M•Cirthy's Chairmanship of the Irish Parliamentary party was held on Monday, in Committee-room No. 15 at the House of Commons. The meeting first discussed the position of the evicted tenants, on whose behalf they authorized Mr. Micarthy to withdraw the remainder of the Paris fund or such part of it as might be urgently needed, the money to be handed over to the Council of the Tenants' Defence Association for distribution. It was announced that the deed transferring to Mr. M'Carthy the shares held by Mr. Patrick Egan in the Company owning `.` United Ireland" had been received. This means, as was explained, that there will be a further contest for. control of the paper. It was in fact stated that instruc- tions had been issued to take proceedings for deposing the present management. Another matter discussed was the work of orga.nisation in Ireland. in connection with which it was determined to hold a., number of meetings and to send to Ireland a strong csntingent of Parliamentary representatives.

A Visit MR. F. MONKS, JP., who is the to President this year of the Warring- America. ton Literary and Philosophical So- ciety, read an interesting and instructive paper, on Tuesday evening, on his recent visit to America. As a member of the Iron and Steellnstitute, which held its autumn meeting on the other side of the Atlantic, he had exceptional opportunities for observation, especially as to matters relating to trade, and his address shows that he made good use of his opportunities. It is hardly possible for anybody to say anything new with regard to Brother JONATHAN and his great country, but it is something gained when emphasis is given to special features. Mr. MONKS was like other travellers,in being made uncomfortably aware that the streets of New York are for the most part in a shockingly bad condition. He noticed also great over-crowding in tramcars ; but remarks as to this and other inconveniences that—" He did not hear a word of complaint from anyone. It was all borne in such good humour that it increased the diffi- culty of explaining it. In a country where JACK was as good as his master, and all men were equal, he supposed they had to take what they could get and make the best of it, for there seemed to be no appeal from the tyranny of the democracy." That phrase " tyranny of the democracy" rather jars on us, coming as it does from a Liberal such as we know Mr. MONKS to be. It is no doubt something strange to an Englishman to see Jack recognised as being as good as his master; but) As there are a hundred Jacks for one master, such a state of things surely tends to the greatest hap- piness of the greatest number, which is the aim of every well-governed State. It may be that the masses in America are in a position to have things their own way; but it would seem that they do not always sufficiently exercise their power, or Mr. MONKS would not have to condemn the influence Of party wire-pullers in municipal and State affairs. Human nature is, to be sure, pretty much the same all the world over; but if things go wrong they can be the sooner righted when the people who feel the pinch have it in their power to apply a speedy remedy. Mr. MONKS noted the abundance of coal and ironstone on the hillsides which was to be had very cheap. It is the same with other primary commodities; and it is these vast natural resources, coupled with the stimulus to energy given by free institutions, that account for the enormous pro- gress which the United States have made during the past century. It is commonly stated that Great Britain is the wealthiest nation in the world; and there has been no ground for disputing the Etatement until recently. Mr. GIFFEN, Secre- tary to the Board of Trade, estimates the wealth of this country to be 10,000 millions sterling; but Mr. ANDREW CARNEGIE, who as an American millionaire may he said to be an authority on the other side, claims that the wealth of America approaches 15,000 millions. There is no question, at any rate, as to the fact that we no longer head the list with our total of manufactures. Against a total annual value of English manu- factures amounting to £900,000,000, the United States have :C1;100,000,000. America now leads the way, whilst others follow; and a young nation which has attained such a pre-eminence may at least feel proud of its material progress. It is true unfortunately of the United States as of England that unskilled labour does not prortionately profit by this growth of national wealth. That involves a problem which has yet to be solved; and when "the way out" is made clear there will be need to exercise what opponents will probably speak of as "the tyranny of democracy." The Fair Traders in this part of country, if there are any loft, will do well to note that, in the opinion of Mr. MONKS, the Protection system in America has increased the cost of living Without increasing wages. It has enabled the large manufacturers to grow rapidly rich at the expense of the mass of the people; and that is not a state of things to be encouraged or emulated. It happens, perhaps fortunately, that the policy of Protection has been so overdone in the M'Kinley Act as to excite something like a revolt—a revolt which, it is to be hoped, will be the means of the masses overcoming the intrigues of the classes. There is one direction, it should be men- tioned, in which, according to Mr. MONKS, we may with advantage Americanise our institutions, and that is in provision for education. He has seen something of the application of technical instruc- . • tion in the United States; and we trust that the additional knowledge which he has gained will spur him on in the admirable task to which he has committed himself—that of securing technical in-. struction for Warrington.

div.head: 11L
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

We hold over several letters under pressure upon our space, including one from an Australian colonist describing his journey out, and a reply by Mr. Dignum to Mr. Gandy. It will be seen that some of the "Letters to the Editor" appear this week on page 6. If our correspondents would study brevity we should be better able to oblige them all.

-- It should be generally known that people who eat mussels do so at their peril. There has been another death through feeding on them, the latest victim being a Bermondsey lad aged fourteen. The percentage of deaths is of course small, but it is not pleasant to those who are fond of the bivalve to know that risk is incurred, however small.

The news reaches us from America that " Mr. Dickerson, Democrat, of Kentucky, has introduced into the House of Representatives a Bill for repeal- ing the M'Kinley Tariff Act and for re-enacting all the laws repealed by that Act." Poor M'Kinley Just when he has become as famous as the late " M'Ginty " he is in danger of being snuffed out.

There are people in Canada who are actually dis- cussing, during the election campaign the possi- bility of annexation to the United Stales. There was talk of this kind in 1837 and in the end the Dominion was pacified with a scheme of Home Rule. Why not try the old remedy—inore Home Rule ? And why not pacify Ireland in the same way?

The refusal of Manchester magistrates to license the new Palace of Varieties establishes an important precedent so far as that city is concerned, and it will have its influence on other licensing justices. It means that no new licenses are to be granted— however " splendid " the case—until the whole question has been dealt with by Parliament. And quite right too.

The militiaman is looking up; his status is to be improved. It has been decided that there shall be prizes for recruits, and there is to be an annual shooting competition for a challenge shield. This is all in the right direction; and when we have gone a little further it will be seen that it is equally desirable to properly equip our volunteers,without sending the hat round to supplement a niggardly allowance.

-- On the face of it, it seems rather hard on Mr. Jerome K. Jerome that, because an unfortunate gentleman used to have " Three men in a Boot" read to him and go to sleep over it,the fact should be adduced in evidence in a lunacy case. If the contention should be that the gentleman must have been out of his mind to go to sleep over such a lively book,lVlr. Jerome as the author may score after all.

A London Correspondent says :—" A sign of the full opening of the London season is that the Prince of Wales has within the past few days resumed his old place among the morning riders in Rotten-row, and that the Archbishop of Canter- bury has now followed his example." How sug- gestive of the harmony between Church and State! But the Archbishop's fashionable ride doesn't quite fit in with the ways or the teachings of the Founder of Christianity.

In a case heard at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, it transpired that a deserter had been " spotted " as a soldier by P.O. Cooper "because of his straight back." This led the NI ayor to ask —" Hasn't a man a perfect right to walk with a straight back through the streets ?" It would seem that the incident has set his Worship think- ing. It would be odd if he should be "run in" by a zealous P.C.; for he walks with a very straight back.

The Emperor William and Prince Bismarck are disposed to hit out at each other. The Kaiser has been saying sharp things of the Prince, and the Prince has retorted with the remark that "he refuses to agree with politics which take away the corn duties and give the Jesuits." The ex-Chan- cellor seems to pay little regard to "The right divine of kings to govern wrong." But how if the ex-Chancellor should be wrong? Let him beware. A cat may look at a king, but must not argue with him.

The alleged case of cheating at cards when the Prince of Wales was visiting at Tranby Croft, Yorkshire, is to come into the law courts; and it is not unlikely that his Royal Highness will be called as a witness to certain proceedings in the matter. Sir William Gordon-Cumming is in a pitiful position ir having signed a document which compromises him; but what a revelation the whole story is of gambling in high life! It is a pity " Society " cannot find something better to do with its time and money.

Poor old "Poet Close"; he died at Kirkby Stephen on Sunday in his 75th year. He would never have been heard of as a " poet " if Lord Palmerston had not made himself ridiculous by granting the rhymester a pension of £5O a year. But the pension was laughed out of existence; and the old man had a grievance ever after against an unappreciative nation. He is said to have remarked that justice would not be done to his genius until there was a ton of marble on the top of him. But why a ton of marble ? A volume of his verse would surely be "heavy" enough.

_ *** NEW STORY.—On Saturday week, March 7th, a new story will be commenced in the columns, of the "Examiner "entitled "Percival Gordon or the Child of the Regiment." We commend it to our readers in the belief that it will be found to be as interesting as previous tales in this journal.

There was a good audience, and Mr. Bisbrown's able description was much appreciated. BASSINETTES.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—ildrt.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 21, 1891.

FOG AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. For the greater part of Wednesday these towns were enveloped in a dense fog, and business was conducted with difficulty. The river traffic was at a standstill. Singular to relate the weather at the village of Weston was bright and fine. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DurroN's Sankev-St.. Warrington.—Advt. LECTURE ON DARKEST AFRICA AT WIDNES. Under the auspices of the Methodist Free Church Mu- tual Improvement •Society, a lecture on " Darkest ' Africa" was delivered by Councillor Snape in the Zion schnolroom, on Thursday night. Mr. Snape described in eloquent aud graphic language, Mr. Stanley's travels through the dark continent, and his descriptions were rendered more interesting and picturesque by a number of lime light views shown by Mr. V. C. Driffield. The sketches in Stanley's cPlebrated book had been photo- graphed on to lantern slides by Mr. Driffield. Mr. W. Clarke, of Dittcn, presided. CaucuLEr. Practical Tailor, Bold-St.,Warrington.—Advt. RuNconN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday. Mr. T. Riley presided, and there were pre- sent Messrs. H. J. Grice, W. Handley, E. W. Humphries, and J. D. Jones (Librarian). The cash statement showed receipts, including a balance of £l9 12s. 3d. in hand, of £27 6s. 7d., and after paying salaries there was a balance of £23 3s. 3d. During January the library had been opened on 14 days, and the issues were as follows : Theology 34, philosophy 14, science 83,history 185, poetry 21, fiction 1,599, miscellaneous 176, total 2,112; being a decrease of 148. 23 books had been consulted in the re- ference department. DEATH OF MR. E. BADLEY OF HALTON. Mr. Edward Badley, landlord of Norton Arms, Halton, died on Sunday last at the age of 58 years. The deceased gentleman, whe was well known and highly respected in Warrington and Runcorn distriet, had sufferedcfor some time from an incurable disease. His remains were in- terred at Warrington Cemetery on Wednesday afternoon. The three coaches following the hearse were occupied by Mr. Edward I3adley, (nephew, Liverpool), Mr. G. Turley (nephew), Mr. John Budge (Warrington), and Mr. Barker (Warrington), Messrs. Price, W. Anderton, J. Jea- cock, F. Furgusson, T. Wright, W. Tandy, John Barrow, and the Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar of Halton, who per- formed the funeralservice. UMRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. 85 W. Durrox's, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

- RUNCORN POLICE COURT. Yesterday, before Major Hazlehurst and Dr. Steele, John Andrews, a navvy, was brought up on remand charged with stealing a coat belonging to Mr. William Craddock, pawnbroker, Church-st., and a pair of trousers belonging to Mr. J. Unsworth, clothier, &c., High-st. The prisoner was sentenced to seven days' hard labour on each charge.—Frederick Egerton, labourer, Halton, was charged with stealing on Wednesday, a goose worth 12s. from the farm of Mr. Parry. It was proved that the pri- soner took the goose from an outbuilding during the fog, but as this was the first offence and he appeared to be of weak intellect, he was bound over in his own recogniz- ances of £5 to appear for judgment when called upon. A NEGLECTFUL FATHER AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. Brundret, and Major Hazlehurst, at Run- corn Police Court, on Tuesday, James Critchley, a chem- ical labourer, was charger' on a warrant with neglecting to maintain his three children who are chargeable to the Runcorn Union. In 1887 the prisoner, who then occu- pied a house in the Rookery, was sentenced to three months' hard labour for neglecting his family, who were found in a most filthy and a half starved condition. Since that time they had been inmates of the Workhouse and had cost the ratepayers £lO for their maintenance. The father had made no effort to provide for them and his whereabouts not being known no action could be taken. This statement was made by Mr. G. Ward, the relieving officer, and the magistrates sentenced the prisoner to a month's hard labour.
WIDNES PARISH CHURCH TE.k PARTY.

The annual congregational tea party in connection with the Parish Church cf St. Mary, and St. Paul's Church was held on Thursday evening, when a large company sat down to a tea provided by Mr. Bray, con- fectioner. Afterwards an entertainment was given, a capital programme being gone through by Madame Annie Williams, Miss Parkes, Messrs. Brady, Wilkinson, Pownall, and A. G. Davies (humourist). Mr. H. Wade Deacon had been announced as chairman, but he was unable to fulfil the engagement through indisposition, and the position was taken by the Vicar, the Rev. G. H. , St. Patrick Garrett, who in the course of his speech,said that during the past year, the congregations had im- proved at both churches, the Sunday schools had grown in numbers, and he had also to report progress in regard to the Bible classes. Their day schools were never in their history more efficient than they were now, but un- fortunately they had been unable to obtain the whole of the Government grant owing to their subscriptions and receipts being less than the amount earned. Be urged them to greater efforts in regard to their churches and schools. UMBRELLAS 11E-COVERED at the shortest notice. —J . & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Adrt. A MERSEY MISSION INSTITUTE FOR RUNCORN. At a meeting of the Committee of the Rungorn Branch of the Mersey Mission on Thursday night, Canon Mait- land in the chair, the altered and improved plans and specifications for the proposed new institute in Station- road, which have been approved by the Liverpool Com- mittee, were submitted and passed.—Mr. John Wilson, oi Greenway-road, is the architect, and the plans show a substantial brick structure, two storeys high, the front facing Station-rd., the rear being in Pig-lane, which is a busy thoroughfare for boatmen and watermen generally. The room on the ground floor will be used as a reading and smoking room,and for entertainments for sailors and boatpeople. The upper room is to be a place of worship where religious service will be conducted on week days and Sundays. Towards the cost of the building there is in the bank the sum of £570 19s. 6d., and a further amount of £57 is promised, but this is far from covering the estimated expenditure, and the help of all those who are interested in the work Mr. Shaw, the missioner, has accomplished and is carrying on amongst the floating population of thc town, ought to be forthcoming. Ten- ders for erecting the new institute are invited from con- tractors and others. CP.ITCHLEY. High Class Tailor. Bold-st.,Warrington.—Advt.

WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. At the weekly meeting held on Sunday afternoon in St. Paul's Chambers, Mr. Howlin, in the chair, the fol- lowing resolution was carried unanimously :—" That we hereby tender our deepest sympathy with two of Ire- land's most illustrious sons, namely, Mr. John Dillon and Mr. William o'Brien, who are at present undergoing six months' imprisonment, for protecting the suffering people of Ireland from the strong hand of felonious land- lordism. We sincerely regret that, seeing their efforts in Boulogne for the past month in tryine•* to establish peace and the once united party have f tiled, there is no hope to bring such a deplorable state of things to a conclusion. We would therefore impress on our countrymen through- out the civilised world, tostand together in one unbroken bond of unity and organisation, and to abstain from doing anything that would increase the difficulties that are now placed in Ireland's road to freedom, feeling con- fident as we are, that the all-sustaining hand, the pro- tector of Ireland's people through long ages of saffering and persecution, will now defend her in this an unparal- leled crisis in her sad and glorious history." Mr. Augustine Creamer delivered a lecture on the Irish ques- tion, and the proceedings closed with a vote of thanks to the Chairman. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notiee.—l. & DUTTON'S Sankey-it., Warrington.—Advt. TRACTION ENGINE ACCIDENT AT HALTON. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Wm. Brookes was charged that he being the owner of a traction eng- ine, did on the 9th February permit it co be used without having a fragms,n stationed in front and also with travel- ling between 5 p.m. and 1 a.m. without providing two efficient lights in front thereof. Enoch Ashbrook, the driver, was charged with driving the engine at a great- er speed than two miles an hour. Two young men named Geo. Grice and James Collier stated that about a quarter to five on the date named the engine was travelling through Halton at the rate of seven miles an hour, and after turningiGalnon'i: Corner it ran into the wall, and was damaged. --;ever,il hours were spent in repairing the engine, and at nine o'clock, the driver started to run to Hallwood without a flagman in front and without lights. Mr. Brookes said he provided the best machinery and paid the men good wages, and thought it hard that he should be summoned for his man's negligence.—Ashbrook said the engine ran into the wall because the steerine, gear broke. He had one light burning all the time. steering Brundrit said the em- ployer was responsible for the acts of his servants in this respect. Mr. Brookes was fined 103. and costs 9s. 6d. in each case. Ashbrook was fined ss. and costs 18s. 6d. or in default 14 days' hard Ihbour. CnrrcitLEr's Tailoring meets the times.—Adrt.

PRESENTATION TO A WORKS MANAGER AT WIDNES. The workmen'employed by the Liverpool Silver and Copper Co., whose works are on the Old Marsh, Widnes, on Wednesday presented their manager, Mr. Joseph Gibbings, with a handsome marble clock and bronze ornaments, in commemoration of his marriage, which took place on the sth inst. The presentation took place in a large room of the works, and the gathering was pre- sided over by Mr. W. J. Wilkins, who said it was very gratifying to find such a friendly feeling existing between employer and employed, and he hoped that feeling would be further cemented by the action of the men that day at such an important juncture of Mr. Gibbings's career. Mr. Gibbings was always ready and willing to ameliorate the condition of all with whom he came in contact, and had striven hard to place that concern on its present ' footing. He wished Mr. and Mrs. Gibbings much hap- piness.—Mr. T. Davies, in making the prescntation,testi- fied to Mr. Gibbings's character and ability, and simliar testimony was borne by Messrs. Baguley and Leathwood. In returning thanks for the present, Mr. Gibbings said when the relations between canital and labour were friendly, both were benefited, and both derived increased profit. He hoped that the good feeling between himself and the workmen which was symbolised by the hand- some present would continue while he had the privilege of managing the concern.—A small balance from the presentation fund it was decided, should be placed to the accident fund of the works,

RUNCORN, WESTON, AND FIALTON WATERWORKS Co. The annual meeting of the shareholders of the Com- pany will be held on Monday afternoon at half-past three. The place of meeting is the Public Hall. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times.—Advt. A CANAL BOAT SUNK IN THE FOG. Owing to the density of the fog two boats collided on the Bridgewater Canal on Thursday morning at Sale. One, belonging to the Bridgewater Trustees, laden with coal, was greatly damaged,and sunk,and the persons on board narrowly escaped with their , lives, some of them being in the cabin at the time of the collision. The loss will be vets, considerable. GRATlON.—lntending emigrants to New York, Boston. Edwards-Moss, M.P. for the Widnes Division has consented to become an honorary member of the Lord Stanley Lodge of the Prescot District of the Independent Order of Odd- fellows. PREMIER SAPP:TIES. Cash or Hire.—Garland, Warrington —Advt. DEATH OF A NOTED CHESHIRE FARMER. Mr. John Markendale, who for forty years was a tenant farmer on the Earl of Stamford's estate, died at Dunham Massey, near Altrincham, on Tuesday night. The deceased was a noted prize sheep and cattle breeder, and at most of the agricultural shows he was a prominent exhibitor, and won many prizes. UMBEELLxS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. Sc W. Durron's Sankey-St.. "Warrington.—Advt. CHILD KILLED ON THE RAILWAY. An inquest was held at Sandbach, on Thursday night, on the body of Paul Cherrington, aged two years, who was killed under singular circumatances. Deceased was playing with three brothers and a sister on the railway near Wheelock Forge, the children amusing themselves by pushing to and fro over the line a pair of truck wheels which had be- come disconnected. The wheels knocked over the deceased, and inflicted fatal injuries. Verdict— Accidental death." LAWN MowEns.—Garland, 51, Bridge-St., Warrington, and at Barlestown.—Advt.

THE NEW ST. HELENS RAILWAY. A series of half-yearly meetings in connection with the railway systems was held on Friday at the board-room of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin- colnshire Railway Company, at Manchester. The first meeting was that ot the proprietors of the Wigan Junction Railways Company, over which Mr. J. W. Maclure, M.P., presided. The half-yearly meeting of the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway was afterwards held, under the presidency of Mr. 11. Seton-Karr, M.P., who ex- plained that the meeting was purely one to receive the report and statement of accounts. The Com- pany, he said, had lately been carrying on negotia- tions with the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincoln- shire Railway Company with regard to making their new line. These negotiations were now practically completed, and they all hoped before long to auth- orise the works to be proceeded with. He formally moved that the accounts be adopted. Mr. E. Chap- man seconded the motion which was adopted, and the chairman and Mr. Chapman having been re- elected directors of the company, a resolution was passed at a special meeting sanctioning the pro- motion in Paarliament of a Bill to extend the time for the compulsory purchase of lands for certain railways, authorised by the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Act, 1885, and the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Act, 1886; to provide for the issue of preference or guaranteed shares or stock, and for other purposes. LECTURE ON "DARKEST ENGLAND"

_ AT RUNCORN. A large attendance assembled in the Greenway- road school last night week, on the occa- sion of a lecture on" Darkest England," delivered by Mr. Charles Garnett, Superintendent of the Star Hall, Ancoats Mission' Manchester. The chair was occupied by Mr. F. J. Norman, who informed the audience that these entertainments were arranged by the officials connected with the Board Schools as an inducement to the scholars to attend regularly at school. About £4O had been spent in that direction, and first class results had followed as both Board Schools had obtained the excellent grant. Mr. Moulton, the head master, attributed that success to the small present of prizes and the entertainments which had been given to the chil- dren to induce them to attend more regularly, and on behalf of the officials he thanked the public for the support they had received. Alluding to the sub- ject of the lecture. Mr. Norman said these was a de- putation to do something to improve the condition of the people who were living in a miserable condition in our large cities and town, and in order to estimate the difficulties that had to he dealt with, he supposed they should visit the slums of our cities and witness the deep degradation that existed. It was altogether impractic- able to do so, and by means of the lantern views and Mr. Garnett's lecture they would be able to form a bet- ter idea of low life and the misery and wretchedness of the poor of London.--Mr. Garnett then delivered his lecture, which was profusely illustrated by lime light views of the slums of Lon 9 don and the lecturer gave minute descriptions of them. In conclusion he gave a. highly interesting account of his mission work in Man- chester, in which he enlisted the sympathies of his audience. The usual vote of thanks was accorded. Mr. Bowyer manipulated the lantern.
