(Applause.) This was a splendid answer to some of the things said in the Vicar's late sermon. (Applause.) The meeting concluded in the customary manner.—During the evening the choir led the singing in a very creditable style, and Mr. Grice presided at the organ.

A. correspondent writes :—" The Wesleyans do not appear to have taken any serious harm from the recent action of the un-Catholic preacher of the Parish Church. Their home missionary services held on Sunday and Monday last were of the most enthusiastic character. It is very clearly evident and it must be gratifying to the Wesleyans and others to see that so far, the intolerant counsels—dictated by indiscretion and bigotry which I Perhaps may have gratified and influenced a few" Well instructed Churchmen," are not the counsels which com- mend themselves to the generosity and common sense of the Runcorn people. I am told that the St. Paul's people never scored a greater success on behalf of their Home Missions, than at their recent anniversary—their plans were well arranged for what the Wesleyans call a" good time" and their best expectations were left a long way behind. A large choir and some capital singing of the old- fashioned type greatly helped to make the meeting one which the worshippers at St. Paul's will never forget. The collection amounted to £56 or nearly 300 per cent. more then was raised three years ago. When we learn that it is only 3 weeks since the magnificent meeting on behalf of the London Mission was held in the same place, and for which the sum'of £l6O was contributed, every- body in Runcorn save the few "Welt instructed Church- men" and their clerical leaderswill say—wiwell done, St. ' Paul's."
RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS' CONCERT AND
BALL.

With the object of raising funds towards the pur- chase of a number of new instruments, the band of the Runcorn Companies of the Earl of Chester's Rifles organised a concert and ball which took place in the Public Hall on Monday evening. The concert was under distinguished patronage and an audience of fairly large proportions assembled, and the aim in view would be to some extent accomplished. The artistes engaged were Miss Clara Moulsdale (soprano), Miss Aimee Roland (contralto), Mr. David Williams (tenor), Mr. Frederick Owens, (basso), Mr. Joseph Cantor (buffo and humourist) and Sergeant James Wood (solo cornet). The pro- gramme was of a miscellaneous description,and the concert was one of a most enjoyable character. The band commenced with the grand selection "Nil Desper- anduin," which was performed in admirable style, and the audience testified their appreciation by prolonged applause. Miss Clara Moulsdale sangthe ballad " Kath- leen Mavourneen" in a charming manner, and in the second part of the entertainment, she rendered with much expression and pathos "Close to the threshold," and in response to an encore, contributed" Dear Little Sham- rock." The items put down to Miss Roland's name were "Sunshine and rain" and "The pretty little flower," and she rendered them with much taste and expression, although her voice was scarcely robust enough for the large hall. Mr. Fred Owens needs no introduction to Runcorn, and it will be sufficient to say he was at his best on Monday evening, and the songs "The Bells of St. Mary's" and " The storm fiend" received full jus- tice at his hands; the latter song being sung with line fire and force. Mr. David Williams is the possessor of a tenor voice clear in tone and of high register, and he delighted the audience with his rendition of" Anna- belle Lee," and "The Parting." A pretty piece of vocalisation was the duet "0 lovely peace," by Miss Monlsdale and Miss Roland and they. fully deserved the praise accorded. The duet "Excelsior," by Messrs. Williams and Owen was also roceived with great favour. Mr. Cantor loses none of his ability to amuse and enter- tain an audience and he retains all his old popularity. During the evening he contributed" Captain Dando," "A journey by rail," and "The trombone," and in response to encores gave "The happy father- land," and "Three old maids of Lee." Mr. James Woods performed the cornet solo "Alice where art thou, in which he disPlaved a musical ability and knowledge of his instrument, of the first order, and he was rapturously encored. In response he gave "In old Madrid," a short but charming solo. The concert was brought to a successful conclusion by . the quartet" Now to the banquet," by the Company, who had previouslysung the Madrigal" Strange adventure" in a most harmonious style. The room was,then cleared for dancing and the ball immediately took place. There -was a good company present, and dancing was kept up until early morn. The Volunteer band provided the music for the first part, and Mr. J. Ravenscroft per- formed the dance music on the piano for the second part. Refreshments were provided by Mr. and Mrs. Jas. Woods of the Bridge Hotel.

TUESDAY.—Before his Honour,deputy-Judge Lowe. THE LIST comprised 30 judgment summonses, 3 default summonses, 72 original plaints, and one ad- journed plaint. DUCKETT V. L.& N-W. RAILWAY CO.—George Duckett, earthenware dealer, Church-st., sued the L. and N-W. Railway Co. for £lss. 2d. compensation for damage done to earthenware in transit from Longton, in Staffordshire, to Runcorn.—Mr. Preston appeared for the Company. —The plaintiff, who was unrepresented, said the goods were consigned by Messrs. C. Harris and Co., and he paid for their carriage to the L. & N-W. Railway Co. When they arrived he found them damaged, and Mr. Scott, local goods agent, also examinedthem. He made a claim six months ago.—By Mr. Preston: Ha did not know the goods were delivered to the Midland Railway Company. He paid the L. & N-W. Railway Co. 153. per ton, and dealt with no other Company.—The goods were delivered to the L. & N-W. Railway Co.—Mr. Preston said the goods were delivered to the Midland Company, and the defendants were merely agents for that Company, and he urged that the plaintiff had not proved that the goods were delivered to the defendants.—His Honour said there was a prima facie case to answer, and as Mr. Preston had no witnesses, he gave a verdict for the plaintiff. A Punucax AND HIS MUGS.—George Duckett, earthen- ware dealer, sued James Woods, landlord of the Bridge Hotel, for 65., balance of an account for two dozen china mugs supplied.—The defendant admitted having given the order, but said the price agreed upon was 305.. and not 365. as charged by the plaintiff. Verdict for the plaintiff. CLAIM FOR THE DEATH OF A Sow.—An action was brought under, the Employers Liability Act, by Charles Edwin Houghton, of Frodsham Bridge, administrator of Charles Edwin Houghton, the younger, against Eliza- beth Reilly, The Abbey Green, Chester, and of Runcorn Bone Works Co., Sutton, for £156 damages. Mr. Parry (instructed by Messrs. A. & J. E. Fletcher, Northwich), was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Mr. John Tatlock, Chester), for the defendants.—Mr. Parry said the claim was made in respect of an accident which occurred on the premises of Mrs. Reilly, by which Houghton the younger was killed. The deceased on the 30th July was employed in the hold of flat filling tubs, which ware hoisted by means of a crane. Whilst a full tub was being raised, the deceased was Ohio.. another. Afrer seven or eight had been raised, the chain of the crane broke, and the tub fell upon Houghton and killed him. It was alleged that the chain was much worn,was defective, and unfit for the purpose for which it was used. To prevent any further similar accident at the , works, only one tub was now used. The deceased was earning about £1 a week, and lie gave the bulk of it to his father towards the expenses of the house, and his death was a serious loss. Mrs. Reilly had paid the ex- penses of the funeral, and at the time said the father would have to be compensated. Evidence bear- ing out this statement was given, and Mr. Mulholland Was about to commence his defence when the Judge said this was a case which might easily be settled, and after a conference the parties agreed to a verdict of £lO and costs. A TRADE SOCIETY CASE.—The Upper Mersey Water- men's and Porters' Association registered office,Waterloo- rd., Top Locks, Runcorn, sued M. M. Moffatt, of Church- street, .Ellesmere Port, waterman, for £25 damages for the detention of books and docments, and for their re- turn or value and for an order for the said books and , documents. Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Linaker and Linaker), was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Churton was for the defendant.—Mr. Churtan took ex- ception to the way in which the, plaintiffs had sued; they had no right to bring the action in the manner they had.—Mr. Mulholland asked for the plaint to be am- ended by adding trustees, but his Honour said he had no power to amend it and struck the case out.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THuRSDAT.—Before Lieutenant-Colonel Gaskell. MISCELLANEOUS.—Jane Drury, Mary Jane Doyle and Richard Remick were each fined for drunkenness.2John Pendergast, Joseph Caldwell. Arthur Clarke, Catherine Hynes, and Mary Ann Walsh, were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, for creating a breach of the peace.—For allowing the chimney of his house to be on fire, Wm. Stevens, beerhouse keeper, Was fined is. and costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit and Dr. Steele. AN EMINENCE ON HIS HEAD.—Frederick Gee, a youth, was summoned for assaulting a boy named Robt. Boyle, of Regent-st. On the 13th inst. the complainant was at Highfield Tannery, and the defendant accused him of tripping him on the previous Saturday. Boyle picked up a small stone to throw at defendant, when the latter threw a large stone which struck him on the head and smashed. The father said the boy had an eminence three-quarters of an inch high on his head. The defen- dant, who pleaded that he did not intend to hurt the boy, was fined ss. and costs, Bs. 6d. DRUNSENNESS.—For this offence a fine of 10s.and costs was imposed upon John Dillon, Joseph Hopkins, Thomas ' Higgins, Robert Ridley, and James Robinson.—Schofield Wifiterbottom and Thos. Millington were each fined ss. and costs, and Norah Wilson 2s. 6th and costs.

ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE.—John Brannan was charged with being drunk in Vicar-st. on Sunday night,and with assaulting P.C. Worth. It was proved that the prisoner struck the officer twice and also threatened to stab him with a knife he had in his hand. The prisoner said he had no recollection of the affair, and he was fined ss.an- costs for the drunkenness and 20s. and costs for the as sault.

div.head: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS;
div.p: WESLEYAN HOME MISSIONS;
MEETING AT RUNCORN.

The annual sermons in aid of the Wesleyan Home Missions were delivered on Sunday in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. Marshall Handles, theological tutor of Didsbury College, and there was a large congregation at both morning and evening service. On Monday afternoon the Rev. T. Champ- ness of the" Joyful News Mission,' preached to a good congregation. In the evening a public meeting was held in the chapel under the presidency of Alderman M'Kechnie of St. Helens, and there were present on the platform Rev. T. Champness, Rev. H. Burson, Rev. Pulford Williams, Messrs. F. J. Norman, J. R. Frith, John Simpson, J. Unsworth, A. Norman, Sister Josephine, of the London Mission, &c. There was a numerous attendance. In the opening proceedings, the chairman expressed his interest in Home Missionary enterprise and his pleasure at being present, and then Sister Josephine described her labours amongst the outcast in London, and in the course of her interest- ing and pathetic narrative she was frequently applauded The Rev. H. Burson read a portion of the annual report, which showed that the income for the past year includ- ing £l,OOO brought from the reserve fund, had beea £44,830. The expenditure during the same period had been £45,204. There was thus a deficiency on the year of £374. Deducting the balance of £l5 which was in hand the preyious year, the deficit on the current ac- count was £3s9.—The Rev. T. Champness delivered a speech, in which, referring to Sister Josephine, he said he would be glad if some one in Run- corn felt herself called to give herself to that kind of work in Runcorn district ; or even if five or six would give half a day each week it Would be a grand thing. (Applause.) One of the chief things Wesley impressed upon the English nation was that there was a possibility for everybody to be saved if they were outside Hell. There was a road from the edge of the bottomless pit to the throne of God. The speaker narrated a number of marvellous conversions which hadl sprung from small causes, and he urged his hearers not to be discouraged from doing the little things because they were not able to do the big things.—ln eulogistic terms Mr. F. J. Norman proposed a vote of thanks to Sister Josephine, Mr. Champness pnd Mr. Williams for their presence and addresses.—Mr. Unsworth seconded the motion, and amid much applause handed the chairman £5, which he and a few other gentle- men had raised towards reducing the deficit on Mr. Champness's mission, and the applause broke forth again when the Chairman transferred the sum to Mr. Champ- ness.—The vote was carried by acclamation.—Mr. John Simpson proposed a cordial-vote of thanks to the Chair- man for once more venturing to place himself under the influence of Wesleyan Methodism. He trusted that he had not suffered in his mind while present that evening, and he hoped no bad effects would follow from his visit. It was very pleasant to find that ministers and members of other Nonconformist churches were so ready to join with them in helping on this great work of home mis- sions. (Applause.) He should not venture to say what he thought about what had recently taken place, but one effect would be that different branches of Nonconform- ists in Runcorn would feel more willing and more ready than before to help each other forward in every way in which they possibly could. (Applause.) He did not think that the specimen of narrow-minded bigotry and exclu- siveness would do the Nonconformists any harm; what the effect might be in other respects he should not say. It was very pleasant to see ministers of other Noncon- formists bodies—and a fortnight ago to see Dr. Preston on their platform. (Applause.) He thought the more fully they. could cultivate a spirit of charity the bet- ter. Christians of various denominations ought to do whatever they could, or at all events occasionally pay each other friendly visits on the occasion of the various anniversaries and rally round each other and help each other on and try to cheer and encourage each other in

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.°

That the alteration of Waterloo Bridge, Runcorn, is approaching completion, and passers by can now have an idea of how great is the improvement that will be effected by the Surveyor, Mr. Barker. That the footpath on either side will be of ample width and pedestrians will be relieved from the trouble and danger of dodging; passing vehicles. That the road at present is in a very bad state of repair but no doubt this will now be quickly remedied. That the design of the ironwork, although plain and unpretentious, has yet a handsome appearance and Mr. Timmins, who made the drawings is to be complimented. That the Vicar of Runcorn's sermon, warning his flock against Dissenters, has aroused the Noncom- formists into unusual activity and put new life into their various organisations, so that, although it raised a great outcry, it was not an " unmixed evil."

That the Cheshire County Council having decided how they will deal with the" beer money" in aid of technical education, some interest is felt as to what course the Runcorn Board of Commissioners will take in reference to the question. That probably they will have to modify the elab- orate report presented some weeks ago, but it is to be hoped they will go in for some smaller and more feasible, yet none the less advantageous scheme. That Mr. Brunner's generous offer to contribute a sum of £5OO or any amount up to that siim provided an equal amount is obtained by subscriptions ought not to be let slit). . . . .

That the advantage of a technical school needs no demonstrating, and surely there are some public spirited gentlemen connected with the towns, willing to dip their hands in their pockets for such an object. That as the children of worl-ing men would be much benefited by the establishment of such a school, they might with justice be called upon to give according to their means, and a shilling from each householder in town would mean nearly £2OO.
That something should at least be done to have a technical school establish ed. _ _ _

That Widnes Local Board • have adopted the Widnes Science and Art School as a technical school, but it is far from meeting the requirements of the town, and application has been made to the Lanca- shire County Council for £5,000. That it is highly probable the town‘will have to be satisfied with a considerably less sum than that, but it is unlikely they will be deterred from meet- ing the needs of the town by such a result of their application. That the second annual soiree of the Runcorn Liberal Club tikes place on Monday evening next, and it promises to be a most successful affair, and to altogether eclipse that of last year. That the petition ot the Widnes Local Board praying for a Charter of Incorporation was con- sidered by tha Privy Council, on Monday, but Mr. Allen, the clerk of the Board, has up to the present, received no intimation on the matter. That before the Charter of Incorporation is granted, a Local Government Board inquiry will be held for the purpose of ascertaining the merits or demerits of the scheme.

div.p: PENKETH.
A CHURCH BAZAAR.

We understand that it has been decided to hold a bazaar on the 27th, 28th, and 29th May in con- nection with Penketh Mission Church, which is a branch of St. Mary's Church,Great Sankey. Arrange- ments are in progress and particulars will shortly be advertised.

div.head: "A Torn IN SWITZERLAND."
div.p: "A Torn IN SWITZERLAND."

Last evening week, in connection with the Wes- leyan Band of Hope, Mr. W. Silcock, of Warrington gave a lecture on a "Tour in Switzerland," illus- trated by lime-light views. There was a good at- tendance. In a very able manner Mr. Silcock gave an account of all the principal places visited during the journey, and of the objects of interest they saw while in Switzerland. A large number of excellent lime-light views of Swiss scenery, &c., were put on the sheet, the lantern being manipu- lated by Mr. H. E. Garnett. The lecture was most attentively listened to, and at the conclusion, a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Silcock was unanim- ously carried.
"COMMON SENSE V. CRITICISM."

On Wednesday evening in connection with the Mutual Improvement Association, Mr. J. Diguum read a paper on" Common sense v. criticism." The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Gandy. The essayist read several paragraphs from the writing of Mr. W. E. Gladstone and ethers en criticism. A description was given of the various books of the Bible, and the way they are pulled to pieces by the remorseless critic. Scarcely two critics have the same opinions, and examples of the different opinions of writers were given. The essayist thought most opinions were worthless, as they were so contradictory. A number of passages were quoted from different Darts of the Bible, and opinions of leading menwere also read. Mr. Dignum thought most of these high- er critics' arguments were groundless in the light of common sense. A description of the writing of Moses was dealt with, the essayist admitting that there may have been additions and alterations to the original text, but he did not think these need trouble us. Atter the paper,which had been listened to with great interest, the following gentlemen offered comment :—The Chairman, Messrs. Peers, Garnett,and White. The essayist replied.after which the meeting closed in the usual way. TEA. PARTY AND ENTERTAINMENT. On Thursday evening the annual tea party and entertainment in connection With the Young Men's Christian Association was held in the Wesleyan Schools, Penketh. There was a large .attendance. Tea was prepared and the tables were presided over by lady friends of the Association. Trays were kindly presented by Mesdames Coop,Walker,Boltou,Aitken, R. Garnett, D. Garnett, Wigfleld, Murray.houghton, and Misses Gandy, Tinsley, Taylor, and Robinson.. After tea the room was arranged for the enterta.ing n- ment,which commenced at 7.30 p.m.,the chair being occupied by. the Rev. T. E. Winder. There was an attendance of about 250 at the entertainment, the room being crowded. In the course of his opening remarksthe Rev. T. E. Winder spoke of the good the Y.M.C.A. are doing in the country, and commended the local branch to the favourable consideration of hearers. This was followed by a gymnastic perform- ance, consisting of dumb bell exercise by the mem- bers of the gymnasium. A clarionet solo was next contributed in an able mannerlby Mr H. S. Jones, accompanied by Miss Mabel Garnett. The next item on the programme was a song. by Miss Newcomb, "Bid me discourse," accompanied by Miss Eustance, for which she was recalled and gave a song, entitled "0 sea, sad sea." Miss Newcomb's contributions were thoroughly appreciated by the audience, and added greatly to the evening's enjoyment. A gym- nastic display on the parellel bars,followed by fenc- ing, was next given,the members of the gymnasium being ably assisted by Mr. A. Towers (Instructor, New Brighton Gymnasium) and Mr. H. S. Browne (Lymm), who went through some wonderful per- formances on the parellel bars. Later on during the evening these two gentlemen went through the Indian club exercises. An amusing recitation in character, entitled " Ticket of Leave," was given by Mr. A. H. Robinson. A humour sketch, entitled a "Lecture on the Phonograph" was also given by Messrs. J. A. Grounds and F. Clarkson of (Widnes) The last item on the programme was bar bell exer- cises by the members,which were gone through in a prompt and smart manner, under the leadership of Mr. W. B. Moston (teacher of the gymnasium). At the conclusion of the programme a vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies who had given trays, to Mrs. Coop, to the Rev. T. E. Winder for his services in the chair, and all the friends who had contributed to the evening's entertainment. The Rev. T. E. i Winder replied and the meeting then dispersed.

LIBERAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT. Last evening a concert in connection with the Liberal Association was held in the Wesleyan school- room, Penketh. It has been originated by Mr. John Mamley, and it was owing to his untiring exertions that the excellent programme provided was got together. There was a good attendance, the chair being occupied by: Mr. C. E. Parker. The first item of the programme was a pianoforte solo by Miss Mabel Garnet, which was gone through'in an excellent manner. A song "The miller and the maid," was next contributed by Miss Perkins. An amusing recitation "Eating a boot jack," in the Lancashire dialect was given by Mr. Furness and keenly appreciated. A song by Mr. Massey entitled "The sentinel am I," was followed by a duet "The Gibsy courcers," In Mrs. Monks and Mr. Mills the latter responding to an encore which the audience heartily demanded. ; The concluding item of the first part of the pro- gramme was a song by Miss Broulhurst, entitled "Friends," which was excellently rendered. The various pieces of the second pa 'n of the programme were contributed by Miss Broadhurst, and Messrs. MaQsey, Furniss and Mills.

div.head: .FRODSHAM.
div.p: .FRODSHAM.

HOME AND FOREIGN MISSION.-011 Sunday, s‘rmons were preached in the Methodist Free Church, Frodsham, morning and evening, by the Rev. H. Fothergill, on behalf of the above missions. The annual public meeting was held on Monday evening, when Mr. Fothergill gave an interesting address on West African Missions, which I was illustrated by lantern views. UNION CHURCH.—The second lecture relating to the history of Nonconformity was given in the Union Church, Frodsham, on Monday evening, by the Rev. John Yonge, of Warrington. The lecture embraced the most notable events which happened to Nonconformity during the reigns of James 1. and Charles 1. The lecturer depicted, the struggle in England between the High Church or Anglican party and the Puritans. Even Scotland was not free from oppression and tyranny, as an attempt was made to introduce inte the Scottish Churches a new liturgy, which was utterly defeated, A splendid collec- tion .)f lantern views was shown by Mr. Robinson, which with the lecture, were heartily enjoyed'and appreciated. THE GAS- COMPANT.—The annual meeting of share- holders was held on Thursday evening under the presid- ency of Dr. Robinson. The report stated that the revenue accounts showed a balance of £495 17s. 3id. which had been carried to profit and loss account, and ' the directors recommended the payment of a dividend of 10 per cent. onordinary shares and 7 per cent. on prefer- ence shares. After the payment of this dividend the profit and loss account would have a balance of £633 6s. 2d. to its credit.—The balance sheet showed that the sale of gas had increased during the year, but owing to the increased price of coal,the profit madelhad decreased, and to pay the dividend recommended £76 4s. 40. more than had been earned had to be taken from the profit and lass account.—The report and balance sheet was adopted and the retiring directors, Messrs.W. Whittaker and E. Imison, were elected. Mr. T. D. Tinimins was re-appointed an auditor. RELIGIOUS TRACT SOCIETY.—In connection with the missionary work of the above society, a public meeting was held in the Town Hall, Frodshatn, on Tuesday even- ing, when Mr. Thomas Rigby, of The Cedars, Sutton, occupied the chair. The other speakers were the Rev. L. B. White, D.D., rector of St. Mary's, Aldermary, London, one of the secretaries of the society, and the Rev. and Hon. R. Grimston. From the report of the secretary (Mr. S. Ormerod) of the Frodsham branch, it appeared that satisfactory progress was still being made. The deputation, Dr. White then gave an interesting 'account of the work of the society in its dealings with other micsionary societies and agencies all the world over. The Rev. R. Grimston thanked Dr. White, as the representative of the society, for the very great help which he had received from the society in the shape of grants of good literature for distribution to the Ship Canal labourers, with whom he had to do, and drew at- tention to numerous instances of men who had been greatly benefited by such.

div.head: .LT3nr.
div.p: .LT3nr.

BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting of the above-named society took place on Wednesday night. There was a good attendance. Mr. Brundritt occupied the chair. The subject of the even- ing was extempore speeches. The evening was most interesting and instructive. HOME AND FOREIGN MISSIONS —Sermons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, on Sunday, in aid of the Home and Foreign Missions by Mr. Jonah Feriday, student from the Manchester College. The congrega:ions 1 at each service were good, and collections were taken on behalf of the missionary fund. On Tuesday evening the annual meeting was held. The chief speaker was tne Rev. D. T. Alaylott, returned missionary from Africa. The recapitulation of his experiences whilst amongst the natives of the Dark Continent proved intensely interest- ing. The Chairman, Mr. G. L. Welford, and the Rev. W. Evans also spoke. The meeting was well attended. THE HISTORY OFNONCONFORMITY.—The last of a series of three lectures on the History of Nonconformity was given by the Rev. John Yonge, pastor of Wycliffe Church, Warrington, in the Congregational Church, Lymm, on Wednesday evening. There was a large and appreciative audience. The subject of the lecture was "Independency under the Commonwealth (1649-1860)" illustrated by excellent views, with the assistance of the lime-light and lantern, the latter being manipulated by Mr. Lee. of Warrington. At the conclusion of the lec- ture Mr. James Mort, proposed a vote of thanks to the Rev. Mr. Yonge and Mr. Lea for their services in con- nection with the lectures, and this was heartily ac- corded.

THE POPULAR CONCERTS.—There was again a capital attendance at the weekly concert in the Bridgewater Rooms, on Saturday evening. Mr. Theo. Nash was in the chair, and delivered an instructive address. A num- ber of boys, members of the choir of St. Peter's, Ought- rington, contributed a couple of glees very creditably. Songs were given by Misses Louie and Daisy Warburton, and Messrs. S. Joynson, E. Smith, J. E. Blakemore, G. Warburton, F. Owen, T. Warburton. Readings of an entertaining character were given by Dr. Fox and Messrs. Chorley and Hall. Miss Warburton played a pianoforte solo very nicely, and a duet between Mrs. E. Smith and Mr. Joynson received due approbation. An excellent all-round entertainment concluded by a vocal valse by the choir boys and a fine rendering of" Good- bye, sweetheart," by Mr. Owen. ZION CHAPEL, CHERRY-LANE.—The annual tea meeting in connection with the above chapel took place on Mon- day evening, the gathering being a decided success. There were about 160 present for tea,thetables being pre sided over by Mesdames W. Moston, J. Moston,Wheeler, R.Mort,E.Holt. After tea a meeting was held. Mr.Moun- field, of Warrington, occupied the chair, and delivered a short and pithy address. Recitations were given and the choir sang several pieces; and songs were also con- tributed by Miss Gallop, Miss Moston, Miss Hewitt, and Mr. R. Haseldine. An amusing dialogue, entitled " Mixem's Matrimonial Mart," was also given. The programme throughout was much enjoyed, and the pro- ceedings terminated by votes of thanks to all who had contributed to the success of the annual gathering. On Tuesday evening Mr. Joseph Mall gave a magic lantern entertainment.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. T. N. Norris (chairman), Wm. Long, Chas. Lister, and Dr. Brabazon. Havpuzi DOGS UratuzzLED.—James Marsh, and Thos. Worthington, for having their Creigs at large unmuzzled, at Lymm, the former on the 14th ult., and the latter on the 17th ult., were fined 3s. 6d., including costs, each. CHARGES OF DRUNKENNESS.—Thos. Henry Percival was charged with bein,g drunk at Lymm, on the night of the 16th ult., but the summons, not being correct, was withdrawn.—Peter Winstanley, drunk on the 14th ult., at Lvmm, was fined 2s. 6d.including costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Kelly, farm labourer, and Joseph Wilkinson, for being drunk and disorderly at Lymm, the former on the 17th, and the latter on the 31st ult., were each fined ss. including costs. ILL-TREATING t DONKEY.—Edward Emerson, aged 17, of No. 7, Back Crossley-st., Warrington, was charged with ill-treating an ass, at Lymm, en the 29th ult., by driving it whilst in an unfit state. A constable deposed to finding the defendant carting oranges about with the donkey, the animal having two bleeding wounds under the collar, and wounds,one "the size of his arm," oa the two fore-legs, also bleeding.—The defendant said he had only boughtthe donkey two days before, and it had the wounds then.—lnspector Wilson, agent to the Royal So ciety for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said he was sent for to to see the donkey in a stable off Back Crossley- street, Warrington, and he found a wound on the animal as large as the palm of his hand, and another into which he could put his finger. The donkey would not he fit for work for a month. He told the Bench that he was not anxious to be hard with the defendant, and would, if the defendant would keep the donkey in the stable till it recovered, find liniments, &c.—The case was adjourned fora month to admit of the defendant doing this, he being informed that if he put the donkey to work before the month was up he would be sent to prison. USING OBSCENE LANOI7AGE.—MaI7 Ann Jackson was charged with using obscene language at Lymm, on the 14th ult. She pleaded guilty, but said she was aggra- vated because of the constable in the case striking her brother, and attempting to strike her. The Bench told ' her her brother could have a free summons against the constable, and the magistrates would then test the truth of her accusation against him, but she expressed no readiness to accept this offer, and she was fined 2s. 64. including costs.
"CRYING EVILS."

Sir,—We are all more or less aware of the fact that a person's imagination is an extremely remarkable article, and that there are many evils which exist only in the imagination of certain people. We had yet to learn, however, what it is that constitutes a " Crying evil "in the imagination of certain great lights of Non- confcrmity. While lecturing on Nonconformity at Wycliffe Chapel on the 12th inst., the Rev. John Yenge is reported to have said that" It was a crying evil that the country rector or vicar should be able to cripple dis- senting Sunday schools by refusing children education in the week unless they attended Church School on Sun- day." This is a very comprehensive charge to make. Words very similar to these were used by the Editor of the " Methodist Times" a few weeks back,and a " country vicar " then pointed out to the Editor (in a letter which he naturally did not publish), that he wag greatly in error in stating that the coun"ry clergy did not respect the consciences of the parents of the children who at- tended their day schools. The Rev. John Yonge and some few others of his party are evidently labouring under adelusion. I do not happen to know what experience the Rev. John Yono'e has had of Church of England day schools. Having had some little experience myself,l can say that such sweeping charges are in the highest degree unjust. The lecture I refer to seems to have the same lofty sentiment running through it that we see embodied in the words of our clerical friend from Manxland—" out with Churchmen." I believe it is the duty of Nonconformist ministers occa- sionally to preach the gospel—but from an outsider's point of view there seems to be a far more noble and im- portantduty resting with them—a duty which they seem ever willing to fulfil, viz., to abuse the Church.—l remain faithfully yours. B. February 17th, 1891.

div.head: WRITERS OF THE GOSPELS.
div.p: THE WRITERS OF THE GOSPELS.

Sir,—Though loth to engage in a newspaper discussion, I have to ask your insertion of the following. I know nothing of Mr. Gandy, save from his letters, which lead me to think that he is an honest but ill-formed contro- versialist. He quotes with obvious approval a passage from an obscure writer, condemnatory of some of the best men who ever lived. If he had taken the trouble to acquire an elementary knowledge of the lives and writ- ings of either Origin or Eusebius, he would not have written as he has done. If he cannot procure the works of either, he may get some notion of their nature by visiting our reference library and consulting: the Dictionary of Christian Biography. I hold that it is wrong for any man to write on these great questions without adequate preparation; of this offence Mr. Gandy is as guilty as Mr. Peers.

There is no evidence that the Nicene Council discussed the canon of scripture, and the fable quoted by Mr. Gandy is as silly as it is untrue. His statement that the Gospels were accepted on the sole authority of Irenceus, whencesoever he derived it, is simply not true. Our existing gospels were undoubtedly used by Justin Martyr, and were accepted by many of the Gnostic sects which arose early in the second century. It is surely obvious that books accepted by both orthodox and heretics must have acquired their authority before the rise of the heresies; and I ani not aware that any modern scholar of eminence, Christian or Sceptic, doubts that our four gospels were written within forty years of the Martyr- dom of St. Paul. There is very good reason for believing that two at least of the synoptic gospels were written some years before the death if St. Paul, but the evidence for this belief is net so overwhelming as is that in sup- port of the belief that all the four gospels were written during the first century of the Christian era. Should any of your readers feel disposed to study these questions for themselves, I can recommend Dr. Salmon's frank and scholarly "Introduction to the Study of the New Testament" as an almost invaluable aid, though of course for a fuller knowledge it will be necess- ary to consult many other works. I donot know whether Messrs. 'Gandy and Peers have any prejudice against things Irish, but the Dublin Professor's " Introduction " is the best work of its kind with which lam acquainted. I commend it to their perusal, and am of opinion that if they will read it carefully, and then with equal care and greater reverence read the work it "introduces," they will not again write so rashly about subjects which they only imperfectly understand.—Yours, _&c,, February 16th, 1891
ALF. J. JOLLEY.

MR. JOHN PEERS AND ANTHROPOMORPHISM. Sir,—ln the discussion eoncerning inspiration it is highly gratifying to note the stress laid by Mr. John Peers on one qualification for the settlement of the ques- tion, viz., the necessity of possessing the "flavour of dignity, honesty, and earnestness." The Bible was written in one of the highly poetical and imaginative languages of the East. Accordingly, it is utterly impos- sible to obtain the truth which these writings were meant to convey without strict attention to the prin- ciples which regulate all such writings. This caution is equally required in reading any of the poetical composi- tions of our own day. To read a play of Shakespeare, or the" In Memoriam" of Tennyson, with literal mathema- tical accuracy would be utterly impossible; and any one who ventured to do so would soon convert the finest eompositions of our language into unintelligible burles- que. Equally, if not more so, would be the case with one who should try the same with the writings of Scrip- ture. Does not Mr. John Peersdo something of that kind when he interprets literally the word " repenting him- self" as applied to God; and in doing so does he not fall short of his own ideal—of possessing "the flavour of dignity, honesty, and earnestness" required for the in- vestigation of such subjects? It is not my intention to answer this question ; I leave it to others better qualified to do so. What I object to in ths letter of Mr. John Peers is a remark of his concerning Theism which, if true, would reverse the verdict of history, and con- vert some of the ablest and profoundest thinkers of the • past into the most consummate fools. "I shall most decidedly object," he says in his letter to Master of Arts, "to his assuming that the God of nature and the anthropomorphic God of the Jews are one and the same. I should indeed be sorry to degrade my conception of the Supreme by such an association." In this quotation there is an invidious distinction drawn between " the God of nature" and "the anthropomorphic God of the Jews "—a distinction which reminds one of the dogma- tism of an infallible authority. If Mr. John Peers only consults the literature of the subject he will find such a distinction to be one mainly of his own " creation" ; if he studies the subject with a little of the "flavour of dignity, honesty and earnestness," so much prized by him, he will find that the Theism of the Jewish religion was handed down to Christianity as one of its richest and priceless legacies. By the " God of nature" I presume Mr. Peers means the same God whom Newton, Herschell, and other eminent interpreters of nature believed in, an6l wor- shipped. Nor did they hesitate to maintain that the God whom they discovered in nature was the same with that of the Jewish Psalmist when he said" The Heavens declare the glory of God," &c. Why such a conception should prove" degrading " it is impossible to see; and with such eminent authorities in the past, one might well pause and consider whether the" degrading "conception was not one of his own "creation." Indeed, for the "degrading " conception there is not the slightest reason, unless it might arise from a consciousness of the great interval between the moral and intellectual endowments of those eminent authorities as compared with the littleness of the " flavour of dignity, honesty and earnestness "which would ven- ture a comparison. As to the question of anthropomorphism, it requires a brief consideration, considering that Mr. John Peers neither defines nor proves his statements. Originally the term Wag applied by Christians to the heathen prac- tise of ascribing the human form to their gods. Except in heathen countries, such a meaning is now obsolete. In our day it is used for the ascription to God of any of the mental and moral features which characterizes man, whether emotion, reason or conscience. Such an ascrip- tion is recorded as derogatory to God, and renders it impossible for man to know him. This argument becomes nugatory from its very de- structive nature. If it is impossible to know God because such knowledge is anthropomorphic, it is equally im- possible to know the existence of our fellow creatures, as such knowledge is also anthropomorphic. No one can see or feel the soul of a fellow creature ;we can infer its ex- istence only because he is himself conscious of possesing a soul. The sameobjection applies to the knowledge of the bodies of our fellow creatures. The child first ob- tains a knowledge of its own body and uses that know- ledge as the standard by which it realizes the existence of other bodies. Accordingly the same argument which denies to man a knowledge of God on the ground of anthropomorphism would on the same grounds exclude man from a knowledge of the bodies of his fellow crea- tures. The same argument would prove equally destructive with several of the most important branches of science. From the time of Hume it is now generally admitted that the senses do not give us the idea of power. This idea is obtained from our own exercise of activity. Such a knowledge is anthropomorphic in all conscience. Does such a knowledge preclude a man from obtaining a knowledge of the forces of nature, chemical force, elec- tric force, &c.? To do so would be to plunge into the superficialities of Positivism and drive back the progress of the ages. Mr. John Peers is still in doubt whether he should be called an Agnostic or not. It is highly- incumbent upon those who write upon such subjects that they should be able to define their own position to separate what they believe from what they do not believe. Otherwise they may attack the truth unknown to themselves. So long as there remains a distinction between the trueand false,

div.head: . . . – -.MOW •
div.p: and between the rational and irrational, so long does it remain highly questionable to attack indiscriminately the beliefs of others. With such a statement, Mr. John Peers should find no fault, for in the discussion of these impor- tant questions his own demand is that a man should be imbued with the "flavour of dignity, honesty, and earnestness. "—I am, Sze., February 9th, 1891.
VERITAS.
INSPIRATION AND REVELATION.

"As incredible praises given to men do often abate and im- pair the credit of their deserved commendation, so we must likewise take great heed lest, by attributing to scripture more than it can have, the incredibility of that do cause even those things which indeed it hath abundantly, to be less reverently esteemed."—Hooker.

Sir,—Mr. Peers says that if we found Euclid affirming that parallel lines would meet if continued far enough, we should not place much confidence in the succeeding propositions. To which I would reply that we could rightly withhold our confidence only from such proposi- tions as were based on the mistake. When the mis- taken conclusion ceased to apply, at that point our judgment would act independently of it. And so with 1 the Bible. Its science is not an integral part of its reli- gious system. To find men speculating on the ori- gination of the physical world is but to re-discover an ineradicable tendency of the human mind. I have seen somewhere a painting in which a chick is looking with thoughtful eyes into the broken shell he has just quitted. That is precisely the attitude of men towards the remote past, an attitude which has characterised them in all ages. Why the Creator should wink at the times of our ignorance it may not be easy to understand. But I think I do see some- thing in the nature cif a sound answer to the question. My plea is that of urgency. Correct knowledge of the origination of things could wait: its pursuit would be a profitable occupation of the creature : his welfare depended to a comparatively slight extent on such knowledge. But that he should know of the existence of a Creator, to whom be was responsible for the right use and control of his life—that was urgently necessary. And is not moral truth incomparably more valuable to a man than physical truth? Without the one life is purely animal at the best : without the other the in- tellect is but robbed of a portion of its best food. And so the revelation was made in such terms as man could grasp, and one nation at least emerged from the chaos of the prehistoric past with the revealdd truth held in a tenacious grasp, to be developed with a swiftness and power which to my mind are simply amazing. In the light of their purer knowledge they moulded existing theories of creation ; and just because they ascribed the creation of all things to their God,their theory, crystaliz- ing round its centre into a firm belief,being committed to writing, was passed on as a purely divine inspiration. But surely God is not to be held responsible for all men's theories about His werks. And to say that because we have in Genesis accounts of the origin of man and things prior to his appearance on earth the claim to divine inspiration is necessarily involved is to open the way to some strange conclusions. For instance, does not any modern cosmogony involve the same claim? Indeed, a fortiori, the most modern should be the most necessarily inspired, as being further in point of time from the creation ! which is (as dear old Euclid would say) absurd. The anthrcpomorphism of the Bible is excessive, but it is nothing Imre. We can interpret the unknown only in terms of the known, and therefore the highest and best unknown in terms of the highest and best known. And with all his faults, man with his intellect, affections, and other powers, is the supreme work of nature, and therefore mu.,t necesarily supply the terms in which his theistic conceptions must be expressed. The Hebrew did this by spiritual intuition, and how true that intuition was is seen in its emphatic ratification in Christ's teaching about the Fatherhood of God. What change or development will take place in our conceptions and terms depends upon the question as to narrowness or breadth of the limits of our finitude. "Now are we the I sons of God; and it doth not yet appear what we shall be." What remains for us to know of God is the corre- late of what we know: how much we know it is impos- sible to say. It is here, I think, that our modern high- soaring Agnostic Philosophy breaks its wings and falls to the ground. The " Unknowable " is altogether incon- ceivable, and there is only one thing that is incon- ceivable, and that is (to use an Hibernicism) Nothing! Therefore the Unknowable and Nothing are identical ? Precisely! The Unknowable has no existence. To call it such is to know it—to know that it is unknowable! Once more the lean kine devour the well-favoureel, well- fed, fat kine ! And so I accept the anthropomorphic conceptions of the Jew as the best possible under our pre- sent finite human conditions. That he imported into it some of the weaknesses as well as the strength of human nature does not destroy the truth of the conception. In- deed it is wonderful to my mind that on the whole the Jewish anthropomorphic ideal is so lofty, compared with the bestial attributes of Hellenic divinities, to say nothing of the abominations enthroned and worshipped by Phcenician, Assyrian, Babylonian, and other oriential peoples of remote antiquity. Amongst them the purity, the righteousness, the mercy of Jehovah, shine out in marvellous splendour. The Hebrew sage may declare that God has repented Him of His wrath ; the expression was one that the people could understand and appreci- ate ; but that no possibility is even imagined that Jehovah could be impure, untrue, unjust, or unmerciful is to me surpassingly wonderful, considering the times and the environment of the Jewish nation.

Then with regard to the matter of the Bible may we pick and choose? We not only may: we must. We refrain at our peril. Our deeper life depends on it. There is a moral as well as a natural selection. There are tares among the wheat,—tares unwholesome, nay, tares poisonous! It is the will of the All-Wise that they grow together until the harvest. But the goodness which has taught the humble brute to avoid the noxious herb teaches us to avoid the moral tare. The moral sense abhors the bloodthirstiness of David, the voluptu- ouseess of Solomon, and the worldliness of the writer of Ecclesiastes. Even the firmest believer in verbalinspira- tion involuntarily yields the principle of selection when he hires another to cut, grind, and bake his spiritual corn. How fiercely he kicks out if he tastes a fancied poisonous ingredient! God consents to be judged by us, and in our very examination of Him he vindicates Himself by enlarging the nsoral understanding. Indeed, the supreme function of religious teaching and enquiry is to widen and clarify the moral sense; and the process must go on until we know even as we are known. Believing this, I was very careful to say, in the penul- timate paragraph of my first letter' that it was Logic and not I that would deny to the Agnostic (the term was not used reproachfully) the right of decision in things inspired or otherwise. Our mental body will not always submit to the strait-jacket of logic. Thus a man may deny the presence ef the atmosphere without ceas- ing to breathe it ; and so also with regard to his spiritual environment. We cannot shut God out, ignore or deny Him as we will. Through ears and eyes, through brain and heart He comes in and takes possession; in Him we live and move and have our being, and all our springs are in Him. The Agnostic may deny Him a name, but he can do nothing more. And if he keeps his heart pure the mephitic vapours of wrong and immorality are as obnoxious to him as to the Christian. And the purer his spiritual air, the more distressful will the impure be. Now the purest spiritual, moral air is the atmosphere of Christ ; there for me Inspiration begins; and whether I travel backward or go forward from Him in the mines of Biblical literature I can tell by the flickering of tke lamp which he has lighted, when I am in the presence of foul after-damp, and air unwholesome and unclean. Mr. Peers has spoken kindly of me, and I thank him, for as coming from him the tribute is welcome. He is personally unknown to me, but his letters of some years in your paper have always seemed to me to bear the im- press of an honest and a thoughtful mind. Honesty is above all price. It is the indispensable condition of all knowledge, even the highest. Does not Christ say—" If any man willeth to do the will of God he shall know of the doctrine whether it be of God ?" To love truth is to be assured of finding it. I trust lam not giving expres- sion to that subtle egotism which leads us to try to make our neighbours agree with us in opinion. Ido not seek a victory; I seek truth. And so, I am convinced does my friend. Our supreme need is Light in this ever- pressing darkness. And we are but

- - "As infants crying in the night; As infants crying for the light ; And with no language but a cry." At the best we are but watchers—and it may be that my friend is in the third or fourth watch of the night, and I but in the first or second—but we have eyes, and they argue the Light : the dawn therefore must come, and its advent will be our exceeding great reward.—Yours &c., MASTER OF ARTS
