div.head: 11 11 E EXAMINER SATUPDA-tY, FEBRUARY 21, 1891
div.p: 11 11 E EXAMINER SATUPDA-tY, FEBRUARY 21, 1891

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. I DRUNK.—Margaret Kelly, a Crewe woman, charged with being drunk the previous night, at Marketgate, was dismissed. THVESDAY.—Before Aldet man Sutton (chairman) and Captain Ridgway. DESERTION FROM THR ARTILLBRY.—CharIes Burns charged with deserting from his artillery regiment, stationed at Woolwich, was remanded to Walton jail to await an escort.

THE CHARGE OF RUFFIANLY ASSAULT BY A NAVVY. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, James White, Ship Canal labourer, of Latchford, was brought up on remand charged with committing, on the 7th inst., a most brutal assault upon Thomas Kelly, a fellow lodger, also employed on the Ship Canal. The prisoner had been remanded because the complainant was lying at the In- firmary, his conveyance to which place had been necessi- tated by his injuries. The defendant now denied the charge. He was remanded for another week to Wal- ton jail, where he had already been a week, the com- plainant being still unable to leave the Infirmary.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNEFIDAY.—Before Messrs. G. Rylands (chairman) and G, Comber. DRUNK.—Thomas Johnson, drunk on the Ist inst., in- Liverpool-road, Great Sankey, and John Shaw, drunk on the Bth inst., at Penketh, were each fined ss. and costs. A DISORDERLY GANG. —James Floyd, Charles Purshaw, Geo. Gowland, John Bradshaw, John Tyndall, and Geo. Tyndall,were charged with being disorderly at Fernhead, the night of the Bth inst. Two constables gave evidence, from which it appeared that they had been guilty of the most disgraceful rowdyism, frightening the whole village; their behaviour indeed being the village talk for several days. Several young men had complained to the con- stables about having been assaulted by the defendants, one of them bleeding in the face, and being without his hat. They had been at the Farmer's Arms at Fernhead, and one of the constables found in a ditch an almanack which was missing from the Farmers' Arms after they left. Floyd had a hat in his hand, thaugh it proved not to be a hat which had been knocked off the head of one of the young men who had been assaulted. They were making a considerable noise.—Wm. Weston said he was coming from Fernhead ' about ten o'clock on Sunday night, and one of the defen- dants, who belonged to Warrington,came with him about 200 yards. As they passed some men, he stopped, and one of them struck him in the face and knocked his hat off. He could not identify any of these men as it was pitch dark. He found his hat.—Henry Bate said he was at the Farmers' Arms on the Bth inst., and left about 10 o'clock. There were a lot of men standing in the road, "falling out " about something, and they knocked him down and cut his head, tore his jacket, and pulled his necktie to pieces ; arid he lost his hat. He could not identify the men, but he saw some of them in the Far- mers' Arms.—Bradshaw, to account for his conduct, stated that two men had pulled his watch out of his pocket and broken his chain.—Purshaw was the only one of the defendants who pleaded not guilty: and they were bound over in the sum of £5 each to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs. RAILWAY OFFENCEL—James Blackburn was charged with passing on the 4th inst, near Glazebrook Station, over the Cheshire Lines Committee's railway otherwise than by the crossing, after having been warned to the contrary. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the prosecution. The defendant was fined 10s. and costs.
THEFTS FROM THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE'S WORKS.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, John Smith and Alfred Lee, a boy-aged 14, were charged with stealing on Saturday afternoon, from the railway siding near Lythgoe's-lane bridge, a quantity of old iron, value 9s. 3d., the property of the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee, also with having stolen a day or two previously from the same place, a quantity of cow horns, value ss.—Mr. Simpson, of the Cheshire Lines detective de- partment, appeared on behalf of the Committee for the prosecution, and said that on Friday a quantity of cow horns were missed, and on Saturday the Inspector caught the two prisoners taking the scrap iron from the siding and placing it against the wall to be thrown over in order to be carted away.—lnspector Wood corrobo- rated this statement, and said he handed the prisoners over to the custody of P.S. Johnson.—Mary Barton, marine store dealer, deposed to the prisoners coming to her place with some scrap iron for sale, on Thursday.— Mr. Simpson said the elder prisoner had been driven away from the yard on three or four occasions.—Smith was sent to gaol for 14 days in each case, and Lee, being too old to be birched, was ordered to be detained in the Bride- well till six o'clock the following night.
DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Freaeria Conroy, drunk and disorderly, at Collins Green, Burtonwood, on the 7th inst., was fined ss. and costs.
RIDING A BICYCLE ON THE FOOTPATIL—WaIter Brough, baker, for this offence at Great Sankey,on the 12th inst., was fined is. and costs.

DISCHARGING A GUN TOO PUBLICLY.—Henry Gotley,for firing a gun within 50 feet of the centre of the highway, at Martinscroft, on the 3rd of January was fined Is. NOT HAVING A HORSE UNDER CONTROL.-401H1 Wearing for being too distant from his horse and cart near Padgate Railway station, on the 9th of January, was fined is. and costs.
DISORDERLY.—Thomas Scarey, for being disorderly on Sunday night last, was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six 'months, and ordered to pay the costs.

BREACIMS or THE SANITARY AcT.—James Gleave was charged by Mr. Kerfoot, Inspector to the Rural Sanitary Authority, with having the drainage of certain cottages at VVoolston in an unsanitary state, and William Booth, agent there for Horsfield's estate,was charged with a like offence. Orders were made for the abatement of the nuisances within 21 days.

line, and after a protracted maul with two opponents, only a minor was secured. After this, Knowles, Thorn- ley, Isherwood, and Holcroft rushed to the Swinton 25, where Rowe got away, and passing to Lawless a try was scored, but disallowed. Half time arrived with only a minor scored. The brief rest evidently had an inspiring influence on the homesters, for they began to attack with a persistency that was rewarded by Rowe scoring a try, a tter Daniels had carried the ball to the line. Harris got into a sprint, but the advantage was not great, until a fine dribble headed by Holker and Harris forced the ball to the Warrington end and a minor secured. Then Jolley put in a fine bit, and Greenall. although tackled by a couple of opponents, relieved his lines. After this Edge by a run and kick got into the home ground, but I Lawless and Sampson completely nullified any advant- age by some telling kicks. Barnes then missed a chance after rapid following up, and Mather, Rowe and Daniels ran the leather to the line, whilst immediately afterwards Sampson nearly dropped a goal, and another minor was conceded, after a very smart piece of play by Randles. Ensuing play found the combatants on the home line, Knowles effecting a fine relief, a rush by Thornley, Craghan and Isherwood improving matters, but a loose dribble by Swinton ended in a minor, and the game ended Warrington 0-1-6 to 0-0-2. Teams: War- rington—Sampson, full back; Daniels, Jolley, P. R. Lawless, three-quarters ; Rowe and Mather, half-backs'; Thornley, Molyneux. Cragan, Knowles, Barnes, Phillips, Holcroft, Randles and Isherwood, forwards. Swinton— Greenall, full back; Batty, Marsden, and Randle, three- quarters ; Edge and Harris, half-backs ; Holker,Mannion, Walker, Lomax, Chapman, Parkinson, Sackfield, Hulme, and Horrocks, forwards. WARRINGTON v. SWINTON.

The return match between the above clubs took place at Swinton on Saturday. Since Warrington so uneN- peotedly lowered the Swinton colours on September 20th, the match in question has been awaited with in- terest, and it was no wonder that en arriving at the Swinton enclosure there was found a company number- ing considerably over five thousand. Like Warrington, neW talent has been introduced in the Swinton ranks,and their smart victory over Huddersfield the week previous had a tendency to establish the homesters favourites for the present conflict. However, there were not wanting those who preferred the chances of the Warringtonians , and the small crowd which accompanied their favourites made their presence heard as regards cheering, when oc- casion required. Both sides were strongly represented,and as Mr. Payne, who had been announced to act as referee, was indis- posed, Mr. Lord handled the teams, and at 3.30, Valen- tine kicked off with the advantage of the slope. James Bate made his mark, and the oval found a resting-place at the half-way flag. Sharp passing by the Swinton half-bac \ts was more than neutralized by the two Bates and Barn es, the latter with excellent judgment giving his side a footing well inside the Swinton quarters. Bumby again got clear, but this time Evans was an ob- stacle not to be passed, and the oval travelling across to Winterbottona, Webster at the second attempt luckily staved off the attack. Barnes got beautifully away,and the Warrington centre's judgment served his team in good stead, for kicking and following up, being ably se- I conded by Jolley, Berry, and Ashton, half-way was the scene of operations. It was now plainly to be seen that whichever side was returned the victors would have to accomplish the task by mere hard work. Both sides strained every nerve to obtain a point, but the defence was admirable, whilst the forwards worked like Trojans' and whereas the Swinton men had the advantage in rushing, the visitors more than counterbalanced the efforts by screwing the pack and their smart following up. After a spell of even, though exciting, play, James Bate got away on the reserve side, but the home for- wards getting the better of a pack, rushed to the visit- ing quarters, Winterbottom almost gettinc, in after a zig-zag run. A clever piece of play by Pearson saved his side, but Donohue came away a moment later, but kicked a trifle too hard in his final essay. The half- way flag was reached, and the visitors' position was further improved by a useful kick by James Bate. A sequence of passes between James Bate, Barnes, and Webster gained a little ground, and Valentine with a strong run and kick took the oval back to neutral territory, but the visiting forwards, all working with a will, soon had the oval back at the Swinton twenty-five. Fair Turner, Jolley. and Holmes each in turn became prominent with indi- vidual efforts, but a fine piece of combination among the Swinton men placed the Warrington goal in jeopardy. J. T. Bate on two occasions cleared finely, and although he reached Pearson on one occasion, the Swinton custo- dian was safe. James Bate next tricked Bumby, and Swinton were once more defending, until a spelt nt pas- sing by Brockbank, Valentine, and Murray looked like ending in a tangible score until Webster came upon the scene and deposited the Swinton man in touch a yard from the line. A fine run by Evans was further aug- mented by a sterling display on the part of James Bate, and the short passing by the visiting forwards for a time nonplussed the homesters, and the oval was again worked to the Swinton end. Brockbank and Bumby soon had the ball back again, and Jolley coming away from the ruck followed up quickly, preventing Bumby from reply- ing. Barnes put in a couple of fine kicks, and again cleared his lines in fine style, and another clever tackle of Bumby by Jolley saw the game at neutral ground. The Swinton men resorted to the rushing game to save their lines, and Davies saving in daring style, the whistle then sounded for the interval with not a point scored. Frank Turner restarted, and Povey and Donohue drib- bling well, Valentine came up in the nick of time and cleared, a smart kick sending the oval to midfield. James Bate and Jolley each showed up with individual efforts, but a fine piece of combination by the Swinton front division placed the home supporters on good terms, but foul tactics penalized the colliers. Fair Turner's kick gained but little, and it was left to Frank Turner and Holmes to rush the leather through the opposing defence, their career not being stayed until the Swintox quar- ters were reached. A couple of apparent chances of scoring were now missed by Warrington, and a pass from Barnes to Webster saw the latter preferring to drop at goal, a minor only accruing. Jolley and Ashton each made a fine, though futile effort and from a kick by Valentine, Boscow was now called upon to show his kicking powers for the first time. A shore run and screw kick into touch showed he was equal to the emergency, and a combined movement, in which Davies and the brothers Turner were the leaders, was responded to by Bothwell, Lomox, and Hallam. J. T. Bate ran and dodged to within reach of the line, when he passed to Jolley, who failed to gain a proper grip of the oval, or a I score would certainly have resulted. The Swinton men I relieved their supporters of any anxiety when Brockbank land Bumby having a trifle the better of James Bate— r who had a minute previously received a nasty knock— worked the oval out of danger, and though Valentine made several efforts to break away, he was foiled by the , accurate tackling of Barnes and Evans. A long pass I from Brockbank saw Murray taking play near the War- rington line, and then Bumby getting away, both Barnes and Webster met the ex-county half-back, with the Iresult he passed to Valentine, and as all opposition had been removed, the Swinton captain ran over, and scored near the corner flag. The same player took the kick at goal without success. Murray nearly got in a moment later, but Evans proved as safe as a bank, and Barnes being prominent with relief, Holmes tackled Winterbot- tam near the centre flag. Ashton made a final effort, but the Swintonians stayed a trifle the better, and in the end won a grand game by a try to a minor. 'reams :—Warrington : J. Boscow, back; J. E. Evans, T. Barnes, and H. Webster, three-quarter backs; James , Bate, and J. T. Bate, half backs; Fair Turner, Frank Turner, H. Ashton, W. Berry, J. Jolley, T. Davies, James Holmes, W. Povey, and T. Donohue, forwards. Swin- ton: Pearson, back; W. Winterbottom, 3. Valentine, and H. Murray, three-quarter backs; W. Bumby and H. Brockbank, half backs; N. Hotchkiss, F. Lomax, T. Bothwell, T. Hallam, Powell. A. Sharpies, G. Sharpies, S. Hall, and W. Evans, 'forwards. Referee, Mr. Lord.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Mr. R. Garnett. _

A YOUNG THIEF.—A lad, 12- years of age, named Michael Lawler, of 48, Hardy-st., was charged with having stolen wearing apparel from the premises of Frank Conolley, 69, Lythgoes-lane ; Thomas Worral. Chester- st., and Thomas Waghorn, 169, Winwick-rd. The articles which had been placed on a clothes line to dry had been taken by the prisoner and afterwards pawned. It was ordered that the lad should be detained in gaol three days and receive six strokes of the birch rod each day. DRUNKENNKSS.—EIizabeth Hedley, was sent to gaol for 14 days for having been drunk and disorderly in Wilder- spool-road on Friday night. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor, Mr. R. W. Francomb (chairman) and Alderman Harrison. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—There were the following convictions for this offence :—Joseph Clare, in Dial-st., on Saturday night, Mary Lee, in Edelston's yard, the same night, Catherine Longshaw, and Charlotte Glover on School Brow, on the 7th inst., all fined ss. and costs. —Michael Riley, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-et., en Saturday night, also with assault- ing Elizabeth Rawlinson, was sent to prison for a month's hard labour.

DISORDERLY AND REFUSING TO QUlT.—Michael Melia, apprehended under a warrant, was charged with being disorderly and refusing to quit the Packet House beer- house also with fighting in Mersey-st., on the 4th inst. Mr. A! Browne, solicitor, appeared for the prosecution, and the circumstances of the case, as detailed by him on Monday week, when he applied for a warrant, have already appeared in our columns. The man was now fined 20s. and costs, with the alteraative of a month's hard labour.

REMOVING GOODS TO AVOID DISTELAINT.—MichaeI Rabbit charged with clandestinely removing his goods during the night of the 7th inst. to avoid distraint for 16s. 9d. rent, was ordered to pay the amount and the costs, or go to prison for 14 days. A DISORDERLY YOTTR.—lhomas Musgrove, a boy, for being disorderly on Sunday night, in Church-st., was fined 2s. ed. and costs.

S LAUGHTHRING WITILOUT LICENSIL—WiIIiam Shutt, was charged by Mr. Norman, Inspector of Nuisances, with slaughtering without a license on his premises, 38 Rawlinson-st., on the 9th inst.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defence. Mr. Norman deposed to finding a butcher killing a pig for the defendant at the place and on the day named, and to the place being unlicensed. Mr. Browne said his client had used the premises for 20 years as a slaughterhouse, and had not the slightest idea that a license was necessary ; and contended that the Act did not apply to the present case, as the place was not used continuously as a slaughterhouse and as it had not been proved that the carcase was to be cut up for sale. His client promised that he would not slaughter there again. —The defendant was fined ss. and cost.

STREET GAMBLING.-Henry Gesling, Frederick Gosling and Win. Gosling, brothers, and all boys, were charged with playing a game of chance in a yard off Winwick- road, on Sunday morning week. As there was T. doubt as to whether the yard was not wprivate one, the Bench dismissed the case.

ILL-TREATING A.N Ass.—Benjamin Scott, of Runcorn, was charged with ill-treating an ass by working it while in an unfit state on the sth inst. A constable said tho donkey, with another, was drawing a load of scrap iron, and on it a wound about the size of the ball of his hand had formed against which a rope by which the animal was attached to the cart,was continually chafing, causing it great pain. The defendant was fined the costs; in default seven days. ALLOWING HORSES TO STAND.— Henry Draper, for allowing two horses and carts to stand longer than necessary in Market-st., on the 11th inst., and James Marsh and Michael Owen for like offences in Butter- market-st. on the same date were each fined the costs.— Frames Williams, a little girl,for leaving a coal truck on the footpath in Battersby-lane on the night of the 11th inst., was fined is. including costs. UNSANITARY Otrinumnisus.—James Finn, John Stan- way, and Ann Patten were charged by Mr. Norman,with not keeping certain closets in Math yard in a proper sanitary condition, and were fined 2s. 6d. each. DESERTING FROM THE ARTILLERY.—WiIIiam Hall was charged with deserting on the 14th of January last, from the Royal Artillery stationed at Gosport. Theconstable who gave evidence against him said his attention was directed to him by seeing him walk so straight ; and from a conversation he had with him he was led to take him into custody. The prisoner said he was on fur- lough from the date in question to the present day.—The Mayor: Has not he a perfect right to walk with a straight back through the streets ? It seems an un- fortunate thing to have a straight back.—Alderman Harrison : Better than having a crooked one.—The Mayor: I don't know. You are not so liable to be dealt with by the police.—The prisoner was remanded for 48 hours.—The Constable: I beg most respectfully to apply for the usual reward.—The Mayor : You don't know that he is a deserter yet. Wait and see. CHIMNEYS ON FIRE.—Ann Thomas was charged with wilfully setting fire to her chimney in Wash-lane, Latch- ford, on the morning of the 10th inst. She denied that she intentionally set it on fire. She was fined is.— Ellen Stuart, for having her chimney on fire on the 11th inst., was fined is.

PUTTINOICLOTHES LINES ACROSS A THOROUGHFARE.— Mary Baguley and Catherine Rawlinson charged with putting up clothes lines in Dial-court, were cautioned and dismissed, the Bench fully appreciating the diffi- culties which they pleaded that they had in finding a dryimg ground.
TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman), E. M. Crosfield, and E. J. Guest.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WiIIiam Stokes, plumber;of 77, Bay Horse-yard, for being drunk and disorderly in that yard, on Saturday night, was fined the costs Bs. 6d. DISORDERLY YOUTHS: THE STICK THE ONLY REMEDY.— Charles Fudge and James Sergeant, boys, apprehended under a warrant, were charged with being disorderly in Church-st., on Sunday night week. Fudge was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and Sergeant was fined 2s. 6d.—ln conn ection with the case a Fudge, whose demeanour in Court was exceed- ingly pert and saucy, Chief Constable Hunt said the police could not use a stick as they formerly did because if they did they would be proceeded against according to law. A good stick would do ttiese boys more good than bring- ing them before the magistrates. Parents seemed to have no control over their children as they formerly had. The defendant he noticed as soon as he got into the box was hard and old, indeed a great deal more so than some who were 50 years of age.—The Chairman said he quite agreed with Mr. Hunt that if an officer had permission to judiciously use the stick it would be a great blessing. He had no sympathy with the sentiment that was goinv, about now-a-days that children should not be touched because of their parents; and if the defendant had a good hiding with a eat-o-nine-tails it would be the best thing that could be done with him. Addressing the boy, the Chairman said: I don't know what you are looking for- ward to, my lad. To judge by your appearance and the face you carry, and the tongue you use, you look as if you were bidding fair fora felon. You are going on the way for ruin.—The defendant declared he was out of the town on the night in question, and his stepmother ex- claimed the same thing in Court. Smoot, CASES.—Mr. G. Riley obtained the following - convictions for non-attendance of children at school : Edward Murray, forgeman, Peter Clough, labourer, 3, School-brow, William Burton, forgeman, 57, Catherine- st., all fined 55.; Thomas Knockton, 27, Erwood-st., John Weaver, forgeman, 18, Blue Coat School-st., and James Travis, forgeman, Haydpck-st., each fined 2s. 61.—1 n the case of Mary Ann Holmes such abject poverty was pleaded on her part, that the child as to whom she was charged, a boy, was ordered to be taken to the Work- house, where, the Chairman remarked, he would be obliged to attend school. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman),

and Mr. J. Fairclough. THE CHAIIGE AGAINST AN ARTILLERYMAN.—WiIIiaM Hall, remanded on Monday, was brought up charged with deserting from the Royal Artillery, stationed at Gosport. His statement that he was on furlough now proved to be correct, but it appeared that his furlough was confined to Manchester, and therefore he had DO right to come to Warrington. He was remanded to Walton jail to await an escort.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.
THATTO HEATH T. 1117INCOUN RECREATION.—These teams met on Saturday afternoon, and after a good match Run- corn won by a goal and a try to two ,tries and two minors.

Si. HELENS RECREATION " A " v. WIDNES Sr. MARY'S.— This match was played at Widnes on Saturday. St. Mary's pressed throughout the game and won easily. Hardman, Kelly, Clarke, and Burgess were the scorers. The final result was: St. Mary's, 3 goals, 2 tries, and 7 minors, to Recreation " A" nil.

LOWTON v. WIDNES VicToara.—These teams met on the ground of the former, before a good number of spectators, on Saturday afternoon. Lowton played up in 'fine form in. the first half, .and scored a try and a minor to the visitors' nil. After change of ends, Low- ton again kept up their form, and scored two more tries, to the visitors one dropped goal. At the close the score stood Lowton 3 tries 7 minors, Widnes, Victoria 1 dropped goal. Smith, Talbot, and Fearnley were the try getters or the home team. WARRINGTON RANGERS v. HALTON VIEW.—The return fixture between these teams was played at Widnes on Saturday. The home team smarting under the reverse of last week got together a very strong team, in hopes of turning the tables upon the Rangers, but the latter again showed surprisingly good form, and in the first portion of the game, after smart play by Clare and Plinston, Edwards scored a clever try which Potts failed to improve. The homesters tried hard to equalize, but could only force a minor. During the second half the visitors penned their opponents, and from a pass Clare lewered the home team's citadel with a capital drop, the Rangers eventually coming out of the fray victors by 1 goal. 1 try, 4 mindh, to Halton View 2 minors. RUNCORN v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.—Owing to nine of the Cheshire men being selected to take part in the county fixture, Cheshire v. Yorkshire, the Runcornians had to meet the Broughton Rangers on Saturday with a mixed team, for the most part taken from the second string, in the presence of about 3,000 spectators. Jack- son, on behalf of the home team, commenced the play, but the ball was successfully returned by Hughes. Then followed even play, Pendlebury being well up in his duties, and preventing a rush which at one time looked serious. Robinson put in a well-timed punt into touch, and subsequently checked a rush on the part of the Broughtonians. Wheeler raised the spirits of the spectators by a neat run, which, however, was more than equally met by a capital punt into touch. The ball was then taken by the Runcornians well into the home team's 25, and a minor resulted. Later on Storer, of the home team, obtained a try from a rush by the home team's forward's, and a goal was kicked by Hibbert. The play throughout was of an enjoyable character, and at the finish of the game, the Broughton Rangers had secured a goal, whilst Runcorn's share was one try, two minors.

Wins v. STOCKPORT.—This fixture was played off at Widnes on Saturday afternoon, before about 2,000 spec- tators. The"home team at once commenced to attack, and some excellent play was witnessed amongst the Widnes backs, consequent upon the splendid passing of Evans and Drummond. Peters, after short sprints several times, had hard lines in getting over, and Widnes continuing the pressure, a minor was conceded to them. Shortly after the drop-out Evans passed to Drummond, and the latter to Peters, who, after a splendid run, got over, but Barber failed at goal. A penalty kick having been accorded to Widnes, theyagain pressed, and another minor resulted. Brennan was next conspicuous with some good play, an forced a minor. Smith passed to Peters, who, after a splendid run, lost possession of the ball just as he was crossing the line. Evans, however, was near at hand, and did the peedful. Gordon failed at goal. Peters again got away, and later Barber, from a pass from Drummond, crossed the Stockport line amid much excitement. Brennan this time landed, a goal. When play was recommenced, Stockport, by a aesperate effort, carried the ball to the home quarters, but Peters relieved by a grand run to the visitors' 25. Stockport kept up the pressure, and by some excellent passing Ogden got over. Potts, however, failed at goal. En- couraged by this Stockport played up well, and after some hard play, succeeded in forcing a minor. At half- , time the score was—Widnes, 1 goal, 2 tries, and 3 minors; Stockport, 1 try and 1 minor. On changing ends the excellent combination of the Widnes team in the former part of the game seemed 6 o fall away, and con- sequently their efforts in the seco/Jd half were not so successful as in the first half. Widnes, however, had the lbest of the game, and forced two minors. The game ended with the score as follows :—Widnes, 1 goal, 2 tries, and 5 minors; Stockport, 1 try and 1 minor. WARRINGTON A v. SWINTON A.—A good number of spectators had assembled round the Wilderspool enclosure when Isherwood started the ball, and for a few minutes the venue of the struggle lay near the Centre, until by the instrumentality of Daniels, Phillips, and Barnes, the scene of warfare was changed to the Swinton line. The ivisitors returned to the home 25, but Jolley was con- spicuous twice in succession, intercepting passes and ilreaching midfield, and being supplemented with a drib- ble by Bandies, the visiting custodian was floored at his own quarter flag. A lot of time was then taken up in Ipacks and scrambling play, but eventually Jolley got grandly away, and his pass not being taken, the ball was forced from the dangerous proximity to the Swin- ton goal. This was neutralized by Molyneux,Thornley, Cragan, and Knowles, but Harris relieved effectually, and Warrington quarters were reached. Daniels then bested Batty for posession, and ran finely ,to the line, and although the ball was passed and repassed no try was secured, the ensuing bouts enabling Swinton to get away to neutral ground. ,A magnificent run by Lawless from Bandies' pass was cheered to the echo but a minor was all that was obtained. Following die drop out, Sampson shone conspicuously, and after Molyneaux had had an effort for a try, a rare bit of exciting play took place, to the advantage of the homesters Some very effective work by 4olyneux, Holcroft, and Knowles at midfield, was then witneqsed, • and directly afterwards Phillips headed rat'linz dribble. Here Mather made a most run through his opponents, carrying the dval over •

PENNE= FRIENDS' SCHOOL v. WARRINGTON RESERVE.- -This match was played at Warrington on Saturday. Penketh kicked off, and soon attacked the home goal, Robinson scoring after ten minutes' play. Laurence added number two, and Hills soon after notched a third. Half-time came with score five to nil in favour of Penketh. In the second" forty-five" the visitors did all the press- ing, and scored five more. Warrington notched a point, and the game ended—Penketh 10, Warrington 1. The scorers for Penketh were Charnock (1), Laurence (1), Hill (2), and Robinson (6.) The visiting half-backs and backs played a sound game, MeTear, White, Wane, Jolley, and T. Charnock fairly out-classing their heavy ,opponents.

div.head: BATTLE IN CHILI.
div.p: BATTLE IN CHILI.

DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNMENT TROOP. LIMA, WEDNESDAY.—lntelligence has reached here that a battle has taken place at Iquique between the insur- gents and the Chilian Government troops,in which, after a severe fight, the latter were completely defeated. The insurgents now occupy Iquique, and have a sufficient force to preserve order. From Iquique operations will be commenced against Valparaiso.

div.head: CHILD MURDER BY A FATHER.
div.p: CHILD MURDER BY A FATHER.

At Lampton, near Hounslow, on Wednesday, Alfred James Bartlett, a wheelwright, strangled his infant daughter Rosina, aged five months, by tying a brick round its neck, while the mother had gone downstairs to light the fire. Bartlett, who afterwards told his wife what he had done, is believed to be demented, and on Tuesday seemed very depressed all day. He was re- moved to the Hounslow Police Station.

div.head: CANADIAN ELECTION.
div.p: CANADIAN ELECTION.
GREAT EXCITEMENT.

Intense excitement prevails in Toronto in connection with the elections. Sir John Macdonald produced at a meeting the other night a printed document which, he said, had been seized by the police in a Toronto printing office, and which contained advice to the United States Government as to the best means of forcing the annexa- tion of the Dominion. Sir John Macdonald holds the original document, which he declares is in the handwrit- ing of Mr. Farrar, editor of the "Toronto Globe." Mr. Farrar on Wednesday published a vindicatory letter, in which he says he prepared the pamphlet for the private information of American friends in Washington, without any concealment or prejudice. Mr. Farrar adds that the Liberal party is not bound by anything he has written, and if it is treason, let those who accuse him put him on his trial.

THE CHARGE OF IN IFE POISONING. The trial of John Webster, on the charge of poisoning his wife at Kirriemuir, was continued at Edinburgh on Thursday. Mrs. Webster, mother of the prisoner, spoke of his habits, and attributed his illness to his wife. Dr. Steel Moon said the prisoner consulted him regarding his illness, and witness treated him accordingly and he re- covered, Dr. Bruce deposed that for a person of Mrs. Webster's condition arsenic was a natural remedy. Dr. Howden, Sunnyside Asylum, Mo ntrose, spoke to the admission of deceased's mother to that asylum in 1873, suffering from melancholia and suicidal mania. This closed the evidence. The Solicitor-General addressed the jury, claiming a verict of guilty. After consulting for eight minutes, the jury returned a verdict of "not guilty." The result was received with loud cheering.
CONFERENCE AT MANCHESTER ON LICENSING REFORM.

A conference on the subject of the reform of the Present system of licensing for the sale of intoxi- cating liquors was held in Manchester on Thursday. The Bishop of Manchester presided, and explaiued that the object of the Conference was to unite not only temperance reformers but men of less pro- nounced views who yet desiredt7o bring about a large diminution in the number of public-houses. He said he had not been able to find any case for granting compensation to a license holder whose license was not renewed, but he was strongly in favour of the expiration of licenses after a specified period of time. A resolution was pro- posed by the Bishop of Salford, and seconded by Archdeacon Wilson, recommending that a certain minimum should be enforced in the number of public-houses in proportion to population, and ad- vocating the adoption of an absolute veto by a three- fourths majority. The Rev. James Clark moved an amendment in favour of reducing the majority to two-thirds, and after discussion the resolution with this amendment was carried by a majority. The Bishop of Manchester thereupon declared that as he was utterly opposed to the idea of compulsion by a two-thirds majority he could take no further part in the Conference. His Lordship left the chair, but was persuaded to return, and the Conference then adjourned for a week.

div.head: MILLIONAIRES' WILLS.
div.p: MILLIONAIRES' WILLS.

The late Nathaniel Clayton's £1,364,496 is the eighth millionaire's estate declared in England during two years. They include a banker, a colliery owner, a woollen manu- facturer, a cotton spinner, an alkali king, a shipbuilder, a baronet, and a manufacturing engineer. The aggre- gate value of their estates was £11,771,834, which is less than a quarter of two at least reported American for- tunes.
WARRINGTON INFIRMARY' AND DISPENSARY. MEETING OF WORKS REPRESENTATIVES.

On Saturday afternocn the annual meeting of representatives of various works in the town on the Workingmen's Infirmary C.ommittee, was held in the Town Hall, Warrington. The Mayor (Alder- man Francomb) presided, and amongst others pre- sent were Major Pickmere and Councillor F. W. Monks.

TER CONTRIBUTIONS. The statement of accounts, showing the sums contri- buted during the yearlBB9-90 by the employes at various works in the town was adopted. It showed that the total of these contributions for last year amounted to £368 10s. 9d., as compared with £403 9s. Rd. for the previous year. In addition there were other items of income including £3B 45. 10d. from the annual concert last year as comparedwith £403 9s. 51d. for the previous year. The total income of the Workingmen's Committee last year was £386 9s. 4P., as compared with £475 lls. 11±cl. inthe preceding year.—The MAYOR said that, from a statement laid before him by Mr. John Roberts, Chairman of the Workingmen's Committee, it appeared that during the eleven years the committee had been in existence it had 'collected no less a sum than £4,283 es. 10d. The first year the concert was held it realised £29 6s. Bd. He thought they would agree with him that the committee had done good work, and must have put a great amount of labour into it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Jonw ROBERTS, referring to the falling off in the contri- butions, &c., last year as compared with 1889, said that there were several special contributions in 1889. He thought there was practically no falling off in theregis- ter of subscriptions.—The MAYOR pointed out that the Whitecross Company, which contributed £3B 4s. 9d. in 1889 had not yet sent in its contribution for 1890. When that came in, as he had no doubt it would, the regular subscriptions for 1890 would be £3 larger than for the previous year.—A delegate from Whitecross here inti- mated there would be a subscription of £3O 14s. 6d.from Whitecross. It was owing to an oversight that it had _ _ _ _ _ . .

not been sent in before.—the MAYOR saki that in that case there would be a subscription for 1890 of £399 ss. 3d., as compared with £403 9s. std. in 1889.—Coun- ciller F. W. Morms also mentioned that the expenses for 1890 contained some of the outlay in respect to the Hos- pital Sunday collection,which they did not in 1889.—The discussion on this subject then dropped. THE COMMITTEES. _ _

After some discussion it was agreed that the working- men's Infirmary Committee for the coming year should Consist of all those delegates who had been returned as representatives of their works.—Some diseussion took Place as to the advisability of reducing the number of the executive committee from 18 to nine, but on a vote being taken it was decided to retain the lamer number. 'The executive committee was then re-apvoiaed with the alteration that the Messrs. Beaman, Taylor, Duncan and Thompson were added in place of four members Whose names were withdrawn. THE APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN.-OPPOSITION TO MR. JOHN ROBERTS.

The MAYOR having intiminated that the next business Was the appointment of chairman of the committee, Mr. JOHN BURTON moved that Major Pickmere be elected to that office.—This was seconded.—The re-election of Mr. JOHN ROBERTS, the retiring chairman, was also moved _ _

and seconded.--:-Major PICEiiERE declined to be put in nomination as he said he could not attend any of their meetings which were held at nights.—Mr. JOHN ROBERTS said he had no desire to stand as chairman unless it was the unanimous feeling of the committee. He had acted as Chairman of the committee since its formation in 1880, and he thought the results had shown that its work had been well done.—A DELEGATE said there had been some dissatisfaction expressed with Mr. Roberts's chairman- ship since a late municipal election in which the matter was brought forward.—Another DELEGATE here objected to the introduction of anything of a political character into the discussion.—The MAYOR said if there was some feeling on that matter there was no reason why it should not be brought forward, unless Mr. Roberts was afraid. —Mr. ROBERTS said he was not afraid of anything : he had done nothing to bring a stain upon his character. He had got something in his pocket that affected some members of the old committee and that would probably come out. If it came out it would make some people - rather ashamed of themselves in the town of Warrington. He did not want to say a wprd on that matter, but what be had said had been dragged from him.—Mr. SIIITHERS said he knew that there had been some friction on the COrnmittoo in consequence of the incidents that had been referred to, and that was the reason why: some people had come forward to give another concert in aid of the In- firmary. He would propose that Mr. Thomas Morris be chairman of the committee.,—Mr. ParrEn said all the facts referred to had been brought by Mr. Roberts before the executive committee, and the members of that com- mittee had expressed themselves as perfectly satisfied.— Mr. HARTLEY said all the dissatisfaction had emanated from Dallam Forge. The committee itself was perfectly free from prejudice, but two delegates had refused to act. The committee was entirely in touch with its chairman.—Mr. BURTON said there was a grievance against Mr. Roberts, and for their last concert there was not a ticket sold in Dallam or Bewsey forges. Iron- workers were generally Liberals, but if they could ap- point a chairman both sides could look up to, it would

be for the interest of the cause, and that was why he proposed Major Pickmere. He suggested that the matter Should be left in the hands of Alderman Davies and Mr. Thomas Morris.—A DELEGATE remarked that that was getting to be a political meeting and nothing else,and Mr. HARTLEY contended that theywere quite able to appoint their own chairman.—Mr. W. UNswonnt thought the tone adopted by Mr. Roberts himself had been the cause of introducing that feeling into the discussion.—Mr. ROBERTS said he had been undeservedly ridiculed more than the vagabond that walks Warrington streets by certain individuals. . He had borne a good deal, and he thought that the old saying was true, that it was the last straw that broke the camel's back.—The MAYOR then took a vote as to whether Mr. Roberts or Mr. Morris Should be appointed chairman of the committee when 20 voted for Mr. Roberts and eight for Mr. Morris, Mr. Roberts being therefore, declared elected. VOTE OF THANES, &C.

It was decided that contributions from the works Should be handed in half-yearly, at tha end of May and November. Votes of thanks were then passed to the resident and honorary medical staff of the infirmary, and also to the Mayor. The meeting then concluded.

div.head: IltON WORKE RS' CONCERT.
div.p: IltON WORKE RS' CONCERT.

On Saturday evening, a concert, promoted by the ironworkers and engineers of the town, was held in the Public Hall, in aid of the funds of the War- rington Infirmary. There was a very large attend- ance, the hall being completely filled in all parts. Mr. T. Morris presided. The CHAIRMAN in opening the meeting, read a letter he had received from Mr. W. H. Bleckley, dated from the Magistrates' Club, London, in which that gentleman said that he "considered it an honour and a compliment to be asked by the Committee of the Ironworkers and Engineers to preside at their concert, but being so thoroughly the workingmen's undertaking he thought they ought to have the entire credit of it themselves, and he, therefore, decided not to interfere. He was exceed- ingly pleased to see the ironworkers and engineers con- tinuing to take such interest in Warrington's noblest in- stitution, the Hospital and Infirmary, and rendering Such valuable assistance. Although it was pecuni- arily, he believed, in a satisfactory condition, the only 'way to keep it so was not to allow its yearly income to diminish. In all manufacturing establishments it Was impossible to avoid occasional accidents, in spite of the most anxious care and forethought. When he first c_ommenced his business life in Warrington, more than 29 years ago, Dallam forge was a small place, but he could recollect some very serious accidents, and it was heartrending to have to send off the poor sufferers who Were injured to Manchester, because there was no in- stitution in Warrington where they could obtain suitable surgical aid, and be properly nursed and cared for. All that was happi.y past and gone, and he trusted that the *Usefulness of their grand hospital might never be cur- tailed fox want of funds. (Applause.) In conclusion, Bleckley expressed the hope that the concert would he a success, and• added that he should be glad if the Committee would allow him to pay their bill for thc use i)f the Public Hall for that concert." (Loud applause.) , Mr. MORRIS then expressed his pleasure at seeing so large a gathering. The friends of the institution had i °sea wondering during the last few days why that , Second concert on behalf of the funds of the Infirmary Was taking place so soon after the one just given. The explanation was this. For some eighteen months or ??,:o years the old working-men's Infirmary Committee tlid not work together so harmoniously as formerly. and Previous to the last concert one part of the Committee lieeeded from the other." The secession party finding 91at the institution might suffer by the withdrawal of their support, determined upon getting a second concert ..1113. Everyone in that room would agree with him that, "lo far as the audience was concerned, the new corn- Mittee had done remarkably well. (Applause.) The programme of music was then rendered in a very :Iluccessful manner. The artistes were Mr. Roberts, Miss Fa manner. Miss Mather, Mr. Mather, Miss Keppie, Mr. Pa' Conway, and Mr. Collins. An excellent orchestral _uarnd, under the leadership of Mr. Peter Caldwell, was Easesent, and gave several selections. Mr. Geo. Riley w ,as usual, a very satisfactory accompanist.

TIIE VICAR OF RUNCORN AND HIS FLOCK. Sir,—As you have given my fellow tiscangniAll a fair description of Canon Wood's bigotry, through preaching and publishing his famous sermon, will you kindly allow me to inform your readers of the feelings of dissatis- faction expressed by eight members of his flock. It is a consolation to find so many not of the Vicar's mind ; no less than eleven from St. Alichae.'s went to the Primitive Methodists Chapel on the Bth inst. Archbishop Whately saia " Those who say the Lord's Supper may not be ad. ministered lay persons not duly ordained are proceeding without any authority whatever." Bishop Ryle writes "Thousands of ordained men in the present day know nothing whatever about Christ except his name." Yours truly, ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, Feb. 16, 1891.

div.head: MR. C. M. PERCY AND THE EIGHT HOURS
div.p: MR. C. M. PERCY AND THE EIGHT HOURS
MOVEMENT.

Sir,—For the courteous reference to myself in your leading columns of February 14th, I thank you. I gather that only my first article on miners and the Eight Hours Movement has come under your notice, and I now send copies of others which followed, and which perhaps make my opinions more clear. _

I need not here set out at length my reasons for strenuously opposing a compulsory Eight Hours bank to bank day in mining operations. As a life-long Liberal I oppose such a proposal as an unwarrantable interference with the liberty of the workman and the employer. I oppose it as a miners' friend, and as a citizen, because it will neither improve the health, or lessen the danger of the miner. I oppose it because it will reduce the pro- duction of coal, and increase the cost,and reduce wages. I oppose it because in all our principal manufactories, iron and steel especially, in which we have severe and increasing competition with other nations, it will increase the cost of those manufactures, and ruin them. You in Warrington know something of the iron trade. Is it flourishing now ? Would you like to see its burdens increased ? Coal is already so dear that iron is not being made at a profit; and iron and steel works are closing. America, our great competitor, is now making 10,000,000 tons of pig iron yearly against something over 8,000,000 tons in England ; and Aerica is putting good coal into railway wagons and selling it at 3s. a ton. The price of coal in England you know as well as I do. Ere many years have passed away we shall have American iron and steel and American coal in England.

You mention that mine rent and way-leave charges amount to several million!, more per year than wages. If you average 180,000,000 tons at Bd. per ton you have 6,000,000, and if you average 600,000 workers at 30s. a week you have £45,000,000.

div.head: Yours truly, C. M. PERCY.
div.p: Yours truly, C. M. PERCY.

Wigan 18 Feb., 1891. P.S.—You will see from the official report of conference procQedings that colliery proprietors are willing to have a joint inquiry as to-1. Present hours of labour. 2. Healthiness of mining. 3. Period of mixing. Day when accidents are most numerous. The miners should accept the offer and have a private inquiry.

C. M. P. [We are obliged to Mr. Percy for his suggestive letter, and for the additional articles he has forwarded for our information. As the subject is of great moment, some of our readers will perhaps say what they think of the important issue which our correspondent raises.—Ed. Ex.]

div.head: SALARIES OF RUNCORN OFFICIALS.
div.p: SALARIES OF RUNCORN OFFICIALS.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me a word in reference to the recent discussion hereon by the Board of Com- missioners. The figures I quoted were takenffrom their own financial statesments, and can be verified by anyone referring to the published accounts.

Under the head of salaries appears the amount for year ending 25th March, 1885, £456 18s. sd. and for 1890 £763 16s. Bd., and whether or not the difference has been spread over new positions or by additions to the already existing ones does not affect my argument. The fact still remains that £306 18s. 3d. was paid in the year ending 25th March, 1890, over and above the sum paid in 1885, and the figures are still growing. The duties now performed by the secretary, with remuneration after the rate of £2OO a year, a collector at £7O and a boy at 6s. per week, were discharged by the former secretary for £l6O. In other words there is an increase of £125 in this department alone. Upon the Board's own showing, the rateable value has increased only £4,485 in the period under review, the amount for the year ending March, 1885, being £50,989, and for 1890, £55.474. The assessable value on which the rates were levied for the latter year was £46,042. That there has been more work I have never disputed, but what Ido contend is, that whereas the rateable value has increased only 9 per cent., the total salaries have risen 67 per cent., and in the words of my previous letter, their expansion is out of all proportion to the growth of the town.

I have never represented that the Law Clerk's salary had been increased from £5O to £lOO. I could not do •so, as it stood at £llO, having been raised from £9O in the late Clerk's time. What I did say was that the Com- missioners proposed to augment his stipend by £25 per annum in place of a gratuity of £5O, which gift the Local Government Board declined to sanction.

I shall not be deterred by such aword as "busybodies" applied by some of the Board—l could not resist a smile when I read the term—neither shall I emulate the ex- ample of those who used it,but I shall continue to exer- du my just rights As 3 xatepaying member of the corn-
BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO., LIMITED.

The twentieth half-yearly meeting of this company, whose works are at Winnington, Northwich, took place, on Thursday, in the Law Association-rooms, Cook-st. Mr. John Crosfield, the chairman of directors, presiding. There was a numerous attendance of shareholders. The report mentioned a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the half-year's working of £154,517 Bs. 3d. This, with £19,837 95. 3d. brought forward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £174,354 17s. 6d. The directors proposed to deal with that amount as follows :—Dividend on the preference capital at 7 per cent, per annum, £14,986 17s. 2d. ; dividend on the ordinary capital at 40 per cent. per an- num, £117,500; amount to be written off patent, accounts, £2,500; amount to be placed to reserve funds £28,829; balance to be carried forward, £10,539 Os. 4d. The £28,829 to be placed to reserve would bring that fund up to £200,000. The profit and loss account showed directors' and office salaries and auditing to have been £7,959 6s. 5d.; general charges and income- tax, £6,009 17s. 2d. and bad and doubtful debts £6B 17s. 11d. The gross profits amounted to £165,198 3s. 3d., and rents-L3,341 16s. 6d. The Chairman said he had much pleasure in present- ing the shareholders with another satisfactory half-yearly balance-sheet. He moved that the directors' report and statement of accounts be adopted, and that the proposed dividend of 7 per cent, per annum be paid to holders of preference shares, and 40 per cent. be paid to holders of ordinary shares for the half-year ended 31st December, Mr. H. Coghill seconded. The motion was carried with acclamation.

Mr. George Jones proposed that the directors other than the managing director be paid £5OO for their ser- vices during the past half-year. It needed no words of his to tell the shareholders that the directors must have worked hard, as was evidenced by the grand dividend they were about to receive. Mr. W. Ross seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The retiring directors, Dr. Hewitt and Me ssrs. Jarmay and Coghill, were duly re-elected. Mess's. T. W. Reid and Co., chartered accountants, were reappointed auditors.

A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman, who informed the shareholders that the directors were petitioning Parliament in order that they might appear by counsel before the select Committee on the .bill for Compensation for Subsidence.

LECTTME AT HIJYTON.-A lecture was given in the Park Hall, on Friday evening by the Rev. Silas Hocking, author of" Ivy," "Her Benny," &c., who took for his title" That Boy." Mr. Joseph Beecham occupied the chair, and there was a full and appreciative audience. The proceeds were devoted to the -Tonic Sol-fa Class funds.

div.head: CANON WOOD'S WARNING AGAINST
div.p: CANON WOOD'S WARNING AGAINST
DISSENTERS.

Sir.—Read in the light of the recent sermon of the Vicar of Runcorn, directed against Nonconformists, the following extracts from a publication entitled " Some questions of the Church Catechism. and doctrines in- volved, briefly explained, for the use of families and parochial schools," will be of interest. The author is the Rev. Frederick Aubert Gace, M.A., Vicar of Great Bar-

ling, Essex. "85. We have amongst us various sects and denom- inations who go by the general name of Dissenters. In what light are we to consider them? A.—As heretics ; and in our Litany we expressly pray to be delivered from the sins of false doctrine, heresy, and schism. "86. Is then their worship a laudable service? A.— No, because they worship God according to their own evil and corrupt imaginations and not according to His revealed will, and therefore their worship is idolatrous. " 87. Is Dissent a great sin? A.—Yes ;itis in direct opposition to our duty towards God. "94. But why have not Dissenters been excommuni- cated? A.—Because the law of the land does not allow the wholesome law of the Church to be acted upon; but Dissenters have virtually excommunicated themselves by setting up a religion of their own, and leaving the ark of God's Church. "95. What class of Dissenters should we be most upon our guard against? A.—Those whom imitate the most nearly the true Church of Christ. "97. But are there not some Dissenters who use the same form of prayer as ourselves? A .—Doabtless ; but the prayers of the Church, being, for the most part, for the priest to offer up on behalf of the people, it must be sinful and presumptuous for those persons who are called dissentine, teachers, to address the throne of grace, usurping lhe priestly office. "98. Is it wicked then to enter a meeting-house at all? A.—Most assuredly, because, as we have said above, it is a house where God is worshipped otherwise than He has commanded, and therefore it is not dedi- cated to His honour and glory ; and 'besides this, we run the risk of being led away by wicked enticing words; at the same time, by our presence we are witnessing our approval of the heresy, wounding the consciences of our weaker brethren, and by our example teaching others to go astray. "100. How do you know that the Church of England is a branch of the Church Catholic? A.—Because she is governed by the three orders of clergy, Bishops, Priests, and Deacons, who can trace back their line in an un • broken chain,to the days of the Apostles, and she is there- fore in possession of what is called the Apostolic Succession without which the Church cannot have exist- ence." Anyone who is possessed of a copy of the Vicar's sermon will be " instructed " by reading it side by side with the above extracts. Whether the explanations of this precious "Minister of God" are used in Runcorn National Schools I are not in a position to know ; but the Vicar has evidently imbibed some of their profane bigotry.— Yours,
NONCONFORMIST.

INFIRMARY WORKINGMEN'S COMMITTEE. Sir,—l was much surprised when reading the report of the annual meeting of the above Committee, to find that my name was given as the representative of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company. There is evidently some misunderstanding about this, as I was not aware that my name had been forwarded until I saw it in your contemporary's issue of Wednesday last. But whether it be correct or not, I shall most certainly refuse to sit again under the chairmanship of Mr. John Roberts. If Mr. Roberts had read to the Committee the corres- hith had taken place between himself and Messrs. Griffiths and nun(..h, it would have put the mat- ter in anahez light, and it would have revealed the real cause of the rupture. According to the tone of the discussion on Saturday afternoon,Mr. Roberts would have the Committee believe, that the withdrawal of the Pearson and Knowles representatives was due to political considerations. I say it was due to nothing of the kind, but it was u, cu- ranted by the insult levelled at upwards of a thousand intelligent ironworkers and engineers. A few days be- fore the Municipal Election in which Mr. John Roberts was my opponent f a certain circular was issued in his interest which inferred that the managers of Dallam and Bewsey Forges, had been dealing unjustly with their puddlers' wages. Why this circular should have been issued I cannot for a moment imagine, unless Mr. Roberts (thinking. I was a manager) thought that he was dealing a most damaging blow at my chances of success,whereas he was believing the fair fame of others. Subsequently another circular appeared having Mr. Roberts' name at bottom,calling upon the workingmen not to be intimidated, coerced, or driven by managers. Now, I don't know what the public opinion is respecting the above, but I think it was a very mean action in- deed on Mr. Roberts' part to allots, the circulation of such libellous handbills, especially when they referred to men, who, till then, had looked upon him as a very great personal friend,and who had worked hand in hand with him for a long period in the interest of our noblest institution. If politics had been the point at issue or had been the reason why the representatives of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles would not sit under the chairmanship of Mr. John Roberts, we should not have been so suc- cessful as we are with the patrons of our concert, or in the choice of a treasurer to look after our accounts. No one .belonging to our party admits that the opposi- tion has been brought about from political motives. It is Mr. Roberts who is responsible for this assertion. If he would be frank enough to define the real cause properly, he would say that he had made use of lan- guage concerning honest men that was libellous, and also that the apology for so doing had to be dragged from him.—Yours, &c.,
S. J. BEAMAN,

_ B.S.—While the ironworkers are much obliged to Mr. Smithies for proposing Mr. Thomas Morris as Chairman of the Working-men's Committee, I may say that a few days before the meeting was held, Mr. Morris had been approached by a deputation from our men to ascertain whether he would allow himself to be nominated for that position. He at once declined on the grounds of the already numerOtlSllS upon his time. Had we intended to place Mr. Morris in the chair, we should have at- tended in such numbers, as would have left the issue of the election of Chairman beyond any doubt. S.J.B.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 21, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 21, 1891.
SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT THE SHIP CANAL WORKS.

News reached Liverpool yesterday morning that a navvy named Kelly, who resided in Scotland- road, Liverpool, and who was one of the Ship Canal gang which left the stage for Eastham by the Gipsy Queen at five o'clock, had sustained shocking in- juries soon after landing, With other men he was hurrying for the workmen's express, and on jump- ing on one of the trucks he slipped, and fell in such a way that the wheels passed over him, and separ- ated his legs from his body. He was conveyed to the Ship Canal Works Hospital in a dying state.
THE FORTHCOMING LIBERAL BAZAAR

All the meetings of ladies which have been held I to promote this bazaar have been largely attended, but the attendance at the meeting held yesterday afternoon was much the largest there has yet been. 1 At this meeting Mrs. Ziba Armitage was appointed president of the committee having in hand the arrangements for the bazaar; Miss Bessie Dutton, of The Willows, Moore, and Miss Beatrice Burgess, of Egypt-st., were elected secretaries to act in con- junction with Mr. C. J. Holmes; and Mrs. Julian Winser, of Grappenhall, accepted the office of trea- surer. The bazaar, it should be stated, will in all probability be held in October, and not in April as • i . mentioned n mistake in a contemporary.
MR. WILLIAM O'BRIEN.

Mr. William O'Brien who has again been con- signed to prison on the sentence of a " Coercion " Court, is like several other of the most active of the Irish party, a comparatively young man. He is a Mallow man and was born in 1852. After being educated at the Diocesan Col- lege, Cloyne, and the Queen's College, Cork, he devoted him- If to journalism. He was for me years on the staff of the ,nd later when he became the

land" he was mainly instru- mental in giving that journal its great circula- tion amongst Irish people. Mr. O'Brien is described as being physically a tall, thin, weakly-built man, with an intellectual look; and one who devotes an immense amount of nervous energy to the service of his country's cause. He was first sent to Parliament by his native place. Mallow, which he won in 1883, after a contest which excited keen interest, the Solicitor-General standing against him. He con- tinued to represent Mallow till 1885, and in that year he was re-elected to Parliament as member for the Southern division of County Tyrone. He was age:di returned in 1887 for the North-eastern divi- sion of Cork, and this constituency he still repre- sents. In Parliament he showed himself to be one of the ablest and mcst active of Mr. Parnell's lieu- tenants. He was committed to prison for six months in 1888 ur der the Crimes Act, and his imprisonment at that time excited much interest, from the stren- uous manner in which he resisted the imposition of indignities upon him by the prison authorities. During 1890 he published a novel entitled "When we were Boys," which, dealing with Irish life, attracted much attention. His marriage with Miss Raffalovitch took place last year. Being sum- moned to appear at Tipperary on the political charge in September, he escaped with Mr. Dillon to Cherbourg, and sailed tor the United States, where he addressed many : tings. What promised to be a very successful An- --,tl mission, was interrupted by the dissensions in the ':rish party at home, and Mr. O'Brien at once returned to France, where he carried on what are known as the "Boulogne nego- tiations" in tile hope of restrxing the union of the the Irish party. Tl.ese well-meant efforts not hav- ing proved successful, he at once gave himself up to ithe English authorities to serve out a sentence of six months' imprisonment which had been passed upon him at Tipperary since his departure for America.
MR. JOHN DILLON.

Mr. Dillon who is Mr. O'Brien's co-prisoner, is a son of John Blake Dillon, one of the rebels of '4B. He is a tall, delicate man, with consumptive tendencies 'which compelled him to .esign his seat in the 1880 'arliament, when he departed o recruit his health on the :arm of his brother in Colo- rado) ; jet black hair, and large contemplative eyes. He is a graduate of the Catholic University, Dublin, where he his proficiency in mathema-

; ybe added that he is a fair classic ! And a very fair linguist. Ile was first returned to Parliament for Tipperary in 1880, . but, as stated above, owing to ill-health resigned the seat; but was elected for East Ma 3 o in 1885 and again in 1886. Mr. Dillon has recently been identified with the "Plan of Campaign" and in November. 1886, while carrying that plan into operation at Loughrea, by receiving the rents of the tenants, was arrested by the police. He was subsequently tried for the offence, and bound over in heavy securities to keep the peace. Mr. Dillon was twice imprisoned under Mr. Forster's Coercion Act as a "suspect," and has been repeatedly suspended by the House of Com- mons. He is one of the most powerful speakers in that Assembly, and, according to one writer, is, or rather was, when the Irish members and the rest of the Commons were at variance, in the habit of , "saying violent things in a melancholy monotone" , At the Mell Petty Sessio-s, Drogheda, on May 11th, 1888, for "having, on April Bth, at Tullyallen, County Louth, taken part in the criminal conspi- racy known as the Plan of Campaign," Mr. Dillon was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The sentence was confirmed on appeal on June 21st. Mr. Dillon was sent to Tullamere gaol, but was liberated in September, 1888. He returned in 1890 from a tour of. the Australian colonies, where he met with an enthusiastic reception and collected large contributions to the funds of the Irish Nationalist party. Towards the end of last year Mr. Dillon, along with Mr. O'Brien, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment at Tipperary, and, having given himself up upon his return from America, is together with his distinguished coadjutor now serv- ing out that sentence in an Irish gaol.

div.head: NEW LANCASHIRE COUNTY MAGISTRATES.
div.p: NEW LANCASHIRE COUNTY MAGISTRATES.

The gentlemen named below have been placed on the I commission of the peace for the county of Lancaster: —The Hon. Robert Gerard,Bispham Hall Billinge ; Major John Richard Pickmere, Cedar Lawn, Thelwall, War- rington; Mr. William Edward Murray Tomlinson, M.P., Lancaster ; Mr. Edward Storey, Crosslands, Lancaster; Mr. Cornelius Edward Beazer, Borsden House, Hindley ; Mr. John James Bleckley, Daresbury Lodge,Altrincham ; Mr. John Saunderson, Bank House, Laneaster ; Mr. Nathaniel Farrington Eckersley, Standish Hall, Wigan; and Mr. John White, Barrowfield,Latchford,Warrington. Of these new magistrates Major Pickmere and Mr. John White are well-known in Warrington. Both of them have been magistrates of the borough for many years. It is scarcely necessary to add that Major Pick- mere was for many years connected with the Corporation of Warrington as Councillor, Alderman and Mayor, besides,taking part in all local movements of a social and philanthropic character. Both Major Pickmere and Mr. White are Conservatives.
WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.

FRlDAY.—Before the Registrar Mr. E. J. Nicholson. A BANKRUPT FARMER.—John Campkin, formerly a farmer, residing at Dutton Hall, came up for his ad- journed examination, and after being further examined by the assistant Official Receiver, Mr. Potter and Mr. Forshaw (who appeared on behalf of the bankrupt) the examination was again adjourned. The gross liabilities are £4,304 7s. 6d. Of this £551 is due to preferential creditors, leaving £3,752 17s. 4d. to rank against the estate. The assets are £1,474 6s. 2d., leaving a defi- ciency of £2,278 us. 2d. A FURNITURE DEALER DOES NOT APPEAL—A debtor named Blumenay, who formerly carried on business in Warrington as a furniture dealer under the title of the London Furnishing Company, should have appeared to undergo his preliminary examination, but on his name being called he did not answer, and the examination was therefore adjourned. The debtor's liabilities have not yet been ascertained, as he has not furnished the Official Receiver with a statement of his affairs. RE CHARLES PAUL.—Charles Paul, now of Wolver- hampton, but formerly trading as a dealer in jewellery, under the style of Armstrong and Company, was fur- ther examinad as to his business and the accounts he had rendered. The case was adjourned.
WARRINGTON YOUNG IRELAND SOCIETY. ANNUAL DINNER.

The arniml dinner of the Warrington Young Ire- land Society was held at the Patten Arms on Satur- day evening, when the host Mr. T. B. Kiernan, provided a most substantial and excellent spread, for nearly 40 guests. Mr. P. Lane, president of the society, occupied the chair, and Mr. P. Mannion- its vice-president, the vice-chair, the Chairman being supported by Mr. D. Donnelly, of the Liver- pool Young Ireland Society, and formerly its vice- presideiku. mi. Niunine, aperktnry nf the local society, and Mr. Bolan, its treasurer. The CuAllows proposed the fitst toast, that of " Ire- land a Nation," coupling with the toast the name of Mr. Donnelly.
- "God save Ireland" having been sung by Mr. Mullins

Mr. DONNELLY then rose to respond CO. the toast. In his remarks he said those present could easily throw back their recollection and fancy what must have been the feelings of those who drank or responded to such a toast in the dark and evil days of 50 years ago. He did not suppose that for many years the hope of ever writing Ireland's name among the nations adopted any other form than perhaps the physical force form, which was perhaps so familiar to some of them 20 or 30 years ago. But fortunately that night they had no difficulty at all in addressing themselves to this toast, and while not at all disregarding the sentiments or aspirations of those who had gone before them, plainly and honestly and freely proclaiming their faith in the toast. The capa- bility of the Irish race to make that toast good in their own good time, lay not in the hopes of their predeces- sors but in the more peaceable and constitutional methods which had been developed of late. (Applause.) No matter how their leaders and those who were lights among them might wrangle or differ amongst themselves, the central idea remained the same, the idea of Ireland a nation. The speaker hoped at some future date to come with his congratulations of the Warrington society on what it had done,on its having succeeded in changine the representation of the town—(applause) —on having altered the condition of the register, on having succeeded in placing in the rown Council some who were not afraid to avow themselves identified with the cause of Home Rule. (9.nplause.) At the same time, he did not attach very much importance to the identification of national societies with municipal politics. Their experience in Liverpool had been that nothing conduced so much as this to dissension and to the breaking up of these societies. It very often happened that local men who had fairly divided claims upon an Irish society were candidates for the same vacancy, and it was only natural that some Irishmen should recognise the claims of one, and some of the other, and consequently split in their favour. Let the society keep out of municipal politics as much as it could where there was any pos- sibility of a misunderstanding, but where there was a chance of united action by all means throw themselves into the contest ; and a society such as theirs was no small factor in a municipal election. (Applause.) After a song by Mr. Thomas Aaron, Mr. KIERNAN, at some length, and in an animated speech, proposed the toast of "Success to the Warrington Young Ireland Society." He mentioned that he had been one of those who commenced the Home Rule agitation, and referred to his presidency over the first meeting of the Home Rule Assseciation in Dublin, and his acquaintance with all the Irish leaders.
Mr. MULLINS responded to the toast. The health of the host and hostess and the chairman were subsequently drunk, and the toasts were duly re- sponded to.
STAG -HUNT.

Yesterday week, Lord Gerrard's hounds passed through Croft, hunting a stag, which even- tually made its way towards Houghton Green, where it was captured at whrt is termed the " Mill- houses " by two young men of that place, and put in a stable. It was afterwards returned to its owner. It is reported that the animal on being captured became exceedingly furious, and cut the young men's hands in a severe manner. ENTERTAINMENT AT THE _BOARD SCHOOL, CROFT.

Mr. A. H. L. Evans, of Haydock, gave magic lantern exhibition in the Board School, Croft, on Saturday evening, illustrative of the "Passion Play" at Oberammergau. The Rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, M.A., presided, and there was a good audience, who highly appreciated the interesting views thrown upon the screen. The pictures were taken from photographs secured on the spot, and were illustrative of the various scenes in the "Passion Play" scenery in and around Oberam- mergau; and the everyday life of the peasants.

div.head: STRIKE OF BREWERY COOPERS.
div.p: STRIKE OF BREWERY COOPERS.

On Thursday morning a deputation, consisting of delegates from the Coopers' Association, waited on the manager of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co.'s, Wilderspool Brewery, Warrington, and presented a letter requesting an increase of wages. This, how- ever, was not entertained. There were only two unionist coopers employed in the brewery, and the delegates forthwith called upon them to leave work on the ground that, the firm did not pay the standard rate of wages. They succeeded in getting another woikman to desist. One of the three is the secretary of the local branch of the Coopers' Association, and the matter will be brought before the association for consideration. The officials at the brewery admit that they do not pay the union rate of wages, but say they grant many privileges to their work- men which more than compensate for this. The men state that they were only receiving 265. per week, whereas 365. is the standard wages of the Mutual Association of Coopers.

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
