FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

How is it that Cheshire manages, to show up so well against Yorkshire? To draw with the big county at Huddersfield was indeed a capital performance, and had they won outright Cheshire would only have had their deserts. They were extremely unlucky not to gain a deciding point, and they deserred it on the afternoon's play. Two dropped goals to a goal and three tries is a somewhat curious record, and we can well understand the intense anxiety of the Yorkshiremen when they saw Cheshire put on their two points early in the game. The home side was not fully representative, and one or two of the new men did not disclose any special abilities. Barnes, of Halifax, was not a model full back, and Wal- ton, of Armley, was hardly a sort of three-quarter to please the Yorkshire critics. Houghton, Crompton, Haslatn, and H. Hughes all did sterling work among the Cheshire back division, whilst the forwards fully held their own.

"Not much satisfaction" says the "Manchester Guardian," "has been extracted by Swinton out of their fixtures with Warrington. They were beaten in the first, and it took them all their time to turn the tables in the second on Saturday. A try by Valentine was the only point that could he secured, se that one can form a pretty accurate idea as to the character of the play. It was full of exciting episodes, and the verdict was in doubt almost until the very last. The Swinton backs worked very hard once they got the lead, but it took them all their time to keep the strangers out."

The following is the list of some other matches which took place, ao. Saturday aftertwon. 3.l...ehester Rangers had a shade the worst of their encounter with nocrulak, Hornets, who had also disposed of the Free Wanderers previously, two matches in one afternoon being a cur% °sky. Oldham proved themselves superior to Tyldesley, and Crompton pulled off their event with Ulverston by means of a dropped goal. Wigan journeyed to Leeds, where they were successful oy three tries to nothing. Widnes, who conquered Wigan a week ago, were too clever for Stockport. All the scoring was done before the changing of ends. Tom Kent assisted Ratcliffe to vanquish St. Helens, securing the first try which led on to victory. St. Helens Recreation did vastly better than their townsmen. beating Nl)ssley with plenty in hand.

The teams of Lancashire and Surrey, both of which had so far beaten all their competitors in their respective divisions, met at Whalley Range on Monday. The game was one-sided for Lancashire, keeping up the magnifi- cent form they have displayed this season, won by four- teen points to none—in other words by three goals, five tries, and nine minor noints to one minor point. The Lancastrians were superior to the Southerns at all points, but especially behind the scrimmages. The Lancashire team was composed as follows :—T. Coop (Leigh), full back ; J. Valentine (Swinton, captain). D. A. Gwynn (Oldham), and W. M'Cutcheon (Oldham), three quarter backs; J. Berry (Tyldesley) and W. Cross (St. Helens), half backs; W. Atkinson (Wigan), T.Brayshav (Wigan), T. Craven (Salford), J. Pyke (St. Helens Recreation), T. Bothwell (Swinton), T. Kent (Salford), R. P. Wilson (Liverpool Old Boys), T. Whittaker (Manchester), and C. V. Rome (Broughton), forwards. Referee, Mr. T. C. Browning, Sale. Touch judges, Mr. A. N. Hornby, pre- sident of the Lancashire County Club; and Mr.Burnand, Surrey.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

The draw for the seini-firs;;1;;;;:i in connection with this year's competition for the Association Cup was made on Wednesday evening at a Council meeting of the Foot- ball Association. It will be noticed that the two favour- ites—Sunderland and Blackburn Rovers—have managed to steer clear of each other. Sunderland v. Notts, at Shcffield. Referee, Mr. J. C. Clegg. Umpires, Mr. W. H. Jope and Mr. R. E. Lythgoe. Blackburn Rovers v. West Bromwich Albion, at Stoke. Referee, Mr. C. J. Hughes. Umpires, Mr. S. W. Widdowson and Mr. R. J. Smith. To be played February 28; kick off at 3.30. It was decided to play England v. Scotland at Blackburn, April 4 ; England v. Wales at Sunderland, March 7 ; and England v. Ireland at Wolverhampton, March 7. The final for the Association Cup will be played at the Oval, on March 21.

The Blackburn Rovers failed to carry their appeal against the decision of the League. They would dearly like to replay their game with Everton, as they fully believe in their ability to reverse the result, and thus improve their chance in the championship. But the League would not stultify themselves, and the match stands as victory for the Liverpool club. The meeting of the League was taken advantag,o of to present the cup to the present champions. It is of handsome design and has ccst 50 guineas. The North End intend to make a great effort to carry off the honours for the third year in success:on.

Four of the most powerful clubs in England are left in for the senn-finals of the Football Association Cup. The weakest of the lot are West Bromwich Albion,ex-holders of the trophy. They managed to knock out Sheffield Wednesday, but never displayed the cleverness which won thern the cup three years ago. They will be lucky to run into the final. Notts had a very hard fight with Stoke, and at the finish were only a goal to the good. Stoke have shown up prominently in the competition, but they were fortunate to be drawn at home in the first and soccnd rounds. The ?moment they venture away they fail to score and are wiped out. Notts played far better botball in the second half, Daft making many brilliant runs on the left wing. Thraves, who has taken the place of Toone in goal, gave much satisfaction in this responsible position.

The Rovers made no mistake in their tie with their old and tried rivals from Wolverhamptln. There was no denying the superiority of the cup holders, whose scientific movements were vastlyin advance of the in- dividual spurts of the "Wolves." The passing of the Blackburn forwards was a treat to look upon, and they took the ball half the length of the field repeatedly. Southworth set his men a splendid example which they were not slow to follow, and they gave Rose plenty Of occupation under the bar. Two goals counted against him, but he saved many others. The Rovers' defence was sounder than that of the Wanderers, the last named falling away very markedly towards the close.

After so many hard tussels with Sunderland Albion it waS generally anticipated that Notts Forest would suc- cumb to Sunderland, and se they did. The absence of Russell. their best half back, told a tale on the Forest, who collapsed in the last 20 minutes, and were decidedly beaten. Many persons are already looking to Sunder- land as the probate winners of the cup. If they meet the Rovers the game should be one of the keenest in the history of the competition.

div.head: LATI,4IST NEWS.
div.p: LATI,4IST NEWS.
STRIKE OF MINERS.
Yesterday fifteen hundred miners struck work at the Tyne Coal Company's pits, Hebburn-on-Tyne, in sym- pathy with the Silksworth men.
THE TOKAR EXPEDITION.
The " Times " second edition contains Cairo telegrams stating that a sandstorm has delayed the march on Tokar. Osman Digna is encamped two miles north of Afafit.
ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.

At a meeting of Conservative and Liberal Unionists held at Tavistoclx yesterday Lord Ebrington, member for the division, confirmed the announcement of his intention not to seek re-election owing to ill-health. Colonel W bite Thompson was unanimously adopted as the Unionist candidate at the general election in place of his lord- ship.

div.head: CARDIFF TRAMWAY STRIKE.
div.p: THE CARDIFF TRAMWAY STRIKE.

The strike of tramway employes continues at Cardiff. The service was partially resumed on Thursday morning by aid of the inspectors and outside labour. There is a good deal of excitement, and large accessions of police are on dusy.
Another section, from Canton to the docks, was opened yesterday morning, the police accompanying each car. The men held a mass meeting yesterday.
RESIGNATION OF SIR RICHARD MOON.

At the I,alf-yearly meeting of the London and North- Western Railway Company at Euston, yesterday after- noon, Sir Richard Moon, who has occupied the position of chairman for the past 30 years, resigned that position, on the grounds of ill-health. A resolution expressing the regret of the shareholders at the loss of Sir Richard's services was moved by Mr. W. H. Smith, M.P..seconded by Lord Colville of Culross, supported by the Right Hon. D. Plunket, M.P., and carried unanimously. Lord Stalbridge was afterwards elected chairman of the company.

div.head: WHITECHAPEL MURDER.
div.p: THE WHITECHAPEL MURDER.

• A Chatham correspondent says that IMrs. Sadler, the wife of the accused man, John Sadler, was visited on Thursday by an official from tht. Treasury. She, it is stated, admits that it is perfectly true that on more than one occasion Sadler had stood over her for more than a quarter of an hour with a knife in his hand.
THE INQUEST RESUMED.

The inquest on the body of Frances Coles, the victim of the last 'Whitechapel murder, was resumed yesterday before Mr. Wynne Baxter. Mr. Charles Matthews ap- pearel for the Treasury, and Mr. Lawless represented the man Sadler, who is at present detained in Holloway Gaol. The first witness was Mrs. Anne Shuttleworth, eating-house keeper, Welper-st., who said the woman, whom she knew as Frances, came to her house the day before the murder, and waited there until a man came. The man wore a peak cap, pilot coat, and looked like a sailor. Sarah Treadway, wife of the proprietor of the Marlborough Head public-house, deposed that Sadler was at her house with the deceased on Thursday night. Mr. Matthews said these witnesses were called to corro- borate a statement that the accused man had made, ad- mitting that he was at these places with the deceased woman, and to enable the jury to judge what amount of credence they could give to Sadler's statement. Mrs. Fleming, deputy of the lodging-house. White's-row, said the deceased aid accused slept there on Wednesday night. On Thursday night deceased left at midnight. Sadler came in at three o'clock. He had blood on his face and hands, and said he had been rob- bed. He asked where Frances was. Constable Bogan deposed to finding deceased drunk at the Dock gates at 1.15 a.m. on Friday. He saw her again at two in Mint street.
FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT.-EIGHT PERSONS KILLED.

NEW Youx, FIID.4,Y.—A fatal collision between passenger trains occurred at seven o'clock this morning in the Fourth Avenue Railway Tunnel, near Eighty-Fourth-street, in this city. It is re- ported that several of the carriages caught fire and that some of the passengers were killed and others injured. A Woman is stated to have been burned to death. NEW YORK, FRIDAY.—The latest reports on the acci- dent on the Central Railway show that eight persons were killed and a large number seriously injured.
YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The Lord CHiNCELLOR took his seat on the Woolsack at twenty minutes past four. THE FACTORY Biu..—Lord THRING moved the second reading of the Factory and Workshop Sanitation Bill. The Bill was intended to secure the inspection of places which were not reached by the present factory act, and to provide for ample means of sanitation.—Lord NORTON supported the Bill. Lord DE RAMSEY on the part of the Government offering no opposition, the bill was read a second time.
The House adjourned at ten minutes to six. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past three o'clock.

THE LONDON WATER SUPPLY.—Upon the London Water Commission Bill, Mr. BAUMANN crititised the pro- posed commission, and defended the present companies. The discussion was continued by Professor Stuart and Sir Algernon Borthwick. Sir Wm. Harcourt followed. Aftor further discussion the bill was read a second time.

NOUS& OF LORDS REFORM. —Mr. SMITH replying to Mr. Bryce said that state of public business 'would not permit of legislation to reform the House of Lords. Mr. LA.BOUCHERE gave notice that he should oppose such Bill. .(Laughter.) WELSH DISESTABLISHMENT.—Upon going into Com- mittee of Supply, Mr. PRITCHARD MORGAN moved a motion in favour of the disestablishment of the Church of England in Wales as an anomaly and in- justice, and as having failed in the promotion of the religious interests of the Welsh people. The Church of England he contended was out of har- mony with the National sentiment, and was in no sense the Church of the Welsh people by whom Non- conformity had been universally adopted. He quoted statistics to show the over - whelming preponder- ,ance of attendance of the Welsh people at Nonconformist churches and begged the House to do away with the Established Church in the Principality which was opposed to the feelings of the Welsh people Speaking of the services of Mr. Gladstone in the cause of reli.ious liberty, he expressed hope that his voice could be heard and also the voices of Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain in favoar of the resolution. Mr. ABRAHAM and ,other Welsh members expressed their approval by cries of `• Clwych," " Clwych." Mr. DILLWYN seconded the resolution. He believed that it expressed the unanimous feeling of the Welsh people on the subject. Mr. GLADSTONE who arose,amid cheering from the Welsh members said the resolution did not quite give expression to his views in one or two particulars. He bore testimony to the noble efforts of Nonconformists in Wales to make provision for their own ministers of religion. He could not deny that upon the whole the enormous majority of the Welsh were outside the pale of the Church. They had declared their opinion in a constitu- tional, lawful,peacefal, and regular manner, and the de- mand of a just people would insist upon being heard, and upon a just, equitable, and conclusive settlement. (Cheers.)

The custom of wearing black for the dead dates back to the times of the Romans, since when it has always been popular ansongst Western nations. The great mortality of Mir country, considering its sanitarY arrangements, has, given birth to a number of• shops exclUsively for the SALE OF MOURNING. These' shops, subsisting entirely on one department}, are compelled to charge- exorbitant prices, as nway a bereaved one is able to testify, having found to her cost, when the funeral was over,. that she had made a bad bargain. Whilst making these statements we wish to, draw the attention of Lutes to two facts: 1— That we'are manufacturers of Mantles, Costumes. aid Milliner'.; doing a larir WHOLESALE TRADE ill these departments, and That we supply our customerrs at the WHOLESALE PRICES. 2. - REPORTED CAPTURE OF TOKA.R. __- ROME, FEB. 18.rtr.—A telegram received here from Saukim states that news has been received there of the capture of Tokar by the Egyptian troops. The despatch also mentions a report that the expedition will now pro- ceed to Kassala, but adds, that this is doubtful, owing to the smallness of the force at Colonel Hailed Smith's dis- posal.
